en: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the glorious ocean of virtues!
Having bowed to the illustrious Śākyaketu, the God of Gods beyond gods, who is accompanied by the hosts of deities,
who crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, the treasury of all virtues, the Lord Buddha Gautama— the Lion’s Roar in saṃsāra, the remover of all fears, the parasol of Dharma, the Sovereign of Sages—
I shall proclaim the jewel of the Dharma, spoken by the best of sages, which is desired by all the world.
Then King Aśoka, eager for the twenty-two stories, spoke again to Upagupta, who was staying at the Kukkuṭārāma: (Dak O.2)
"Venerable One, I wish to hear the auspicious discourse on the service of caityas, so that this nectar of the Dharma may likewise emerge from the lotus of your mouth. (Dak O.3)
Having heard this request, Upagupta commanded:
"Listen, Aśoka; I shall proclaim the twenty-two avadānas."
I. Discourse Encouraging Merit:
The Blessed One, the Teacher, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Leader of the World, dwells in Rājagṛha, at the Gṛdhrakūṭa, that abode of bliss of great splendor. (Dak_1.1)
Together with a great community of twelve hundred monks,
and with eighty thousand great bodhisattvas.
Honored and placed at the forefront by gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, and humans, he stood like the full moon in the sky surrounded by planets. (Dakṣa 1.3)
Illuminating the assembly with his great radiance and surveying the gathered multitude,
he once again taught the Dharma, which is auspicious in the three times.
He proclaimed the holy life that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end, possessing good meaning and good phrasing, entirely complete, pure, and immaculate.
Then Ānanda, knowing the Self, with palms joined in reverence and full of joy, bowed before that omniscient King of Dharma with devotion. (Dak_1.5)
O Blessed One, out of a desire for the welfare of humanity, I wish to hear; O Lord of Speakers, King of Orators, please teach the supreme teaching among all teachings. Dak_1.6
When he had thus made this earnest request, the Lion of the Śākyas himself then entered there into a sublime meditative absorption that revealed the supreme Dharma.
Then, from the opening between his beautiful eyebrows, there issued forth that [light] which dispelled the darkness,
like the garland of rays of the midday sun illuminating all directions.
Then his disciples, along with the assemblies,
showered the Blessed One with beautiful flowers that were tossed by the wind, like young creepers upon a mountain.
Then the earth, together with the oceans and the mountains, trembled in its six ways;
flowers fell from the clouds, musical instruments resounded, and the celestial rishis broke into song.
Then all the hosts of gods come to Gṛdhrakūṭaka:
Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Śakra, Hari, Kāmeśvara, and the others. (Dak_1.11)
The Asuras, the Khecaras, Gandharvas, Kiṃnaras, and Mahoragas,
as well as the world-protectors and others such as Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his kin.
There, having circumambulated the Blessed One and prostrated before him,
all the gods and other hosts set out ahead in wonder.
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, having arisen from his meditative absorption and surveyed the assembly, remained silent with a smile.
Then Ānanda, the one of great wisdom, perceiving the Sage’s acceptance,
rose suddenly from his seat and addressed the Blessed One.

O Blessed One, though afflicted by thirst, I desire to drink the nectar of your speech issuing from the lotus of your mouth, just as one tormented by heat desires the water of the mountain-born [Ganges]. (Dak_1.16)
In this world, there is someone very wealthy, learned, an enjoyer of pleasures, and fortunate; another is poor, diseased, and miserable; and yet another is a skilled artisan, but a fool. (Dak_1.17)
"O Blessed One, by what ripening of karma would someone go to the celestial realm or to an extremely terrible hell? How might such a thing come to be? (Dak_1.18)
O Lord of Debaters, for the sake of the welfare of all the world, tell me all of that, having shown favor to me who am submerged in the ocean of existence. (Dak_1.19)
When this had been said, the Blessed One then spoke to that best of monks,
displaying his own power for the sake of the welfare of the entire world.
O noble one, listen to that which is auspicious and inauspicious for beings submerged in the six realms of existence, if it should please your heart. (Dak 1.21)

O highly fortunate one, it has been heard before that living beings, born from the four wombs and always following their respective courses of action, consist of both the existent and the non-existent. (Dak 1.22)
Egg-born, sweat-born, spontaneously born, and womb-born:
birds and the like are said to be egg-born; humans and the like are womb-born. (Dak 1.23)
Worms, insects, and the like are born from moisture; gods and others are of spontaneous birth;
and these are seen by the wise through their karma, vows, and virtuous conduct. (Dakārikā 1.24)
According to the specific state of their destiny, living beings are born thus in the four continents of great energy, subject to the ripening of their former karma.
Beings born within the six realms of existence— whether inferior, superior, or middling—
are each assigned their respective destinies, O monk, through the ripening of their karma.
This action—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is born of body, speech, and mind;
from it, people experience its fruit, both mundane and supramundane. (Dak_1.27)
Then Ānanda spoke again to the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World:
"Reveal the manifestations of those worlds that are the root of evils. (Dak 1.28)
O bull among speakers, tell me in detail all those various actions that have been performed by body, speech, and mind.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, hear clearly from me the fruit of good and evil for human beings:
through dharma one attains joy, and through what is not dharma, the arising of sorrow.
And again in detail.
The action of physical misconduct is revealed as being divided into three types:
taking what is not given, the destruction of life, and likewise sexual misconduct. (Dak_1.31)
The wise one has declared that vocal misconduct consists of four types: lying, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. (Dak 1.32)
The wise know that mental misconduct is divided into three types:
covetousness, malice, and wrong view; these are the three kinds. (Dak 1.33)
He who abandons compassion, being malicious through the killing of other living beings and so forth, and performs acts of beating and injury—that is called "prostration to living beings. (Dak_1.34)

The wise know that taking what is not given consists of seizing property through greed for another's domain, by means of injustice and force, and through theft, falsehood, and unrighteousness. (Dak 1.35)

Women observing vows, those practicing dharma, impure women, courtesans, and the wives of others—sexual misconduct with these, whether through attachment to a relative or otherwise, is called *kāmamithyā* (sexual misconduct). Dak_1.36.
When, for the sake of awakening others from attachment to sense objects, from greed, from affections, and from fears, one speaks with what is untrue, that is called false speech. (Dak 1.37)
When one conceals one's own fault so that the fault of another is revealed, and strikes with words poisoned by a vital wound, the wise know this as harsh speech. (Dak 1.38)

Through conduct and behavior that are wicked, one comes into conflict with kinsmen and friends; and by practicing slander toward those won over by one's own virtues, one is considered a fool. (Dak 1.39)
That which, by means of divisive speech in their presence, unsettles the minds of others so that mutual hatred arises, is considered to be *saṃbhinnapralāpa* (frivolous speech). Dak_1.40.
One who, with a mind of greed, covets the abundance of another's wealth and so forth—this should be known as *abhidhyā* (covetousness); such a person is attended by the wicked. (Dak_1.41)
When another person attains excellence such as a beautiful body and so forth, if one should wish with a corrupt mind, "May misfortune befall them," this is called malice (vyāpāda). (Dak_1.42)
In the next world, neither merit nor demerit exists, nor do pleasure and pain; having heard such a difficult-to-understand treatise, he holds wrong views and is an atheist. (Dak 1.43)
Thus, by means of the very evil of the ten unwholesome actions, that fool is tormented by various afflictions through the messengers of Yama in the next world.
Therefore, Ānanda, I have said that the fruit of the tree of the body arises;
whatever karma has been performed by whomsoever, by that very [karma] they experience its result.
Living beings are submerged in a lake of birth, death, and old age;
therefore, like one who is terrified of a most fearsome serpent, they should be full of dread. (Dak 1.46)
Gods, asuras, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings—
these six classes of beings are born therein through their virtuous and non-virtuous karma.
Having heard this, Ānanda, grieving for the worlds, terrified by the irresistible cycle of existence, had the hairs on his body stand on end with rapture. (Dak_1.48)
Then Maitreya, his senses subdued, rose from his seat and spoke for the benefit of the worlds to the Lord of the universe: Dak_1.49.
O Blessed One, Buddha, Lord of Heroes, who increases the joy of the world,
speak of various excellent qualities, full of compassion and the perfection of fruits.
Hearing the encouragement toward merit is difficult to obtain, as is the merit of renunciation;
likewise are the bathing of the image, the fragrant paste, the parasol, and the consecration of the relics. (Dak 1.51)
The mandala, food, drink, clothing, and the description of flowers and so forth; prostration, incense, lamps, monasteries, and beds and seats. (Dak 1.52)
"O Lord, Sovereign of Speakers, tell me the number of these twenty-two discourses, which are manifold and profound, beginning with 'The Field' and ending with 'The End'."
O Sage, O Blessed One, please explain all six perfections: ethical discipline, patience, as well as diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Dak_1.54
The Blessed One said:
Excellent, excellent, O Maitreya, you who act for the benefit of the world! Listen, O one of friendly mind, to this auspicious discourse that inspires merit. (Dak_1.55)

Having attained human birth, which is difficult to reach through hundreds of arduous deeds, and having secured this rare opportunity while death— inescapable and most terrible— stands perpetually before them,
those by whom a sufficient provision consisting of self-restraint, charity, and discipline has not been made; [how will they fare]?
Having fallen into the precipice of the fierce ocean of saṃsāra, they will encounter sufferings.

Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as fleeting as a flash of lightning, a bubble, or a wave—even when such a human state has been reached, how can one fail to remember merit when the favorable conditions are present? (Dak_1.57)
Having attained human birth, cross over that great river of suffering;
for in this state, one should perform only meritorious deeds, since for humans, merit is like a wish-fulfilling gem.
By whose power you have now once again attained human birth—therefore, increase your merit here, for that is the cause of your happiness. (Dak_1.59)
That human birth which you have obtained by relying [on merit], and which is now endowed with various qualities such as the nobility of form and high lineage—
that merit alone is your friend and the sole kinsman of the worlds in other births.
Therefore, perform this repeatedly, for it brings about the accomplishment of all goals. Dak_1.60 //

By relying upon those very merits, you have attained sovereignty esteemed by the world, which is the abode of Lakṣmī; therefore, you should cause those merits to increase further, for one must never diminish the side of those who have been benefactors.
Desist from evil; perform most noble merit;
subdue the difficult-to-tame horse of the mind that craves sense objects;
and, like the lords of sages, be constantly devoted to the welfare of others.
As long as the serpent of death, whose venom is unbearable, does not bite.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Story Encouraging Merit, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
II. Discourse on Encouraging the Hearing of the Dharma:

Having understood this wondrous and fleeting opportunity—which is as difficult to encounter as the meeting of the hole of a sea-turtle’s two ears with the opening of a whirlpool in the ocean—[one should listen to the Dharma].

Listen for even a moment to the words of the Sage, which are exceedingly difficult to encounter in this world; they are the sole armor for the city of tranquility and the remover of the fear of calamity.

That human birth, free from the defects of the eight inopportune states, which is difficult to obtain even in many hundreds of eons, has now been attained; therefore, you must indeed exert yourselves to hear the Dharma. (Dak_2.2)

In this existence, which is as flickering as a drop of water on the tip of a young leaf and is encircled by the web of afflictions, the birth of one who does not contemplate the true path of action is fruitless in this world. (Dak_2.3)

Not by those gone to hell, nor by hungry ghosts, nor by animals, nor by those with impaired faculties, nor by the teachers of the gods, nor by those dwelling in the borderlands, nor by those wounded by the sword of false views—
[can the truth be seen] while the Sun-like Sage has not yet risen, when the light of wisdom has not appeared in the Victor.
The nectar of the words of the Lord of Sages can be drunk by both men and gods.

Therefore, having abandoned all unwholesome actions and recognizing one's own task to be the supreme noble Dharma, one must listen to the Dharma with diligent effort; for from this, all virtuous qualities arise.
This jewel of speech from the Lord of Sages first produces joy in the wise at the mere hearing of it; thereafter, it destroys the mass of powerful, heavy, and dense darkness;
and finally, at the conclusion of reflection and meditation, it makes manifest the entire continuity of the cycle of birth.
It constantly shatters the entire series of afflictions and is the treasury of all prosperity.
It removes the calamities arising from intense existence and bestows the unsurpassed bliss of nirvāṇa;
having understood these words of the Sage to be thus, listen now with pure minds. (Dak_2.7)
Thus ends the second chapter, the story of the encouragement to listen to the Dharma, within the collection of twenty-two avadānas.
III. Discourse on the Rarity of Human Birth:

Having attained that which carries one to the further shore even of the ocean of existence, which plants the seed of supreme awakening for the sake of auspiciousness, and which exceeds even the wish-fulfilling gem in its abundance of virtues—who here would render this human state fruitless? (Dak 3.1)
He who, having attained human birth through the abundance of wholesome deeds over many eons, does not out of delusion accumulate even the slightest wealth of merit in this world,
encounters intense sorrow when he departs from this life to the next.
Like a merchant returning home empty-handed from an island of jewels. (Dak_3.2)
Human birth is not obtained again through unwholesome paths of action;
when human birth is not obtained, there is only suffering—where, then, is happiness?
There is no greater deception than this, nor is there any greater delusion than this:
that having obtained such a moment as this, one does not perform much wholesome merit. (Dak 3.4)
For a sin committed in a single moment, one dwells in Avīci for an eon;
how much more so for a sin committed over many lifetimes—what need is there to speak of a happy rebirth?
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Human birth is exceedingly difficult to obtain, comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke in a vast ocean. (Dak 3.6)
Thus ends the third chapter, the Discourse on the Rarity of Human Birth, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
IV. Discourse on Generosity:
Abundance of food, drink, bedding, and seats; jewels, garlands, garments, and ornaments;
fame, supreme virtues, and young women—all this is said to result entirely from generosity. (Dakārikā 4.1)

Radiance of command, abundance of enjoyments, excellence, nobility of form, sweetness of complexion, vigor, eloquence, good fortune, beauty, health, and long life—this is the desired fruit resulting from giving. (Dakārikā 4.2)
Horses, silken garments, elephants, white fly-whisks adorned with many flowers,

parasols, palaces filled with music, the sounds of honeyed drums, flower garlands, young women, food, necklaces of jewels and other gems, cities, towns, the earth, and lordship over the world of the gods— [all these are attained].
And the state of perfect buddhahood is described by the Buddhas here as the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree of generosity.
And women, whose eyes rival the delicate and stainless petals of the blue lotus, whose thighs and hips are kissed by swaying girdles, whose red garments have slipped down,
and whose creeper-like brows are arched as their breasts heave with trembling, fall into servitude.
This is the manifestation of generosity, which is skillful at shattering the door-panel of stinginess.
Those best of men go forth with horses whose heads are bowed under the weight of chowries, with elephants whose mouths are turned upward by their bits and whose rutting ichor has been broken,
and they are honored by servants adorned with ornaments who join their palms in reverence beneath the raised parasols.
The sages always declare that such is the fruit of that gift previously acquired.
Adorned with necklaces, golden bracelets inlaid with diamonds, armlets, and crowns studded with gems, these kings always sit upon lion-thrones;
in the midst of their harem women, they sport with various diversions.
The sages declare that to be the fruit of giving, which is like the playful stride of a tiger.

In a palace inlaid with jewels, gems, and gold, adorned with parasols and banners, resounding with the songs of lutes, harps, and flutes, and illuminated by the radiance of precious stones— where Śakra, accompanied by Śacī and surrounded by thousands of women, takes his delight.
The sages declare that such is the fruit of giving from what was previously acquired.
The giver always becomes beloved by people and is attended by many who approach him as virtuous men;
his stainless fame spreads through the quarters, and being confident, he attains those various lofty states. (Dak 4.8)

Upon the dissolution of the body, having attained birth among the gods in places where various abundant and radiant enjoyments are complete— amidst vast wish-fulfilling trees blooming with clusters of diverse blossoms—
he dwells for a very long time in the Nandana gardens and others, experiencing supreme happiness without weariness as he pleases.
Through the act of giving, one attains a state of preeminent form, served by hosts of celestial maidens.
Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one [into the next life] and cannot be shared by thieves and the like;
generosity is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind,
and it is the comfortable vehicle that removes the exhaustion of the journey through saṃsāra.
Generosity is not merely inclined toward the enjoyment of various pleasures; it is a true friend that is ultimate.
With girdles fastened upon their hips, voices sweet as song, eyebrows dancing with playful grace, large and lovely eyes reaching to their ears, and garlands clinging to the ends of their hair—
these women themselves come into the service of the meritorious, their broad hips heavy with the weight of their breasts.
Śauddhodani spoke of that greatness of giving, which yields its gathered fruit.

The lover repeatedly drinks the honey, red as the bandhūka flower, which has been offered by his beloved as a solemn oath; it is placed in a splendid golden vessel, fragrant with crushed mango blossoms, and contains floating blue lotuses that have settled therein.
Those of pure intellect declare that in this regard, generosity is the supreme cause for the highest good.
Having thus heard these virtues of giving, O gentle one, apply yourself with a disciplined mind to the very act of giving;
for in the great terror of the three worlds, there is no other kinsman for humanity superior to generosity.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Discourse on Giving, within the collection of twenty-two edifying tales (*avadāna*).
V. Regarding the discourse on the desire for merit:

Whatever is seen in the world that is most beautiful, beloved, or pleasing—whether it be form, lineage, dear ones, wealth, or happiness—the virtuous declare that these are produced solely by the artisan of merit; indeed, this is the merit of a person who performs wholesome deeds. (Dak_5.1)

Adorned with rows of exceedingly lofty, elevated, and white banners, their bodies beautified by waving yak-tail fans, kings of abundant merit traverse the earth with vast armies of elephants, horses, infantry, and chariots that stir up the dust. (Dak_5.2)

Wearing variegated garments of silk, Kāśika cloth, and fine linen, their limbs adorned with strings of pearls, gold, and jewels—only certain men bear such splendor; this is a praise of the merit of their past conduct. (Dak_5.3)
A very long life, birth in a noble family, a beautiful body, and freedom from the fear of disease;
abundant wealth and the excellence of a retinue—these arise from the great maturation of merit. (Dak 5.4)
That a universal monarch, though endowed with the most excellent jewels and a thousand sons,
enjoyed the earth as far as the boundaries of the ocean— that is the vast fruit of the jewel of merit.
Seated in the center of a most excellent and variegated lotus, eternally saluted by the lords of gods and asuras and others—
it is through his merit alone that Brahmā always shines, outshining even the world of Brahmā with his splendor.
That the Teacher of Gods is always worshipped by the hosts of gods, nāgas, asuras, and siddhas, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, and supreme kinnaras— that is the vast fruit of the jewel of merit.
Leaving behind their physical form, vigor, and craft, men depart helplessly from this world to the next, driven by the winds of karma.
But merit alone follows one here absolutely and brings about happiness;
because it cannot be taken away by others, merit is the supreme wealth among all riches.
Even those winds of universal destruction that scatter even Mount Meru with their force in the ten directions are not capable of destroying one's merit.
Merit does not undergo decay even by the waters of the four oceans, which surge forth unrestrained during the dissolution of the world.
Even when the earth is being consumed by the seven sun-fires, which are like blazing coals of light,
a single merit is not burned.

Having thus heard the sage’s words, which were indeed the truth, Maitreya—whose hair stood on end with joy and who was terrified by the insurmountable nature of cyclic existence—[was moved]. (Dak_5.13)
Then Maitreya, having heard these words of the Sage with great joy, bowed at the lotus-feet of the Jina and spoke thus to the Tathāgata: (Dak_5.14)

Furthermore, what would be the fruit of establishing images of the Buddha, restoring ruined [shrines], and so forth? And what would be the fruit of those reliquaries containing the relics of the Jina? (Dak_5.15)
The Blessed One said:
One who restores ruined stupas and images of the Sugata,
endowed with the power of supernatural faculties, shall become equal to a universal monarch.
Having become meritorious and powerful, one's faculties will not be impaired;
then, having experienced happiness at the end, one is born into the state of perfect buddhahood.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, tiger among victors, it is well; you are truly praiseworthy, O Lord.
Tell me, O ocean of wisdom: by whom has this been done? (Dak_5.18)
When this had been said, the Blessed One, for the sake of causing wonder among the worlds,
performed a single sign and remained there in silence.
Then, like lightning coming from the sky, he arrived radiant with rays of light;
having illuminated the entire assembly, curiosity arose among them all.
Maitreya said:
O Blessed One, this is a marvel; what is the cause of this wonder?
Whose manifestation of an object is this that has appeared, radiant with rays of light?
The Blessed One said:
Maitreya, the radiance of the palace adorned with jewels and of the king has arrived, illuminating everywhere in all directions.
Maitreya said:
"O Blessed One, surely this [splendor] has come to him by means of such radiance. By whom was such radiance attained, and what is the cause of it that has arisen in my heart? (Dak_5.23)
The Blessed One said:
But now, Maitreya, I shall show you this king;
for by virtue of his former merit, he possesses great supernatural power.

Then King Ratnavyūha, having ascended his jeweled celestial palace, traveled by means of supernatural power through the expanse of the sky to where the Blessed One was; having approached and arrived there, he suddenly appeared in that place.

Then that king, having seen the Blessed One endowed with the thirty-two marks, golden-hued, his body radiant with a splendor exceeding a thousand suns, was filled with serene faith; he descended from his celestial palace, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One, although he already knew of the king's arrival, asked:
"O Indra among kings, is all well with you, both externally and internally?"
"O illustrious one, you who are devoted to the Dharma, speak of that which leads to union;
O tiger among kings, you who desire our welfare and are dear to all beings, speak of that which grants liberation. (Dak 5.26)
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, performed three circumambulations, and presented the offerings, he bowed down and spoke to that guru: (Dak 5.27)
O Blessed One, as I reflect thus, you have acted for my welfare;
seeking my highest good, you have everywhere treated me, a mere forest-dweller, as a teacher. (Dak 5.28)
"I have no other task, O Blessed One; it is solely out of a desire to see you and to hear the Dharma that I have always come here. (Dak_5.29)
The Blessed One said:
"I shall teach you correctly, O best of kings, for you,
O ruler of the earth, are a worthy vessel for the principles that constitute the true nature of dharma."
Listen, O mighty-armed king, to the most excellent and supreme dharma of kings:
protect the power of royal duty and practice the path of political ethics.
It is as follows:

Just as one would constantly protect a tree laden with fruit and flowers for the sake of the citizens, so too, O King, you should always protect those who are the constant support of the ruler; by acting thus in every way, all will be well.

Just as a fruit possesses its quality and its flavor through the power of ripening, so too, O Lord of Men, might there be strength and the glory of victory; yet even so, these [qualities] are powerful over people.
And listen again, O Great King.
A foolish person, looking upon things as empty, engages in evil;
in the night of dense darkness, one thinks, "This is the time for sinful deeds. (Dak 5.34)
The sages, who have perfected their souls and possess divine vision,
perceive that in some places there is nothing at all, while in other directions the world is entirely filled with those whose wealth is asceticism.
Therefore, O best of kings, become one whose soul is devoted to that [practice];
taking up a skull as your choice, go to dwell in the houses of your enemies. (Dakṣa 5.36)
Wherever a doer of evil who desires happiness goes,
there and right there he is struck by the weapons of suffering born of his own misdeeds.
Wherever the aspiration of those who perform virtuous deeds goes, there too it is honored by the value of its fruit through their merits. (Dak_5.38)
Therefore, with all effort, one should abandon the entire accumulation of evil;
having conquered the fury of hatred, perform virtuous deeds. (Dak_5.39)
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with great effort through various methods.
When the thorn of hatred remains in the heart, the mind finds no tranquility, it does not enjoy the bliss of joy, and it attains neither sleep nor steadfastness. (Dak_5.41)
Evil people, who are like the sky, do not go to destruction merely by being hated;
however, when the mind of anger is slain, all enemies perish.
Blazing with the fuel of conceptual construction, the living being first burns himself with the fire of anger; he may then burn others, or perhaps not at all. (Dak_5.43)
Old age for the beautiful, anger even for those with sight, and the destruction of virtue, wealth, and pleasure—therefore, one should restrain anger. Dak_5.44.
He who, through persistent effort, destroys anger born from the occurrence of the undesired and the obstruction of the desired, is happy both in this world and in the next. (Dakārikā 5.45)
Therefore, having completely conquered hatred, protect the mind with diligence;
for it is impossible to guard the training while failing to guard the flickering mind. (Dak 5.46)
Untamed rutting elephants do not cause such agony here as that which the elephant of the mind, when unrestrained, inflicts in the Avīci hell and other realms. (Dak_5.47)
If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness, all fear has vanished and every excellence has arrived. (Dak 5.48)
Therefore, having composed the mind and maintaining mindfulness, protect it with effort;
for from the mind alone do both fear and well-being arise in every respect. (Dak_5.49)
Having abandoned the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other vows?
Knowing this, O King, always protect your subjects with righteousness.
And again, O Great King:

That king who gathers the fruit of his realm like one who plucks a tree that yields its bounty, does not find sweetness himself but destroys the seed; he ruins the country because it is difficult to bear his taxes, and the king indeed finds no joy in the Dharma.

Therefore, do not punish the subjects unjustly; protect the kingdom with justice. For those kings who bring about the welfare of their subjects, it is their subjects who carry away their suffering. (Dak 5.52)
And again, O Great King:

Those kings who are always pained by the suffering of others as they are by their own, and who find happiness through the happiness of others as they do through their own, and who are thus ever equal toward all—such kings possess every virtue at all times. (Dak_5.53)
They fulfill their sovereignty through Dharma; they constantly carry prosperity through Dharma;
they satisfy the worlds through Dharma; and they obtain their desires instantly through Dharma. (Dak_5.54)
And again:

Through generosity one obtains enjoyments, not by harming others nor through the delusion of ignorance; for those who possess wealth in this world by means of oppressing others will encounter suffering in the next world. (Dak_5.55)
The self, O Bhārata, is a river with sacred bathing places; truth is its water, virtue its banks, and compassion its waves.
One who is skilled performs his ablution therein; for the inner self is not purified by mere water.
Purity comes through truth, not from entering water, which only destroys the external impurities of the body.
By truth the gods always abide; indeed, the stability of the earth rests upon truths alone.
Heavenly realms do not come from leaping off mountain precipices, nor are protective guardians equal to ethical discipline.
Humans who slip from the mountain of immoral conduct fall into sufferings within the great oceans.
Liberation comes through knowledge, not from the emaciation of the body; it is not made wet by rain any more than it is by the summer heats.
A man devoid of knowledge is just like one who has merely bathed in muddy lakes. (Dak 5.59)
Having heard this, O Indra among kings, his hair stood on end with joy as he thought:
"In this most terrible cycle of existence, how shall I deliver myself? (Dak 5.60)
Then that lord of kings, terrified by the fear of cyclic existence,
became devoted to the Blessed Buddha and once again took refuge in him.
“O Blessed One, O Buddha, Lord of Heroes, having heard this, my mind finds it pleasing. O Lord, I entreat you: please grant me the prophecy of my awakening. (Dak 5.62)
Then the Blessed One, the Teacher, knowing her virtuous intention, prophesied:
"In no long time you shall become a Tathāgata."
The Arhat named Ratnākara is the Perfectly Awakened One, the Leader of the World,
the King of Dharma, the Lord of the World, the Omniscient One, the Arhat, and the Sovereign of Sages.
"You shall become a teacher, the lord of all vidyās, a mine of virtues;
having then performed the work of a Buddha, you will remain for a long time."

Then that lord of kings, having first accepted his true blessing and bowed down, announced with joy, "I shall depart," and mounting his celestial chariot, like a merchant who has gained great profit through his wealth, he set out for his own home— his very own kingdom.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Discourse on the Desire for Merit, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
VI. The Story of the Restoration of the Image: Then, filled with curiosity, the monks said this to the Blessed One.
"Blessed One, by what merit and by what wholesome deed has this king become so exceedingly handsome, beautiful to behold, and captivating?"
Of what city is this man the likeness, who possesses such excellence and a wealth of beauty that is very difficult to find even for a god? (Dak_6.2)
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, that protector of the earth, blazing with the splendor of great merit,
was the supreme king Ratnavyūha of the city of Vaiśālī."
And what would that city be like—prosperous, flourishing, and delightful; abundant in food, beautiful, and filled with virtuous and learned people? (Dak 6.4)
It was sixteen yojanas in length and breadth, likewise;
it was filled with various festivals, and the wicked were driven far, even further away.
As was the mind of the city folk, so was the king’s mind;
it was filled with vast gardens and beautifully adorned with lotus ponds.
But on the sides, the birds were indeed made to play [their songs] with the humming of bees.
His queen was Saṃpannā, and his son was Śubhavyūha;
he was handsome and beautiful to behold, possessing a form like that of the flower-bowed god of love.
He attained all royal splendor along with the honors due to a king;
he was fully endowed with the science of archery and had reached the further shore of the knowledge of the treatises.
Endowed with the power of great supernormal faculties, possessing a radiance equal to that of a universal monarch,
knowing the methods of the scriptures and traditions, he is wise and has accomplished all that was to be done.
Such is this Lord of the Jewel of Kings, powerful throughout all the world;
through his former wholesome deeds, he has obtained such a fruit.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, furthermore, endowed with what root of merit did that king possess such splendor, and by what action?"
The Blessed One said:
Maitreya, listen!
Long ago, Maitreya, in a previous birth, he was a boatman;
that boatman lived constantly upon the shores of the ocean. (Dak_6.11)
Due to the influence of his ill fortune, no merchants arrived; therefore, he was miserable and in great distress, for he could not take on any ferry fare. Dak_6.12.
Then he thought: "Alas, alas!
What shall I do now? I have not obtained food or anything else. (Dak 6.13)
"May no one ever experience such suffering"—
thinking thus in his mind and recollecting the Jina, he remains.
Then that boatman’s mind took no pleasure in staying there;
as he was walking along the seashore, he saw at a certain spot a single shrine that was very extensive, containing a decayed stūpa for the relics of the Tathāgata.
And seeing that the interior of the stūpa had been broken by cowherds playing with stones and bricks, he reflected and said this:
"By what evil-souled one was this destruction of the shrine committed?
This unsightly shrine is now being restored by me. (Dak_6.15)
He performed that consecration (saṃskāra) wherever there were broken parts and so forth,
as well as in places where the plaster had crumbled, using stone or even brick.
And having regarded him as a boatman, he acted auspiciously as before.
Then, by the power of the Buddha, at that time and in that place,
three hundred merchants with their wares arrived at his assembly.

For the purpose of crossing the river Nadīśa, those merchants, joined by the caravan leader, called him and spoke thus to that man: Dak_6.18. "Those merchants, having summoned him, spoke to that caravan leader."
"O boatman, we are going to the Island of Jewels by all means;
having considered this, may you, as our guide, protect us here from the ocean."
Having heard this, that steadfast fisherman, after considering their income and expenditure, hoisted his boat before them and said:
"Sirs, you ought to remain here on these vehicles for now;
recollecting your own deities and maintaining firm fortitude, stay. (Dak_6.20)
Having agreed, saying "So be it," the three hundred merchants bowed to the ship, offered prayers to the ocean, and having boarded the vessel, began to cross the sea by degrees.
Then all those merchants, their minds filled with joy and possessing great enthusiasm and delight,
became certain that the success of their supreme voyage was assured for them.
Then, in due course, they entered the ocean, which was not yet deep and whose rows of foam were stirred by waves upon which various schools of fish moved about;

it was as dark blue as a stainless sword-blade, like a cloudless sky melted away by the heat of the sun’s rays, and having gradually reached the middle of the fathomless sea, the traces of its shores had vanished on all sides.
Then it became the time of evening, when reaching the shore was extremely difficult,
at a time when the sun’s rays were faint.
A great portent, most terrifying and formidable with Garuḍas and venomous serpents, arose in tumultuous waves.
With its waves breaking apart and its foam scattered, and with a terrifying roar produced by the lashing of fierce winds,
it became as perilous as the time of the world's end, agitated by the great tempests of universal destruction.
Clouds, with flickering tongues flashing like streaks of lightning and possessing many crests like blue serpents, shrouded the path of the sun, resounding with continuous and terrifying thunders.
Then that boatman, seeing those merchants despondent about their own lives and overwhelmed by fear, summoned his courage and said to them:
"Do not disregard me; do not act rashly; do not fear, do not fear! Remember the Buddha, remember the Buddha!"—thus he addressed the merchants.
Having heard that, those merchants performed the recollection of the name "Bauddha" and paid homage.
When this had been said, by the power of the Buddha, that great portent vanished in an instant.
Seeing that, she joyfully ferried them to the shore.
Then those merchants said to him:
"O boatman, it is well; through your favor we have reached the shore."
Having spoken thus, and having given him an exceedingly high crossing-fare with great hospitality and profound respect,
they announced, "We are departing," and then they set out.
The boatman, having taken them and placed them on board the vessel, turned back and stood waiting.
Then the ferryman, having received the kārṣāpaṇa fare for crossing, remains in comfort, well-provided with clothing, food, and drink.

Monks, in the past, through the roots of merit acquired by repairing the dilapidated stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata during his birth as a boatman, that Ratnavyūha attained such a form and superhuman power of miraculous eloquence for that king.
Then, O monks, they said:
"Blessed One, it is well, Sugata; we have been awakened. That king is indeed praiseworthy;
tell us again, what kind of eloquence does he possess?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, that king ruled his kingdom with righteousness;
he protected all his citizens like a father protects his son, and all the people heard his fame, glory, and renown.

Having performed his duties according to the law, he gave gifts to those who sought them: food to those seeking food, drink to those seeking drink, and clothing to those seeking clothing; thus, O monks, that king brought about well-being within his own realm like the thousand-eyed Indra.
Then, at one time, that king, having assembled everyone, had a hall constructed.
In the assembly of that king, a certain monk arrived—
one who was lame and afflicted with leprosy due solely to his immoral conduct and evil deeds.
Clad in foul-smelling, filthy garments of loathsome appearance, one will be reviled by all the world, and no accomplishment through speech shall be found. (Dakāratantra 6.24)
Then, having seen him, the king reflected upon this and questioned him:
"O monk, why have you come here? And how is it that your feet are lame?"
The monk said:
"O Great King, what is the use of this evil deed of mine? In my youth, I was born with a clubfoot and my body was afflicted by leprosy. (Dak 6.26)
The king said:
Even by taking up the going-forth, how is it that your body is thus?
You have neither staff nor bowl, nor do you have the robes;
you have come here as a monk in name only.
The monk said:
For how could I know, O King of kings, that I am unworthy of the staff and the robe? Being so unfortunate and devoid of merit, have mercy on me, O God among gods! (Dak_6.28)
The king said: "O monk, may you be worthy of offerings through your fame and well-conducted; follow one who is endowed with virtue.
Having spoken thus, the king gave him a staff, bowl, robes, and other requisites, and fed him with great honor.
Then, O monk, by the mere sight of the king, Khañjapādasnāyu became one whose limbs were soft.
Gradually, the leprosy and other ailments dissolved;
not even a mere remnant remained.
Then that monk went from that place to another region.
Then all the people, struck with wonder, spoke thus:
"Aho! The great king is meritorious, having become a treasury of Dharma;
by the mere sight of him, that monk’s leprosy and lameness of foot were completely cured."
Then the king reflected.
What is the cause of this illusion, or what is real for that monk?
Such is the wonder that has come upon me.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, how did that monk become the cause for those who had arrived there by means of illusion?"
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Maitreya, I shall tell you the reason for this:
that monk did not go to beg out of illusion, but because of his natural disposition. (Dak_6.29)
But, monks, by this mere sight of the monk, the king—whose body was the Dharma—was thus freed from his lameness of foot. Dak_6.30.
Then, monks, they said: "This is most wonderful and marvelous!
Even while established in the state of a monk, how did he become lame in his feet? (Dak_6.31)
Neither a god, nor a seer, a siddha, or a rākṣasa, but even as a king born among men, how could he possess such eloquence? (Dak 6.32)
The Blessed One said:
"That monk was one who did only a small service; do you wish to hear his story?
O bulls among monks, listen as I relate his account. (Dak_6.33)
Those men who, out of negligence, act with malice toward their parents— who are indeed Brahman, the God of gods— [commit a grave offense].
For this reason, one should not cause even one's parents to suffer distress.
Those who in their families properly honor, properly revere, and properly maintain their mother and father with comfort.
Alternatively, she should perform honorable service for her parents with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and seating, as well as with that same attentive care and irreproachable conduct.
For what reason?

Men with moon-like faces, broad and excellent bodies, large eyes, and physiques resembling the morning sun, endowed with auspicious fame, obtain a kingdom free from the fear of enemies; all this indeed results from giving to one's own teachers and maternal relatives.
Listen as I relate the deeds of that bhikṣu in his former lives.
Long ago, monks, there was a city named Kāverī.
In that city lived a merchant named Kuśīda, who was extremely impoverished due to his lack of merit and generosity in previous lives.
(Dak: 38) He had two sons:
one was a boy and the other was a youth.
Then, when his father had passed away,
the younger son caused enmity toward his mother;
he constantly addressed her with anger and harsh words.
And having given food and drink only in limited measure, he himself always consumed it.
Then, with that anguish in her mind, the mother spoke to her son.
"My son, what have you done? Your younger brother is but a child, not yet knowing how to eat; he drinks only milk—how shall I sustain him on such meager food?"
Having heard that, out of envy and anger toward his mother, he kicked his mother with his foot and uttered these words: "Ah, what!"
Nevertheless, although the dart of suffering remained in her heart, she herself pacified it and spoke;
thinking, "O my sons, may you not experience the ripening of this karma," she remained there.
Then that merchant’s son, because his anger had not subsided, spoke to his mother with resentment:
"O mother, do not stay here in my house; go wherever you desire. The mother replied:
"Where must I go, my son? What offense have I committed, my child?
Do not speak such words; do not give way to sudden anger."
Then, having rendered his mother's words as if they were not spoken, he remained under the control of his own will by means of his son Dahara.
Then his mother remained there, looking after her youngest son.
Thereafter, because that young son had not yet abandoned his domestic duties, he experienced a most grievous suffering.
A transformation occurring in his foot causes it to become afflicted with leprosy and crippled.
Certain tasks and actions are not easy to perform.
Because of his lack of power, he gradually wraps himself in his own evil deeds and becomes poor.
Then, because his objects of perception were gone and his right mindfulness was likewise lost, he experienced nothing but suffering, like the distress caused by a firebrand. (Dak_6.37)
Then he thought:
"Alas, alas! What a great misery for me! Now what shall I do? Where indeed shall I go? (Dak 6.38)
"I shall say, 'May I become even a mere monk,'" he said;
having spoken thus, out of shame he did not speak with his mother and departed from his own home.
Then, after the lapse of three fortnights, he passed away.
Then, as the ripening of karma resulting from having committed an injury against his mother, he was reborn in the hells.
Then the messengers of Yama seize them and cast them into other hells.
Therefore, having been lifted up, they are led toward the prison; but he, who has done harm to his mother, is sent out through the gate with the utmost width and great height.
Then he entered further inside;
there his door was closed.
Having entered further inside, as soon as he had entered, a massive iron wheel appeared upon his head.
The door-panel was closed.
From that sin, a wheel—blazing, fiercely flaming, and become a single mass of fire—spins;
it revolves over his head, and from it, pus and blood flow forth.
That is its nutriment.
Then he said:
"Alas! How painful is this sensation! By what evil deed has it come upon me? Is there no protector at all who might come when thus invoked? (Dak 6.39)
For karma draws one far away, and from afar karma sets one in motion;
karma carries one forth to that place where karma ripens.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
By the ripening of that karma, a wheel—blazing, fiercely aflame, and obstructing my life-force—is borne upon my head. (Dak 6.42)
Thus it is said.
Then, from the sky, a sound issued forth from that house.
Who protects you, a wicked sinner who has defiled his mother?
When someone like you arrives here, he is liberated from that suffering.
Thereafter, at the end of a hundred years, such a man arrived at that iron house;
as soon as he had entered, he fell from it, and a wheel appeared upon the head of that newly arrived man.
That son of Kuśīda, having been released from those hells, was born once again into a poor family.
There, his mother and father passed away;
being left all alone after their death, the remainder of his evil karma was not yet exhausted, and he became afflicted with a lame foot and leprosy.
Thinking, "In this very life, having become a beggar, I shall say, 'I am a monk,'" he departed from his own home.
Thus, monks, that monk of immoral conduct, through that fault of his mother and that transgression, becomes afflicted with leprosy and lame in his feet;
it does not happen through illusion, but rather as the ripening of his own karma.
Then his younger brother, being small in age, was properly honored, revered, and well cared for by their mother.
By that act of offering alms-food, the world of the ancestors was fully satisfied.
By the power of that merit, having been born as the son of King Ratnavyūha in a great royal lineage, he became Prince Śubhavyūha.
Therefore, monks, one should not even conceive in one's mind the thought of doing harm toward one's mother and father.
When this had been said, Maitreya, with the hairs on his body standing on end from joy, addressed the Blessed One as follows.
"I am awakened, Blessed One; I am awakened, Sugata.
By one so devoted to evil, such a thing was experienced."
By what means and through what effort does the destruction of that monk's transgression occur?
The Blessed One said:

For those humans who, having passed away from this very world of saṃsāra, have been reborn in a mother’s womb— having carried them for ten months and giving birth with great hardship, she sustains them by providing her breast milk— it is not possible to escape the consequences of doing harm to such a mother, even through deeds that are difficult to perform.
Then the Blessed One spoke again:
O Maitreya, a king named Ratnavyūha, possessed of supreme merit, again reflected one day.
"I am old and my limbs are utterly decayed; how much longer shall I remain?
By the power of destiny, I shall certainly and inevitably go to my death. (Dak_6.44)

Reflecting that the entire kingdom and the enjoyment of its objects are entirely useless, causing most terrible fear, agitated by the terror of the serpent of death, impermanent, and devoid of essence, his mind no longer found delight in dwelling in the household;
then, having addressed Prince Śubhavyūha and his minister, he spoke thus:
"Son Śubhavyūha, here I am, surely overcome by old age with my faculties decayed;
then, even though overwhelmed by disease, I would certainly go to my death. (Dak_6.45)
Therefore, I wish to go forth by the excellent and praiseworthy path, before death strikes me down while I am still attached to the household life. (Dak 6.46)
Therefore, my mind finds no delight in remaining here, as I am terrified of cyclic existence by the many fears and anxieties; I shall go for refuge to the Buddha. (Dak 6.47)
"O son Śubhavyūha, by the power of my former merit, Gautama Śauddhodana has prophesied for me:
'Awakened by him, you will before long become a Tathāgata.
May I myself become a Buddha."
"In the western direction, in the world-system Campakavarṇā, there is a single buddha-field;
I shall go there."
Therefore, you ought to act exactly as I have instructed;
having protected your subjects, conduct yourself according to the principles of righteousness.
Do not distress the world with your sufferings; practice your family dharma, and indeed, give gifts with faith, endowed with compassion even toward others.
Do not commit killing, taking what is not given, or sexual misconduct; do not engage in lying, slander, harsh speech, or divisive talk. Dak_6.50.
Abandon covetousness, ill-will, and faults such as wrong views;
maintain all these with a firm mind.
"For this is indeed taught by the Sugata to be the root of all evils;
even if this is done, no calamity shall befall the king. (Dak_6.52)
From this day forward, you shall be the sovereign lord of all worlds,
the instructor of all dharmas, and the bearer of the welfare of all sentient beings.
For what reason?
Through righteousness the kingdom prospers; through righteousness wealth increases.
By means of righteousness riches are accomplished, and by means of righteousness the attainments of desire are achieved.
Through the attainment of desires, liberation is reached; of this there is no doubt. (Dak 6.54)
By this path of knowledge, the king instructed his son, just as an elephant is restrained when it is bent by the fear of the goad of knowledge. (Dak 6.55)
Having heard those words, which were like nectar, he bowed to his father, saying:
"O Father, as you have commanded, I shall attend to the protection of the subjects."
Having thus given these instructions, the high-minded King Ratnavyūha then awakened his sons, wife, and others, and departed joyfully for a Buddha-field.
Listen again, Maitreya, to the account of the journey along the royal roads.
Then that king, acting as a traveler on the road, beheld an old drainage channel.
The water was not flowing before; it was made to flow by seeing him. By whom was it not flowing previously, yet now has it been set in motion? (Dak 6.59)
While the king stood there exclaiming "How wonderful!", a voice spoke to him from the sky:
"O Great King, you are meritorious; by your power this [river] has been set flowing. (Dak 6.60)
"O King, you must surely understand this: since this water-channel is broken within, you yourself are indeed the very embodiment of Dharma. (Dak_6.61)
The king said: "And I myself was not recognized."
Therefore, the king proceeded to a vast forest tract;
having arrived there, he beheld trees laden with fruits and flowers.
When another tree stood there alone, having been uprooted by its very roots,
it rose up as before the mere moment the king beheld it.
Then a voice spoke to him from the sky: "O King, this tree is indeed praiseworthy; for though it is insentient, having risen up, it has come here. (Dak_6.64)
The king said: "I myself was not even recognized."
Immediately thereafter, three Brahmins arrived on the paths; one was afflicted with leprosy, another had lost his eyesight, and the third always possessed a healthy body.
Seeing them, the king reflected and asked them:
"O Brahmins, where are you going, and from which land have you come here?"
The Brahmins said:
"It is well for you, O Great King, that you are renowned as Ratnavyūha; we have no other business, we are going there to that king. (Dak_6.67)
Merely by being seen by the king, those with impaired vision regain their sight;
they become beautiful-limbed and well-nourished, and heaps of evil are cast off.
Then the brahmin friend said:
"O friend, I have attained a state of great wonder! For what reason has your sight been restored now, even though you were deprived of it? (Dak_6.69)
"You who were afflicted with leprosy on every limb shall once again possess beautiful limbs;
by the mere sight of this very man, my friend, you who were thus deformed shall indeed today become one of beautiful limbs. Dak_6.70.
"Be present now; let us question him, O friend.
He is the cause, for he is not a man of limited vision. (Dak 6.71)
"O sir, from where have you come? O bull among men, your self is accumulated with merit; you shine with a splendor that surpasses all."
The king said:
"O Brahmins, do you not know that [the city] is renowned as Ratnavyūha? How, O auspicious ones, can I go there now in such a state? (Dak_6.73)
Then the brahmins, filled with affection, joy, and gladness, pronounced blessings upon that king.
"O Lord of the Earth, may victory be yours! May all that is desired by your mind be attained—may it be so, O you who are resplendent with the glory of merit. (Dak_6.74)
Having said, "So be it for me," he honored the brahmins with exceptional hospitality and dismissed them.
Then the brahmins, having attained faith, departed for their own hermitage.
Maitreya said:
"By what sins does one become one-eyed, and how does one become afflicted with leprosy?
Such is the teaching of the twice-born;
alas, what a misery for a man! (Dakṣa 6.75)
Being thus questioned by Maitreya, the Blessed One spoke to him again.
"What you saw was not seen; what you spoke was a false oath. Because of that, you have become blind; you were intent on your own interest, not on performing the welfare of others. (Dak 6.76)
A twice-born man who, having embezzled wealth for the king's business, was made a treasurer, is led back to his own home after giving a small portion to another. (Dakṣa 6.77)
Due to that ripening of karma, the twice-born man’s body was afflicted with leprosy;
for whatever action is performed, one experiences its fruit accordingly through its maturation.
Maitreya said:
I am awakened, O Blessed One; I am awakened, O Sugata.
Then that king reached the buddha-field in the world-system Campakavarṇā.
Having seen in that buddha-field a shrine named Vimalaprabhā, which was delightful, beautiful to behold, and inspiring, his mind was filled with supreme joy, and he took refuge at its hermitage.
Having sat cross-legged and straightened his body, he remained established in the delight of meditative concentration;
then, at that very moment, he attained the five superknowledges.
In due course, he became the Tathāgata, Arhat named Ratnākara.
Maitreya said:
"Blessed One, what kind of fruit results from the restoration of dilapidated stūpas containing the relics of the Tathāgata?"
O Lord, please teach us all regarding the establishing of reliquaries and images of the Tathāgata: from what source, by what means, and what kind of fruit would result for those who do so? Dak_6.79.
The Blessed One said:

Wealthy, with all sorrow destroyed and every strife eliminated, he is a vessel for the joy of the eyes, a treasury of the glory of good fortune, possessed of increased strength and limbs of lovely form;
he is illustrious, radiant, beautiful in appearance, skilled in eloquent speech, and has his senses and body fully subdued.
The wise donor, having fashioned an image of the Blessed Buddha, becomes free from distraction. (Dak_6.80)
As many atoms as there are in the stupas or images of the Blessed One, so many kingdoms shall the maker of them certainly enjoy in heaven and on earth;
and having experienced all the bliss of the perfection of the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms, he shall enjoy it all.
Beforehand, one attains the state of a Buddha, which is free from birth, old age, and misfortune.

He whose beautiful body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and who is characterized by the [minor] marks of a universal monarch shall, at the end, become a Victor who has conquered the enemy of the faults—this is for one who fashions an image of the Tathāgata. (Dak_6.82)
The non-deficiency of the sense faculties, distance from womanhood and the miserable destinies, birth as a human, a noble lineage, and speech that is authoritative. (Dakārastava 6.83)
Birth, sacred learning, tradition, fortitude, the attainment of desired prosperity, devotion to appropriate goals, and freedom from affliction by passion and other defilements; (Dak_6.84)
Excellences esteemed by the virtuous arise for those who, out of joy, fashion images of the Buddha or stūpas for the sake of living beings; this is called "perfect awakening. (Dak_6.85)

He who makes an image of the Lord of the World does not fall into servitude, nor into poverty, nor into the state of a messenger, nor even into a low birth; nor shall he suffer any deficiency of the sense faculties in this world. (Dak_6.86)
This merit regarding the activities performed at shrines should be understood in brief;
it is not possible for all the Victors to describe it in its entirety, so how could I do so? (Dak_6.87)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Story of the Restoration of the Image, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
VII. Discourse on Bathing.
Immediately thereafter, Maitreya said to the Blessed One:
"Please describe the fruit of bathing the reliquaries and the images of the Buddhas. (Dak_7.1)
The Blessed One said:
"O Ajita Maitreya, listen to the supreme fruit of bathing; for the sake of the world's welfare, I shall speak of [bathing] at shrines and before images of the Buddhas. (Dak_7.2)
Whoever bathes the Sugata with various fragrant perfumes, or offers worship with flowers, incense, and unguents with a joyful mind, or with the sounds of musical instruments fit to be heard—
[they attain] the pollen-dust of the filaments of golden lotuses blooming in the Mandākinī.
When she has pervaded [the world], he who bathes at the end, cleansed of all the impurities of the Kali age, attains liberation.
In the Mandākinī, which is agitated by the heavy blows from the full and lofty breasts and hips of celestial women,
and which casts forth the fragrance of the overflowing sweet nectar dripping from blooming golden lotuses,
the hosts of gods daily delight in water-sports.
This is the fruit of bathing the venerable Buddha with various kinds of scented water.
Thus, Maitreya, there is great benefit in meritorious deeds performed toward the Tathāgatas; even a very small amount yields a vast fruit.
Then, at that time, in order to sever the doubts of all those in the assembly who were present, the Blessed One emitted a divine radiance from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
Having illuminated the triple-thousandfold world system with that radiance, it shone as far as the very peak of existence.
In one part of that great city, Dharmakośavatī, there lived a merchant named Dharmamati.

He was very wealthy and possessed of great enjoyments, with an extensive retinue and abundant riches and grain; he was endowed with houses, fields, gardens, male servants, female servants, and messengers.
Then, by that radiance, the entire house, both inside and out, was illuminated.
Then, having touched his body with that radiance,
With a gladdened mind, he speaks.
"Aha! Whose power is this, which has never been before nor will ever be again?
Whom should I ask who is the cause of it?"
Having said this, he became silent.
Then, by means of the light from the net of rays of the Blessed One, he spoke this verse:
For this [account] concerns the power of the Buddha, the Teacher of the World;
therefore, with every effort, perform acts of devotion toward the Buddha. (Dak_7.5)
Therefore, recognize the Buddha as the one who grants liberation to sentient beings,
releasing those submerged in the ocean of existence from the net of afflictions.
A refuge for those who are without protection, a destroyer of disease and sorrow, and a deliverer of all sentient beings from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra. (Dak 7.7)
Having said this, he disappeared.

Then that merchant Dharmamati, having offered worship preceded by an act of homage with flowers, incense, and other offerings born of serene joy toward the Buddha, the Blessed One, scattered a handful of flowers upon the Blessed One.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, all those flowers remained like a pavilion of flowers;
the incense settled like a mass of clouds, and his head was adorned as if with a variegated array of white, blue, yellow, green, and crimson.
Then that merchant, having developed serene confidence in the Buddha, the Blessed One, and having paid homage, remained in comfort while recollecting the Buddha.
Then, because that merchant was short-lived, he passed away and, through the power of his merit, was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Then, having bathed in the Mandākinī together with celestial women, he remains there in the enjoyment of blissful play.

Then, through the ripening of his own merit, having sat within a jeweled gabled chamber, he wandered from heaven to heaven, enjoying himself and sporting; and in due course, he became known as Ratnamatī.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, saw him in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, extolling the praises of the Buddha.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, seeing that the divine son’s peaked pavilion was so well-heated by his roots of merit, replied with a verse:

By whom was your body made to resemble polished gold, and why does your body possess this incomparable splendor like the beauty of a lotus and a blue water-lily? From where has this radiance issued forth from your body?
And by whom was your face made to resemble a blooming lotus, shining with the luster of refined gold?
Tell me, O deity, what is this fruit born of karma that is being experienced?
The divine son Ratnamati said:
That Sun among Men, together with his disciples and adorned with excellent marks,
having performed that wholesome deed, shines even more brilliantly than I;
his face, pure as the moon amidst the waters, is lovely to behold.
Śakra said:
Oh, what a field composed of virtues and free from all defects, wherein you have sown the seed for the sake of attaining the desired heaven! (Dak 7.10)
Who would not worship the Buddha, who is as fair as a magnificent heap of gold, whose beautiful eyes are as long as pure lotuses,
and by whom [the merit] produced through his service is bestowed upon the immortals?
The joys shone forth like the full moon in the heavens.
It is indeed the natural law that three thoughts arise in a son of the gods who has recently been reborn.
From where did he pass away? Where was he reborn? By what karma?
He sees that, having passed away from among humans, he has been reborn among the sublime Trāyastriṃśa gods because he had developed a serene mind toward the Blessed One.
Then this thought occurred to that son of the gods:

"It would not be fitting for me to approach the Blessed One for a visit while my term of exile is still unfulfilled. Thinking thus, that son of the gods— his body radiant in all its limbs, his form anointed with the fragrance of the Jewel-Crest and other perfumes, and surrounded by many thousands of sons of the gods— together with that very same jeweled gabled palace, approached the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, having scattered divine flowers over the Blessed One, he sat down before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of that son of the gods, gave a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths.

Having heard it, that son of the gods shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry;
having seen the truths, he uttered this inspired exclamation three times.
"Venerable Sir, this has not been done for us by our mother, nor by the deities, nor by the king, nor by our circle of beloved ones and kinsmen.

Rather, it is because the Blessed One has dried up the oceans of blood and tears, crossed over the mountains of bones, closed the gates to the states of woe, opened the gates to heaven, and established us among gods and humans. And he said:
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils, has been closed;
the most meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the way to Nirvana has been found by me. (Dak_7.12)
Through reliance upon you, I have today attained the pure vision that is free from all defects;
I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the noble ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods, free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
O Sage, whose sight is so difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes, today your appearance has borne fruit.
Then that son of a god, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, filled with joy, departed for heaven toward the celestial realm.

Then that son of the gods, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer whose crops have ripened, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to his own abode with the very same splendor with which he had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, the monks, their minds filled with doubt, asked the Blessed One:
"What actions were performed and accumulated by that son of the gods such that he possessed such splendor?"
That son of the gods was endowed with only a meager root of merit.
Then the Blessed One, having remained silent for a moment, addressed the entire assembly of monks and spoke as follows:
"O monks, what has become a source of wonder for you? I shall explain its cause; listen."

When a seed is sown in the earth, from it there arises a sprout, and from that a well-grown creeper with beautiful flowers, many branches, many leaves, and fruits; in the world, things of this kind are to be understood in the same way. (Dak 7.15)
For when a seed is sown, the sprout from that seed is indeed great;
just as the sprout from a seed [arises] from the earth, so too does the creeper arise from the surface of the ground, surpassing all other great plants that have grown.
With many branches and leaves, possessing various kinds of flowers, and established with fruits of many different types within its interior.
In the same way, humans plant the most excellent seed in the field of a worthy recipient; the tree born from that is never inferior, it does not go to ruin, and it bears fruit constantly. (Dak_7.16)
Therefore, for any monk, the sprout of a seed is greater than all other seeds; indeed, the seed of merit is the most excellent of seeds. (Dak 7.17)
For what reason?

Monks, in the past, in an age long ago, incalculable eons back, in the country of the Mallas, in the forest of the city of Kuśinagara, there was a single stūpa containing the relics of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. In that city lived a merchant named Śāntamati, who was destitute of wealth, extremely wretched, and utterly poor.
His younger brother was named Vigatamati;
the two of them joined together and, through many efforts, they sought to acquire wealth, yet it was not successful.
For what reason? Because they were devoid of past merit and generosity.
Then, under the teaching of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, there lived a lay follower named Prakṛtipariśuddhi.
Possessing that mind of Dharma, he establishes a mind of compassion and constantly teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings.
Namely as follows:

Whoever, in the future time, shall worship even a relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed, or shall worship a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata— for them, the fear of all karma, including even the unwholesome and painful states arising from malicious speech, shall not prevail.

Whosoever among human beings circumambulate and worship a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata for the sake of avoiding their own faults, they shall, through that act, have the dissolution of faults such as the killing of living beings resulting from negligence regarding what should and should not be approached.
Auspicious is the Dharma, the completely pure Dharma; purified are former evils through the Dharma.
Oh, how wonderful is the Dharma—the supreme noble Dharma, the purifying Dharma, the Dharma that brings about auspiciousness! (Dak_7.18)
Then that poor man, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, was filled with faith and went regularly to listen to the Dharma.
Then his younger brother, devoid of affection, said to his brother:
"Brother, why do you abandon the bounds of propriety? What is the use of hearing the Dharma? It is not possible to live with you."
Having said, "I shall live as one sent by others," he departed from his own home and, acting according to his own will,
became the servant of another.
Then that poor brother, having become agitated in mind due to their separation, nevertheless calmed his own thoughts and remained intent upon reflecting on the teachings of the Dharma.
Then one day, a certain monk, wearing saffron-colored robes and carrying an alms-bowl, stood at the doorways to beg for alms-food.
Seeing him, he quickly entered the house and saw that nothing was there;
there were only a few grains of rice for his own food. Taking them hastily, he gave them to him.
The monk also, having taken it exactly as it was given, said to him:
Even among the poor, there are those whose nature is meritorious; yet among the poor, generosity is rare.
Therefore, by the power of your merit, may your poverty be destroyed.
May it be well with you, O auspicious one; may it destroy all that is inauspicious.
May there be devotion and serene faith in the Buddha, by means of which you may attain rebirth in heaven.
Having said this, he vanished.
Then this thought occurred to that poor man:
"What should I do now? Alas! Shame on my birth and my life!
For one deprived of wealth, death would be better."
Again, this thought occurred to him:
I have heard the Dharma from the lay follower named Prakṛtipariśuddhi:
"Whoever, in the final age, shall worship even a relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed,
or shall worship a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata..."
Their previous karmic obstructions will come to an end.
Through the destruction of evil, the mind becomes purified; through the purification of the mind, the Dharma becomes purified.
Because of the complete purity of the Dharma, the fruit is obtained by that very means.
Thus have I heard: "The Dharma is completely pure."
Then this thought occurred to him:
"I should worship the Tathāgata in such a way. But he too had passed into nirvāṇa; nevertheless, there is a stūpa for his relics, and I should worship that.
Again, this thought occurred to him:
If one is devoid of the complete assembly [of requisites], with what indeed should one worship?
Flowers, incense, likewise perfume, lamps, and food offerings—if worship is performed without these, what fruit of worship is obtained? (Dak_7.22)
Thus the poor man remains, grieving with a dejected mind.
Then, as if with a goad favorable to merit, it urged on that one who had heard the Dharma.
This thought occurred to his mind:
"It would not be fitting for me that I should worship the reliquary stupa of the Tathāgata with mere water, nor perform a bath with it.
Thinking thus, he took an earthen jar, bathed on the riverbank, and with a purified mind, taking up water, he bathed that stupa.
Then, after the lapse of days and months, on one day he went to fetch water for the ritual bathing of the image at the shrine.
Then, having taken water and gone there, he performed his ablutions;
at that time, various kinds of jewels fell from the water-jar. (Dak_7.23)
Then, having seen those things, Śāntamati was filled with serene faith, and this thought arose in his mind:
I pay homage to the stūpa, to the shrine, and to the realm of phenomena;
with a pure mind, I offer precious jewels to the shrine.
Then, having turned back, he proceeded along the bank of the river;
there he saw it strewn with jewels by a poor man.

Having agitated the flow of the river, it cast up its essence— abundant with diamonds, lapis lazuli, pearls, and rubies, as well as karketana, sapphire, topaz, and the like— onto the sandy bank. (Dak 7.26)
Through the power of the Buddha’s merit, even a poor person may, before long,
obtain such gains of jewels as these, which are like a dream.
Then that poor man, having taken those things according to his own desire, returned once more to his own home and, reflecting, said:
"Oh, what a field consisting of virtues and free from all defects!
By serving it for even a very short time, I have attained the fruit-bearing state. (Dak_7.28)
Then that great lake became filled with wealth; it was as if it had been completely filled by the masses of rivers from all directions being poured into it.
From that time forth, honored by the king, the royal ministers, and the brahmins, he became esteemed by virtuous people and beloved by the world.
Excellent, virtuous man! You are renowned throughout this world.
Then that merchant, his mind uplifted and filled with joy and gladness, directed his heart toward the Buddha with serene faith.
Then, after the passing of days and months, this thought occurred to him:
Oh, how the power of the Buddha bestows inconceivable perfection!
A heap of alms has been obtained, and the suffering of poverty has vanished.
Then that merchant, with great honor, had jeweled gabled pavilions constructed for the stūpas.
Having bathed them with various scented waters, circumambulated them three times, and prostrated with his head at their feet, he joined his palms and made this aspiration:
"O Blessed One, may I have such serene confidence in the Tathāgatas in future births, and together with these jeweled gabled pavilions, may I be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Having said this, he constantly attended upon that stūpa.
Then that merchant, having fulfilled his worldly duties and having developed serene faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One, passed away.
Having passed away, he was reborn in the city of Dharmakośavatī as Dharmamati, the preeminent merchant.
Possessing great wealth and vast enjoyments, and endowed with extensive riches and grain, he inspired faith in me during this very life and performed worship with devotion;
all of that he now presents before me.
In the beginning, the waters appeared, shining like a string of pearls;
the flowers were like a heap of blossoms, and the incense remained like a mass of clouds.

Then, because that merchant’s life was short, having inspired faith in the Buddha, he passed away and was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods of exquisite splendor. By the ripening of the fruit of his own merit, he sat within a jeweled gabled chamber and came there this very night;
I have taught him the Dharma.
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, in that age, was that poor man is this very son of the gods named Ratnamati, who, having heard the Dharma from me, returned to his own abode."
In the past, as soon as he had performed a ritual bath for the reliquary stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, he became very wealthy.
Subsequently, he constructed a gabled pavilion made of jewels; by the power of that very vow, he was reborn in the heavenly realms together with that jeweled gabled pavilion.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Discourse on Bathing," within the collection of twenty-two avadānas.
VIII. The Story of the Gift of Saffron and Other Substances.

Now, at one time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by kings, royal ministers, wealthy men, and caravan leaders; he was venerated by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

The Buddha, the Blessed One— renowned, a recipient of great merit, and honored with great veneration for his robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, together with the community of disciples— was being worshipped for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, displaying his own power, taught the Dharma to the assemblies in order to eliminate the pride, intoxication, and arrogance of those whose minds were haughty.
