Having heard that, the people gathered in the assembly were filled with joy.
At that time, in Rājagṛha, there was a certain merchant named Sautīrṇa,
who was very wealthy, possessed of great enjoyments, and had acquired an extensive retinue;
he had brought home a wife from a family equal to his own.
He dwells happily together with her.
He reflects:
"That is not appropriate; rather, our father was one who lived by the fruits of his own actions."
"I too shall do likewise."
"If he was a gambler, I shall act as a gambler;
if he was a merchant of the great ocean, I shall act in that same way."
Then, having heard it being told by someone that "I know our father was a sea-merchant," he thought this and said to his wife:
"Beloved, it is solely by my own karma that I was born into a merchant family; therefore, I wish to go to the great ocean, the mine of jewels.
You should remain at home attending to household duties; do not be afraid.
I shall return before long. For my sake, remember the deity, maintain your fortitude, and do not act rashly."
Having heard that, his wife said:
"Do not say that, O Lord, my husband; how indeed can I remain? For what woman by nature is not distinguished [by her need for protection]? Who protects women in your house? (Dak 8.1)
For whose sake do you seek wealth, since you have no son?
O Lord, be at peace with whatever ancestral property you possess.
What is the use of many material things when only affliction arises from them?
For those possessed by afflictions there is constant suffering in saṃsāra; whence could there be happiness? (Dakārastava 8.3)
For those who possess many possessions, there is constant affliction, suffering, and great fear; therefore, do not exert effort in the pursuit of such useless wealth. (Dakārathama 8.4)
The husband said:
"Do not speak thus, my beloved, for this is my family duty;
one should not abandon the family duty, whether it be low or even great."
For householders in particular, wealth is indeed the very root of embodied beings;
for one who is deprived of wealth, where is there a friend, and where is there happiness? (Dak_8.6)
All women are won over by wealth alone, and even a man is won over by riches;
through wealth one attains honor in the world; therefore, one should acquire wealth. (Dak_8.7)
The wife said:
"O Lord, how can I remain all alone without my protector?
It is like a night devoid of the moon, when the house is shrouded in darkness. (Dak_8.8)
And again:
For, without their husbands, women consort even with others, like birds pecking at lumps of meat fallen upon the ground. (Dak_8.9)
In the realms of existence, there are objects of greed such as women, flowers, and fruits;
whose mind would not be deluded upon seeing women, even if it were not yet subject to rebirth? (Dak_8.10)
How can the untamed elephant of the mind proceed upon the path of the righteous?
For if it should go by a wrong path, it will surely fall into hell. (Dak_8.11)
Especially by a woman is that dharma attained which is so very difficult to obtain;
therefore, O Master, do not go away yourself, abandoning me who am thus terrified. Dak_8.12.
For what reason?
Listen to this single story, O Lord; I have heard it said somewhere regarding my mother that a Brahmin woman becomes a courtesan through a sin conceived in her mind. (Dak 8.13)
The husband said:
"How could a Brāhmaṇī woman born of a noble family become a courtesan, O beloved? This is a wondrous and marvelous thing, occurring merely by being thought of in the mind. (Dakārtha 8.14)
The wife said:
And there was the city of Kośalā, vast and magnificent,
crowded with learned men and graced by virtuous people.
In that city lived a very wealthy Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas; he dwelt there together with his wife, enjoying himself in pleasure and play. (Dak_8.16)
Then, at the tenth division [of his life], that best of the twice-born died,
abandoning his dear friendships and all his prosperity, rendered helpless.
His wife was indeed a Brāhmaṇī woman, yet she was childless and still in her youth;
remembering the virtues of her husband, her mind became distressed. (Dak 8.18)
As the days passed, she became utterly distressed by the separation from her husband and the loss of their love;
though her body was treated with cooling remedies, it felt as if it were burning with a fierce, blazing fire.
What use is a bed of rags from a *kāmalaka* tree, comparable to the bed of a female monkey? And what purpose is served by other such services for it? (Dak 8.20)
Then, having summoned a physician, she was presented to him;
the physician, having grasped her hand, examined the pulse once again. (Dak 8.21)
Seeing this, he then said:
"She is comforted not by medical treatment;
for her, the disease of separation, no physician or medicine will prove effective."
Having reflected thus, that physician returned to his own home, having observed the pulse and taken another [medicine] according to his judgment. (Dak 8.23)
For, as soon as the unconscious woman touched the man with her hand, his heart indeed became cool by that mere touch. (Dak 8.24)
With her heart composed and surrounded by her attendants,
she looked at them all with her eyes and spoke very softly.
"By whom was my hand asked about today, and by whom was my body touched?
O friend, tell me, what is the nature of your well-being and happiness? (Dak_8.26)
The attendants said:
O Lord, without you, physicians have been appointed by those established in their own interests out of mere desire;
for what medicine could one prescribe after seeing the suffering of the sick and the lack of leisure? (Dak 8.27)
The Brahmin woman said:
Whether it be a woman or a man,
whoever has been born healthy within my heart—
such a person born in happiness has, for me, instantly brought peace to their affliction. (Dak 8.28)
The attendants said:
"The physician was not a woman, but a man who heals the world;
having observed merely a vein, he has gone to his own home. The Brahmin wife said: Dak_8.29 Dak_8.29 / The Brahmin wife said:
"Aha! By the mere touch of a man's hand upon my heart, such bliss has arisen; how can there be pleasure for the sake of mere play? (Dak_8.30)
By the mere thought of this,
that practitioner becomes a serpent;
then, having abandoned this life, she is impelled by the winds of karma.
In the beautiful city of Pāṭaliputra, she was born as a courtesan; known by the name Kāmarati, she was adorned with beauty and grace. (Dak 8.32)
In due course, she became a young woman, proud with the intoxication of love; and there, her mother Ratīlolā spoke to her daughter.
"In our family traditions, you must practice the profession of a courtesan;
for with your exceptional beauty and charm, many people will be attracted to you. Daughter, sport with many wealthy men! (Dak_8.34)
From that time forward, Kāmarati repeatedly engaged in the customary practices of her own family.
Then Kāmarati passed away and fell into hell.
"O Lord, I too shall become like that; this I shall say to you."
"Do not fear, O dear beloved! Well said, well said! You shall indeed not become so; therefore, remain firm in your resolve. (Dak 8.35)
Then, disregarding the words of his wife Satīrṇā, he took his merchandise and set out upon the great ocean accompanied by many merchants.
His wife was not yet young, being of middle age and childless;
then, after some years had passed, she became anxious and distressed for the sake of a son and for the sake of her husband, yet her husband did not come back. She said:

"Why has my husband not returned? The merchant has been gone for a long time. Without him, how can there be the birth of a son for me? As my age advances, the extinction of my lineage is certain. (Dak_8.36)
Her husband, Sautīrṇa, has not returned even after a very long time;
with a dejected mind, she remains with the dart of grief fixed in her heart. (Dak 8.37)
Then, with great hospitality, Sautī honored those merchants who had returned;
having offered fragrant substances to the Tathāgata and discarded [the previous] letter, he placed it in the hand of another merchant and sent him away.
Then that merchant handed the letter into the hand of his wife.
Then his wife, having taken the letter,
inquired after his welfare.
"Is my noble husband well? Is all well with every matter?
Have all his affairs been accomplished? May no ailment afflict his body. (Dak_8.38)
He said, "All is well; do not fear," and having spoken, he went to his own home.
Then his wife remained there with her mind full of longing, her thoughts dwelling on the expectation that her husband would arrive.
Then, when he had returned, by the turn of ill fortune,
his ship was destroyed in the ocean of the dissolution.
Then, having recollected it, he uttered the name of the Buddha;
at that very moment his life departed there, and by that act he went to a happy rebirth.
All possessions perish, and even life itself is lost;
no news of him returns, whether he be dead or perhaps restored to life.
Twenty years passed, and he eventually met his end.
As the days passed in succession, she grew old, her hair became white and matted, and she became hunchbacked;
nevertheless, her affection did not perish, and it remained through her constant remembrance of many deities.
Then she thought: "These fragrant perfumes have been sent by my husband for the Buddha, the Sugata. (Dak_8.43)
How shall I worship the Lion of the Śākyas, that ocean of virtues,
now that King Ajātaśatru has forbidden the worship of the Buddha?
Then she thought: "Standing upon the roof-peak of the palace, I shall worship the Tathāgata with sandalwood ointments. (Dak_8.45)
Then, with a mind full of devotion and great joy,
she worshipped the mandala with sandalwood paste along with flowers.
Then, having joined her palms in reverence and bowed down, she spoke again with respect: "Is my husband dead, or is he perhaps still alive? (Dak_8.47)
Not even news of him has arrived; how is this, O Blessed One, O Sage?
You are omniscient and all-seeing; there is nothing that remains unknown to you. (Dak 8.48)
"O Lord, O Sage, you will grant me a vision of yourself—whether it be as 'is' or 'is not';
for a longing to behold my husband’s lotus-like face has arisen within me. (Dak 8.49)
Having thus made her request, she passed those days;
then, for the sake of rest at night, she went indeed to the dwelling of her own home. (Dak 8.50)
Then the Blessed One, the All-Knowing, perceiving her intention and manifesting his own power, spoke with a Brahma-like voice through his supernormal power: "Well-spoken! (Sautīrṇam).
Your wife has already crossed over; she does not know that you have passed away.
Therefore, assuming a divine form, descend from heaven and manifest a dream of your celestial body.
Thus, from the moment that thought arose, having beheld the divine body of the Blessed One— the merchant who had crossed over—
the nature of things (dharmatā) is such that three thoughts arise in one who has recently been reborn.
From where did he pass away, how was he reborn here, and by what karma?
He saw that, having passed away from among humans, he had been reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three due to his gift of saffron and other offerings to the Blessed One.
Then the divine son Sugandhamukha— his body adorned with swinging, stainless earrings, necklaces, and half-necklaces, his crest-jewel of gems,
and his limbs decorated with saffron, tamāla-leaf paste, and other unguents— having pervaded four *krośas* with his fragrant scent during that very night,
descended from the heavenly world wherever he went and settled in the storehouse of his wife.
Then she saw this dream.
The husband said:
"O beloved, know this: your husband's death is certain for me alone.
You do not understand; do not be afraid—he has come here from the heavenly realm."
Not by anything other than the power of the Buddha, nor through the offering of saffron and the like, but having enjoyed the bliss of the divine realm, I abide in the play of happiness. (Dak 8.52)
Those humans who offer Kāśmīra saffron and gośīrṣa sandalwood to that most excellent Sugata will indeed obtain fragrant bodies in the abodes of the immortals.
With a mind full of faith toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and likewise the Saṅgha, be heedful;
act in such a way that you may, before long, attain the auspicious path as I have described.
Thus, through the power of the Jina, having instructed his own wife in the Dharma, he returned to his own abode.
Then, having seen such a dream and awakened, she was overcome with great wonder and her mind became agitated by grief.

Then, rising from her seat and reflecting again in her mind, she realized this was a true dream; with the hairs on her body bristling from grief, her frame trembled, and surely tears flowed from her eyes. (Dak_8.55)
Then, having attained composure, he indeed bowed to the Sugata:
"Protect me, O Blessed One, Teacher; O Lord, grant me your favor! (Dak_8.56)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the supreme Sugata, being well-pleased,
performed the maṇḍala as before and was worshipped for eight days.
Then, by the power of time, she too met her death and was reborn as a divine maiden among the well-governed Thirty-three gods.
At that time, there was a daughter of the gods named Sugandhagandhinī;
she remained for a long time in heaven with her husband in perfect happiness.
Then, having conversed with the Blessed One and offered him saffron and other gifts, the two were reborn in the worlds of the gods.
Therefore, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One to attend upon him and speak with him.
Then the divine sons and daughters, Sugandhamukha and his consort, having suffused four *krośas* with their fragrant scent,

illuminated the entire great monastery of Jetavana with a sublime radiance during that very night; they filled the Blessed One with rains of sandalwood and other sweet perfumes and sat before the Blessed One to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition and nature of the two devaputras, Sugandha and Mukha, delivered such a Dharma teaching that penetrates the four noble truths;

upon hearing it, those two, the man and the woman, shattered with the vajra of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, he uttered this inspired utterance three times:

"Venerable Sir, this which has been done for us by the Blessed One was not done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our circle of beloved kinsmen and relatives, nor by our ancestors, nor by recluses and brahmins.
The doors to the states of misery have been closed, and the doors to heaven have been established."
Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many evils, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the way to Nirvāṇa has been found by me. (Dak_8.60)
Through reliance upon you, I have today obtained a ship free from defect and attained the most pure vision;
I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the Noble Ones and crossed to the further shore of this ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods, free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
O Sage, whose sight is so difficult to obtain even in thousands of lifetimes, today your appearance has become fruitful.
Having bowed down and paid homage at the two feet of the Blessed One, filled with joy and announcing, "We shall now depart," they departed for heaven, facing toward the world of the gods.
Now, monks, while they were dwelling devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first watch of the night,
they saw a magnificent radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having seen it, they were filled with doubt and questioned the Blessed One.
"Blessed One, has Brahmā Sahāpati, or Śakra the lord of the gods, or the four world-protectors approached the Blessed One for a vision this night?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it was neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the Lord of Devas, nor even the four World-Protectors who approached me for a vision; rather,
it was that merchant Sautīrṇa who had set out upon the great ocean."
Then, after that merchant had crossed over, he gave me fragrant substances such as saffron and sent another man in his place.
When the merchant returned, by the turn of ill fortune, his ship was wrecked in the midst of the great ocean; having fallen into the sea, he passed away.

His wife was a celestial maiden named Sugandhagandhinī; having become devoted to me, she stood upon the roof-peak of the palace and worshipped me for eight days with fragrant substances such as saffron,
and she made this aspiration.
"O Sugata, please send me to the place where my masters are.
By the power of that meritorious aspiration, she was reborn among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
They approached my presence during this very night; I taught the Dharma to them, and having seen the truths, they returned to their own abode.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"One should do what is beneficial to the Three Jewels and not what is harmful. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves during my lifetime and after my parinirvāṇa.
Then, monks, having become filled with doubt, they questioned the Blessed One.
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that he has now crossed over [to safety], yet these items such as saffron and other fragrant goods were sent,
and without having obtained a sight of you, he passed away in the midst of the ocean?"
The Blessed One said:
Listen, O monks!
Long ago, monks, there was a certain regional king.

Not far from him, on the bank of a river called Ajiravatī, in a delightful and expansive area adorned with various trees and shrubs along the flowing stream, there lived a seer named Dharmaruci. He used to go regularly to hear the Dharma.

Then once, having heard public rumor that fear had been instilled in wild animals along the path to the hermitage of a sage, the king, having equipped himself with bow and arrows, went to the hermitage accompanied by his attendants.
Upon reaching the hermitage, he paid homage to the preceptor and remained there comfortably, engaged in various pleasant conversations and stories.
Then that sage, seeing the bow and arrow, spoke to the king.
"Enough of this, O King; having prepared your bow and arrows, you have arrived. I am not wicked."
Or have you perhaps become afraid upon seeing me, O King?
Then that king, having massaged Karṇa and paid his respects, said:

"O Teacher, do not speak thus; it was not out of fear or despondency toward you, but rather, having heard public rumor that fear had been instilled in a wicked creature at the edge of the road, I have come."
Then the seer said:
"Do not grieve, O King, for in these essence-less cycles of existence, one may become an offender through mere negligence; thus it was said to you, O Lord of the Earth. (Dak 8.63)
At times when one has fallen into distress, even though one sees, one does not see;
even though one has heard it, it is not realized by you. Therefore, O Upholder of the Earth, this has been said.
If someone were to strike you with a weapon while you yourself were harming some living beings,
you should then become composed and act with a firm mind.
O King, listen further as to why you have been thus instructed:
if one strikes with a weapon when the life-force has already departed without cause, [it is a grave offense].
Indeed, by that suffering of the living being, through its lamentations and wailing, it surely causes further cursing;
for it becomes a thorn of fault.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; non-violence is the supreme austerity;
non-violence is the supreme knowledge; non-violence is the supreme state.
Then that king, saying "So be it; it is indeed true," bowed at the feet of his guru and returned with his companions, diverting himself on the road with various stories.
Then, having emerged from the river,
he was seen when he had reached its middle;
at midday, scorched by the rays of the sun, he saw a female deer resting in the shade of a tree after drinking water.
Then, suddenly forgetting his teacher’s words, the king pierced that female deer with an arrow;
he had pierced the arrow into her belly.
Then the female deer, with a human voice, spoke thus to the king:
Excellent, excellent, O Great King! You have performed a supreme vow;
you are a bull among kings, of the noblest divine lineage, and most righteous.
"I am not a human being, O best of men, but a doe living within your domain; I have grown old on the grass and water belonging to you. How then, O King, could I trouble you? (Dak 8.70)

O King, since by relying upon you—who are the abode of Lakṣmī—you have attained a kingship esteemed by the world, and since you are the protector of the world in times of calamity and fear, how is it that you have been pierced by my arrow? (Dakṣa 8.71)
"For I would have been of the animal species, weak and submerged in the river of ignorance;
my food, sexual union, and sleep—such is the way of beasts, O King. (Dak_8.72)
"You are not one whose authority is limited to a single dharma; you are the judge of both dharma and adharma, renowned as a protector of the earth and praised by all the world. (Dak_8.73)
O Great King, you who possess such power are the protector and lord of the weak and the distressed; how then have you been robbed of your life from me? Dak_8.74.
"I am heavy with child due to these special circumstances; what will become of the one dwelling in my womb?
I might not see his face, and therefore he shall not see my face. (Dak 8.75)
And again:
I am not of the lion species, nor of the tiger species, nor of the bear species, nor indeed of the sow;
I am not of the wolf species, nor of any cruel species. For what reason have you pierced me with your own arrow?
O King, such is the conduct prescribed for hunters who are fierce, cruel, shameless, untruthful, and wicked. (Dak 8.77)
Then, having heard these words, the king was like one pierced by a dart; with a faltering throat, he was unable to give a reply.
Having remained silent there for a moment, that king spoke to the female deer.
"What do you think, O doe? Even now, though I have come for the hunt, I am not stained by transgression; the word of my guru is not otherwise. (Dak 8.78)
Just like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, having encountered this [opportunity], you have acted with joy;
it was done neither by a cruel mind nor out of a state of hatred.
The female deer said:
What do you think, Great King: through your clarity of faith, do you regard your own body and the bodies of others as exactly equal? (Dak 8.80)
O King, how is it that you do not know the happiness and suffering of all beings?
For you are indeed the taker of my life; what more need be said than this?
Having said this, that doe passed away.

Then her husband, the deer, arrived; having caught her scent, he looked about, and seeing her body lying dead like a severed trunk, he suddenly fell to the ground. Gradually regaining his senses, he uttered various piteous lamentations with the most profound sorrow.
Alas! O you who delight my life, how can you depart all alone?
Having abandoned me now, by whom and for what reason have you been struck down there?
With equal straightforwardness and equal knowledge, and possessing prowess equal to my own, how could I forget your virtues and consider this forest so terrifying? 8.83.
There are no other friends for you; indeed, you have but one beloved. Now that you have cast aside affection, how is it that your life has been lost?
Then he spoke to the king.
"This woman is as dear to me as my own life; she is my wife, who has taken away my very existence.
She is a woman for whom I have the greatest affection—how could she have taken away your life? (Dak 8.85)
Then that deer was cursed by him.
Just as my wife was struck down and killed by you while standing in the middle of the river, so may you meet your death in the middle of the ocean.
"May I become one of the lowest caste among the four castes," saying this, the deer slowly returned to his own hermitage.
"What do you think, monks? At that time, on that occasion, I was the seer;
he who was Sautīrṇa was the king."
Due to a deer's curse, he became a merchant and passed away in the midst of the ocean;
however, by recollecting the name of the Buddha with joy and through the gift of saffron and other offerings, he was reborn among the gods.
Monks, there is great merit in giving fragrances such as saffron to the Tathāgatas; indeed, there is great merit in giving fragrances to the Tathāgatas.
And listen again.

The Lord of the Gods repeatedly plunges into the Mandākinī— the river of the world's supreme being— which is expanded by the hands, breasts, hips, and thighs of the playful women at its bathing-gates, and which possesses full-blown, radiant lotuses,
out of reverence for that Supreme One. He does so again and again with his beloved wives, who are overwhelmed by passion.
The fruit [of this] arises from the offering of scented water, water for the feet, incense, flowers, garlands, and perfumes. (Dakārikā 8.86)

When the universal monarch, experiencing supreme physical bliss in the Gaṅgā— which is joined with streams of saffron water that move through the sky, fragrant with the scent of camphor and cooled by contact with the fragrance of sandalwood— rejoices together with beautiful women.
Therefore, by the renunciation of saffron and other such things, [one should offer them] to the Buddha, the venerable Lord, who is a treasury of a multitude of virtues.
Having performed worship to the supreme Sugatas with the sounds of clay drums, lutes, and kettledrums, one hears the voices of gods and humans and attains a distinguished, divine ear. (Dak_8.88)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Story of the Gift of Saffron and Other Items," in the glorious *Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā*.
IX. The Discourse on the Gift of Parasols.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way: "Blessed One, those who offer a magnificent parasol to the Buddhas or to their stūpa-images..."
O Lord Sugata, please tell us: what would be the fruit of those [deeds]?
When this had been said, the Blessed One remained silent for a moment,

and then he manifested this great sign in order to display his own power, to bring about the worship of the Buddha, and to produce mental clarity in the minds of those who were not yet clear-minded toward the Buddha. Immediately thereafter, the great earth shook in six ways.
As far as the subterranean realm of Rasātala and even unto Mount Sumeru,
such wonders as these and others occur.
Namely as follows:
Narrow places become wide;
elephants trumpet and horses neigh.
Various musical instruments within the houses resounded of their own accord;
the blind regained their sight, and the deaf recovered their hearing.
The mute become capable of speech;
those with impaired faculties obtain complete faculties;
and the insane become free from their delusions.
Those afflicted by poison become free from poison;
those who harbor mutual enmity attain loving-kindness;
and pregnant women give birth safely.
Those bound by fetters are liberated from their bonds;
those without wealth obtain riches;
and the hungry have their bellies filled.
Those afflicted by disease become free from their ailments,
and the gods dwelling in the intermediate space release a rain of divine flowers.
(Dak: 87) Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having directed his vision of knowledge downward, descended from the heavenly realm at that very moment.

For the sake of honoring the Blessed One, he himself held a divine parasol made of gold and jewels of immense proportions and arrived there on Vulture Peak Mountain together with hosts of gods, while ten million drums resounded.
Making a sound.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, beheld the Blessed One, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, blazing with glory like a mountain of gold. The Blessed One was covered by parasols made of gold and jewels;
having circumambulated him three times and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down before the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed them with a discourse on the Dharma, inspired them and gladdened them.
Impermanent is cyclic existence, impermanent is the treasury, impermanent are friends along with sons and wives;
impermanent is the king and various enjoyments—everything in cyclic existence is indeed impermanent.
"Generosity is an ornament in the world; generosity wards off miserable rebirths;
generosity is a staircase to heaven; generosity is auspicious and brings peace.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with his retinue, having heard the Dharma, returned once more to the celestial realm.
(Dak: 88) Immediately thereafter, the members of the assembly, their minds informed by that cause,
and having understood their disposition, the monks, filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Blessed One, where were these roots of merit performed, from which such worship as this for the Blessed One and the community of monks has arisen?"
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in other previous births; their conditions have been gathered, their causal factors have matured, they have arrived like a rushing torrent, and they are inevitable.
Since I performed and accumulated these actions, who else shall experience their results?"
Monks, deeds performed—whether auspicious or inauspicious—are not ripened in the element of earth, nor in water, fire, or air.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, in the great city of Kṣamāvatī, there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One named Kṣemaṃkara, who now dwells together with his disciples.
Now at that time, in a certain district, there was a royal capital— delightful,

prosperous through supernatural power, well-supplied with food, crowded with a multitude of people, and filled with learned men. In that royal capital, there was a great Kṣatriya who had been consecrated on the head.
Possessed of great heroism and supremely righteous, the King of Dharma governed the kingdom in accordance with the Dharma.
Then that great consecrated Kṣatriya, having heard the spoken eulogy and praise of the Tathāgata Kṣemaṃkara, attained supreme faith.

Then, at that very moment, having prepared various articles for worship, he dispatched a messenger to extend the invitation with the speed of a horse, the speed of an elephant, and the speed of a chariot. Arriving there in due course, he made his request to the Tathāgata.

"O Blessed One, Kṣemaṃkara, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the great consecrated kṣatriya, has sent an invitation to you; O Great Sage, may you come today on the fourth day together with your disciples and the assembly."
Having spoken thus and prostrated before the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara, he returned to his own realm.
Then, on the fourth day, that great consecrated kṣatriya, having prepared flowers, incense, perfumes, parasols, banners, and flags,
offered a handful of flowers.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, those flowers became spread over the head of the Tathāgata Kṣemaṃkara.
Then, monks, they asked the perfectly enlightened Buddha Kṣemaṃkara:
"Venerable Blessed One, from where has this invitation come?"
The perfectly enlightened one, Kṣemaṃkara, spoke thus.
"A great kṣatriya, consecrated by royal aspersion, has extended an invitation;
we must go there. Let the monks prepare themselves! (Dak 9.2).

Then, on the fourth day, the Tathāgata Kṣemaṃkara, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surrounded by a multitude of monks— the Blessed One Kṣemaṃkara, who was self-controlled with a self-controlled retinue, peaceful with a peaceful retinue, liberated with a liberated retinue, marvelous with a marvelous retinue, disciplined with a disciplined retinue, and an Arhat with an Arhat retinue— [proceeded].
Free from passion, he was surrounded by a retinue free from passion; serene, he was surrounded by a serene retinue— like a bull surrounded by a herd of cattle,
like an elephant surrounded by a troop of calves,
like a lion surrounded by a pack of fanged beasts.
Like a royal swan surrounded by a flock of swans;
like Suparṇin surrounded by a flock of birds;
like a brahmin surrounded by a group of disciples.
Like the horse Bālāha surrounded by a host of steeds;
like a guide surrounded by a company of travelers;
like a hero surrounded by a host of warriors.
Like a caravan leader surrounded by a multitude of merchants;
like a guild-president surrounded by the citizens;
like a provincial king surrounded by a host of ministers.
Like a universal monarch surrounded by a thousand sons;
like the moon surrounded by the host of stars;
like the sun surrounded by a thousand rays.
Like Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by hosts of Gandharvas;
like Virūḍhaka surrounded by hosts of Kumbhāṇḍas;
like Virūpākṣa surrounded by hosts of Nāgas.
Like Kubera surrounded by hosts of yakṣas;
like Vemacitra surrounded by hosts of asuras;
like Śakra surrounded by hosts of the thirty-three gods.
Like Brahmā surrounded by the Brahmakāyika gods, like a tranquil ocean, like a rain-bearing cloud with its water, or like a lordly elephant free from rut,
he moved about with his senses perfectly subdued and his deportment undisturbed.

Accompanied by many followers of the host of gods, praised by various sons of gods, and heralded by the sounds of songs and musical instruments, the Blessed One Kṣemaṃkara arrived at that royal capital. King Mahākṣatriya, the consecrated monarch, heard that the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara had arrived at their royal capital; and having heard this, endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, he went toward [the Blessed One].
The Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kṣemaṃkara, approached him; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kṣemaṃkara and sat down to one side.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One, Kṣemaṃkara, exhorted the consecrated Kṣatriya king with the dharmas that bring about awakening.
Then that king, having conceived faith, invited the perfectly enlightened Kṣemaṃkara to the royal palace and served him with food of a hundred flavors.
He covered [the Buddha] with a golden parasol worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Then the Blessed One, Kṣemaṃkara, the perfectly awakened one, began to rain down the rain of Dharma.
Excellent, excellent, Great King! By means of this supreme vow of great merit,
the lowering of the parasol,
such a fruit as this is obtained.
That a universal monarch travels through the sky with elephants, horses, foot-soldiers, and chariots, accompanied by his thousand sons and the seven precious jewels,
while the rays of the sun are blocked by the parasol resembling the halo of the moon—
that too is a noble fruit produced from the gift of a parasol.

With the rays of the sun obscured by their golden parasols, seated upon the shoulders of majestic, well-trained elephants, adorned with excellent ornaments of many jewels, and rivaling the splendor of Śakra,
these sovereigns who rule over the four continents travel through the sky with effortless ease.
That is the fruit resulting from the offering of flowers and parasols at a reliquary stūpa of a Tathāgata.
(93) Listen again in detail:

By the gift of a parasol to the Tathāgatas, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), a righteous king of dharma who has conquered with his fourfold army and is endowed with the seven jewels. They are as follows:
The wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the woman-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure;

thus he is endowed with these seven treasures. Furthermore, the universal monarch has a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, handsome in form, and crushers of enemy armies. He is thus possessed of a thousand sons.
Having completely conquered this great earth, including the oceans—making it entirely free of thorns, without the use of force or weapons—he shall dwell upon it.
He will rule the kingdom righteously as if the earth were a single city.
"In such a form you shall become a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakravartin), a lord of the four continents," he thus prophesied.
The Blessed One, by means of his supernatural power, returned to his own monastery through the path of the sky just as he had come.
Then that king had a stūpa built for the Tathāgata who had entered parinirvāṇa, measuring one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
A large parasol was set out and honored.
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king—was he someone else? It was I myself.

Because I placed an umbrella with faith upon the stūpas of the Perfectly Awakened One Kṣemaṃkara, having thus performed such worship, I became a universal monarch and experienced infinite happiness within saṃsāra."
Now, by that very same Śakra, the lord of the gods, such honor and worship as this has been paid to this Tathāgata, together with the parasol.
Therefore, monks, knowing the Buddha, the Blessed One, to be the Teacher, you too must show him honor.
Likewise, during my lifetime and after my parinirvāṇa, even toward beings in saṃsāra, such noble speech as this should be inferred.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Story of the Gift of the Parasol, within the *Puṇyaprasādana* collection of twenty-two avadānas.
X. Discourse on the Planting of the Seed-potential.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:

O Blessed One, having heard your words on the benefits of the parasol, I have attained great joy. Furthermore, O Lord, Ocean of Wisdom, please tell me: what is the fruit for those who place relics within a stūpa dedicated to the nature of the Jina?
At that time, that Blessed One also dwelt right here on Vulture Peak for the sake of compassion for the world.
The Blessed One said:
Excellent! Listen, O Great Being, to the fruit arising from the enshrinement of the relics;
I shall describe that merit and its distinction for the sake of all-enlightenment. (Dak_10.2)
For example, at one time in the southern region, a king named Dharmakalpa reigned.

His kingdom was prosperous and flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, riots, and tumults, devoid of thieves and disease, abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, and he governed his realm as if it were an only son dear to him.
At a later time, he played, took pleasure, and amused himself with the queen.
While he was thus playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, after the lapse of a month, a son was born who was handsome and beautiful to behold.
Gracious, having transcended human appearance and possessing a complexion endowed with the divine elements, he illuminated the entire city with this radiance.
Upon seeing him, his parents, other members of the world, the assembly of ministers, and the beings who had come out of curiosity were struck with great wonder and thought,
"From where has such a distinguished being come?"
Then, at that time, the village headmen and the officials appointed over the districts of that king came to the king and said:
"O Great King, in various places within your realm, floods of treasure have appeared."
Some say they were born as those who had emerged from a submerged hoard of gold.
Some say they were born from a flood of silver as their cause.
Some say they were born immersed in a treasure of jewels.
In this way, eight other successive leaps of the treasure were produced.
"What shall be the name of the boy? they asked.
The kinsmen said:
Oh, the power of merit! For by his very birth, with a radiance clinging to the [nine] elements, (Dak: 97)
The entire city was illuminated;
moreover, eight deposits of relics (dhātu) emerged.
Therefore, let the boy’s name be Dhātustejarāja-kumāra; thus his name was established.
Thereupon, through various excellent provisions, he grew rapidly like a lotus in a pond.

That wise, discerning, intelligent, faithful, auspicious, and noble-minded youth was intent upon his own welfare and the welfare of others; he was compassionate, high-souled, righteous, a lover of dharma, and by nature affectionate toward his subjects.

Later, at another time, intoxicated by the pride of his physical form and overcome by great strength, he became deeply curious about the extent of his own kingdom’s domain and set out to see what else existed therein.

Accompanied by great royal splendor, making the sounds of various musical instruments resound, surrounded by his retinue and attendants, and encircled by thousands of mares and thousands of elephants, he went forth with such magnificence that he rivaled Śakra and was treated with honors befitting Śakra.
Then, he heard the report that the king was coming to show his presence throughout the village and the countryside.
Then all the people, having prepared all the articles and provisions according to their respective capacities, approached the king and honored him with the enjoyment of all those things.
(Dak: 98) Then that element of splendor arrived at a ground with a most extensive and level surface not far from here.
Thereupon, the king’s mind became eager to sport with the speed of a horse.
Then he allowed the king’s companions to rest there;
then the king exerted the speed of his horse a second and even a third time.
Then, carried away by the horse with extreme speed, he traveled until,
having been abandoned by the horse in a most distant land, the king fell into a swoon;
a fainting fit came over him.
In an instant, the king regained consciousness;
the horse had vanished from sight.
Then all the accompanying people, having lost sight of the king and being broken in heart, turned back.
Then that king,
not knowing the path by which he had returned and being ignorant even of the directions,
left that realm of his own will and went elsewhere to a distant land.
Then the king saw a city named Ramaṇaka not far from there,
and he approached it;
as he did so, four apsarases emerged— beautiful, lovely to behold, and gracious— and they spoke.
"Come, O element of fire! Welcome to you!

This is our house of food, house of drink, house of clothing, and house of bedding, filled with jewels, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of gold and silver; come, we shall enjoy ourselves."
Having agreed, saying "So be it," he experienced pleasure with them for many years.
Nevertheless, because that being had performed meritorious deeds and cultivated virtue,
they restrained him from proceeding along the southern path.
The more he was turned back from the southern route, the more intensely he longed to go;
and as he continued following the southern path, he again beheld a city named Sadāmatta.
There, acting as a gateway, eight even more beautiful, more lovely, and more pleasing celestial nymphs emerged from that place and said:
"Come, O Dhātutejas! Welcome to you!

Here is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of beds and seats; it is filled with jewels, pearls, diamonds, beryls, conchs, crystals, corals, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves!"
He experienced pleasure with them for many years;
nevertheless, because that being had performed merit and cultivated wholesome deeds,
even they could not obstruct his path toward the right course.
The more he was turned back from the southern path, the more intensely he yearned to go;
yet, as he continued on the southern road, he again beheld a city named Nandana.
He became their gateway until sixteen more celestial nymphs emerged from there, even more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more gracious than the previous ones.
They said: "Come, O Dhātutejas! Welcome to you!

Here is our house of food, our house of drink, our house of clothing, and our house of beds and seats; it is filled with jewels, pearls, diamonds, beryls, conchs, crystals, corals, and various kinds of gold and silver. Come, let us enjoy ourselves!"
He experienced delight with them for many years;
nevertheless, because that being had performed merit and cultivated wholesome deeds,
even they could not obstruct his path toward the right course.
The more he was restrained from the southern path, the more intensely he yearned to go.
Then, proceeding again by the southern path, he saw a palace named Brahmottara.
Having approached its gate, he saw thirty-two apsarases emerge from it—more beautiful, more lovely to behold, and more gracious than those before—and they said:
"Come, O Dhātutejas! Welcome to you!"

"This is our house of food, house of drink, house of clothing, and house of bedding; it is filled with jewels, pearls, diamonds, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, and silver. Come, we shall enjoy ourselves."
He experienced delight with them for many years;
nevertheless, because that being had performed merit and cultivated wholesome deeds,
even they could not obstruct his path of generosity.
The more he is turned back from the southern path,
the more intensely he yearns to go.
Just as he was proceeding along the southern path, from that path he saw, as he continued on the southern road, a vast expanse of burning sand;
then he approached the shores and beheld the sand glowing with flames as if scorched by fire.
Seeing that, and with his mind overwhelmed, he thought: "How can I go?
Where indeed, O friend, shall I go?"
While he was thus situated, a fierce creature arrived;
it was neither a horse, nor a donkey, nor a camel, nor a cow, for its facial form was unlike any of these.
A single creature approached him and said:
"O Mānava, let me descend onto your back; for how can I travel upon this ground of sand?
If your foot, as delicate as wheat, were to tread here, it would surely shatter as if struck by a mallet."
Therefore, mount upon my back; I shall carry you to the opposite shore.
He then descended, and as he was being carried away with speed,
that creature reached the shore at that very moment and vanished.
(Dak: 102) Then, traveling by the southern path, he sees something blazing at a certain place;
he is tormented by that flame.
He asked, "By what karma?"
"I was the fire that burned the forest;
it was due to that karma."
He is seen once again,
being incessantly devoured and shrieking by crows, vultures, and other scavengers.
He asked: "Who was he, and by what karma?"
He said:
"I am a betrayer of trust;
it is because of that deed."
Furthermore, he was seen eating a glowing iron ball that he was forcing into his mouth.
He said: "Who is he?"
"By means of stealing the property belonging to the Saṅgha."
He is seen once again,
crying out as he proceeds with his feet shattered along a path of iron that has been heated until it blazes with an even sharper edge.
Having seen him, he said:
What are those of such a kind?
And he said:
They break the bridge of Dharma on a treacherous river or on a crooked path;
it is by that karma [that they suffer].
(Dak: 103) Again, two women with disheveled hair stood there, gnawing on their own knees with their teeth.
He said:
"Which women? Or by what deed?
They replied:
"One who does not give, being devoid of skill."
Food was not obtained for twelve years.
Again, going further inward from here, he sees a *śālmalī* tree covered with iron thorns eight finger-breadths long, which he cries out against as he becomes entangled in them.
He said:
Who is this?
And he said:
"One who is addicted to approaching another's wife."

Proceeding again along this southern path, he sees a woman whose two feet are bound with a rope, who is suspended by her neck, and whose hair is tied in a knot with a rope and hung from a tree; she is being devoured intensely at the hips by iron-tusked beasts.
Seeing her, he said: "Who is such as this?"
She said: "Yes."
Having treated one's own master with contempt, he delights in the prowess of others.
(Dak: 104) Again, traveling further along this southern path, he sees [a being] with an iron wheel whirling upon its head; from that head, pus and blood flow forth.
Seeing him, he said: "Who is this person? Why is he so difficult to endure and so full of suffering?"
He said to him:
"Because of my offense against my mother, I am experiencing this unbearable suffering.
Then, traveling again along the southern path from there,
he sees [a being] with a massive body, resembling the interior of a mountain of great height.
His limbs are covered with his own hair, and his mouth is like the eye of a needle.
Seeing him, he said:
"Who is this one of such fierce form and terrifying appearance?"
He said to him:
"I do not give even a small amount of a gift to anyone,
because of the stinginess that obstructs giving."
Again, traveling further along this southern path, he sees sparks of fire raining down upon his head; he is tormented by great thirst.
Seeing him, he said, "Aha! By what deed has this been brought about? He replied:
I do not give water to anyone who has come, afflicted by thirst, to drink.
If he were to go again to drink from it, then he too, having taken up mud and stirred it about, would make the water turbid; for that reason, this suffering arises.
Then King Dhātuseṇa, having reflected that he was certain to go to the next world, turned away from that southern region and returned to his own kingdom.
Then, because his father, the king, had not returned for a long time and presumed him to have passed away, he had a palace built in his son's name.
Various musical instruments—drums, *mṛdaṅgas*, *tāḍas*, *jhallas*, lutes, flutes, *mukuṇḍas*, trumpets, and so forth—as well as parasols, banners, and yak-tail whisks, were placed atop the palace.
And these syllables have been written and set down:
"If the prince Dhātusteja is still alive,
by his auspicious merit, for the sake of his swift return."
Then, having passed away and reached the end of his life, he does so for the sake of attaining a specific state of rebirth.
Having written these syllables in this manner, they were placed upon those [lines].
Then King Dhātustejas, having seen [the body] and not having had it marked by the citizens, was not questioned by anyone.
Then, as he wandered all around, that Dhātu Tejorāja beheld a palace constructed with his own name.

Filled with curiosity upon seeing his own name inscribed there, he reflected: "Aha! My parents, thinking I was already dead, have built this temple with my name and an image of me. He thought, "Now that my father, the king, has done this, how might I see him face-to-face once again?"
For this reason, his mind found no delight in staying there.
Having said, "I shall accomplish the path to liberation and absolute isolation," he departed from that place and traveled elsewhere toward Magadha.
Then, at that time, the beings of Magadha were coming toward Vulture Peak;
thereupon, by the power of those relics, they were seen and asked by him, "Where are you going, sirs?"
They said, "Let us go to Vulture Peak to see the Buddha, the Blessed One."
Hearing the previously unheard name "Buddha, the Light of the World," all his pores bristled with hair and a supreme curiosity arose within him.
This thought occurred to him:
"What if I were also to go to see the Blessed Buddha? And so, he too went to Vulture Peak together with the people.
Then he beheld the Blessed Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, adorned with a celestial luster, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns.

Seeing him, who was auspicious on all sides like a moving mountain of jewels, he was filled with serene faith; having prostrated his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down before him to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood his disposition, delivered a Dharma teaching that penetrates the Four Noble Truths.
Having heard this, he was filled with faith and said this to the Blessed One:
Blessed One, please grant me a prophecy;
grant me a prophecy regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One said:

"Noble son, in the world-system named Dhātuśikhara, you shall become the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, by the name Dhātutejas."
Having heard the prophecy, he undertook the going forth into homelessness.
At that very moment, he directly attained the state of an Arhat.
(Dak: 108) Then, having seen that, the monks were filled with wonder and asked the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, who is this person whom you have prophesied for perfect enlightenment?"
The Blessed One said:
In the southern region, there was a king named Dharmakalpa, possessed of great majesty and most righteous;
this [prince] was the son of that king.
The monks said:
"Venerable sir, what deeds were performed by him, such that he is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing, and has realized the splendor of the state of an Arhat through going forth?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one kalpas ago, a Perfectly Awakened One named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—

endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He dwelt residing near the great royal capital city of Bandhumatī.
Then that Blessed One, having completed all the works of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
Thereupon, King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral rites for the body, caused a stupa one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height to be built.
At that time, a certain son of a merchant, having seen him and being moved by faith, took various reliquaries made of great gold, silver, and jewels prepared by his father,
and deposited the relic within the interior of that stūpa of Vipaśyin.
He made this aspiration:
"By means of this merit, may I receive the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment from the final Tathāgata in the future time, the final period, the final age."
By virtue of the roots of merit cultivated by that son, his father became a king named Dharmakalpa in the southern region;
his son was Dhātustejas, who had also been father and son in a previous birth.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the merchant’s son, is this very Dhātustejarāja.
Because he deposited relics in the stūpa of Vipaśyin, by that cause he has become handsome, pleasing, and most beautiful to behold."
"Arhatship has been realized."
I, too, have been prophesied for perfect enlightenment.
The Blessed One spoke again.
Maitreya, there are great benefits; monks, there are great benefits for those who enshrine relics within the stūpas and images of the Tathāgata—the benefits and fruits thereof are not few.
Listen to that.
At that moment, firmly established on the ground of the perfections of a Sugata, his fame is proclaimed throughout the world, and he becomes the refuge for the entire realm of sentient beings.
If a relic is placed by people within an image of the Victor, supported by an excellence of nature that is exceedingly lofty and stable; Dak_10.4 //
Having attained sovereignty over Śakrī and having enjoyed the splendor and the four continents,
those lords of men finally attain the pure state through their dedication to the element of the Victor.

It is seen that there are mortals in the world of men who are radiant, with faces like the moon, beautiful brows, and long eyes; who resemble excellent gold and are endowed with patience and gentleness;
and who, as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), protect the earth clothed by the oceans.
All that occurs within the image of the Buddha for embodied beings who, with devotion, have projected their own elements [into it]. (Dak 10.6)
Therefore, monks, after my passing, when the world is without a leader, this sutra must be taught.
Upon hearing it, faith shall arise; once faith has arisen, one will act accordingly, and by so acting, that fruit will certainly be attained.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the Story of the Enshrinement of the Relics, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XI. Discourse on the Maṇḍala.
Then, having heard the praise for the fruits of planting seeds in the [Buddha] realms, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya spoke thus again to the Blessed One:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the mandala of the Sugata and that by which it is prepared for the purpose of worship.
O Lord, what is the fruit of those [actions]?
The Blessed One said:
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Whoever constructs the maṇḍala in this supreme abode of the Sugata, Dak_11.2.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One remained silent.
When it had been so performed, the Blessed One reflected.

"May the Bodhisattva Candraprabha come here! As soon as this thought arose, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha vanished from the world-system Candrāvabhāsa; at that very moment, having arrived through miraculous power by way of the sky, he sat down before the Blessed One on Vulture Peak.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One,
he sat down to one side;
he was like the moon itself in the beauty of his form, and like the moon, he shone with a cool radiance.
An area of a yojana all around was illuminated by its splendor.

(Dak: 112) Then that bodhisattva, rising from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, spoke.
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what being present does existence arise as a condition? Through the cessation of what would it cease?
What is it that ceases as existence?"
The Blessed One said:
Excellent, excellent, Candraprabha!
Monks, you too should look upon it and listen likewise;
I shall proclaim this sūtra. Endowed with the ten powers and confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, I roar the noble lion’s roar in the assembly.
That is to say: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.

With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
That is to say: when this does not exist, that does not exist;
through the cessation of this, that ceases.

That is to say: from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact;
from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.

From the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Monks, my Dharma is well-expounded, manifest, revealed, with its crossbar broken, and perfectly proclaimed for gods and humans alike.

While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha attained the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and also attained the six perfections; then the Blessed One bestowed upon him his formal prophecy.
"Excellent, excellent, noble son!
In this world-system of yours, there shall be a Tathāgata, Arhat, named Candraprabha."
Endowed with wisdom and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, unsurpassed— he shall become a teacher of gods and humans in the world. (Dak 114) Dak_11.3 //

Then that bodhisattva, having received the prophecy from the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, being filled with serene faith, circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and departed for his own abode.
Then, monks, having seen that Bodhisattva—who was handsome, beautiful to behold, and serene—they said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, what deeds were performed by the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, such that he is handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing?"
The Blessed One said:
In the past, monks, in a time long gone, ninety-one kalpas ago, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—

endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He dwelt, having approached the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Now at that time, the Blessed One Vipaśyin, the perfectly awakened one, having emerged from this very monastery, was dwelling in the abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
(Dak: 115) Then those masses of people did not venture to remain without the Blessed One.
Then those masses of people said to the monk Sunanda, the supreme disciple of the Blessed One Vipaśyin:
"Where has the Blessed One Vipaśyin gone? Having not seen him for a long time during the day, all the masses of people stood there, longing to see the Blessed One.
The monk Sunanda said:
"I am staying all alone right here in this monastery; even I have not obtained a vision of the Blessed One."

Now at that time, a certain merchant, possessed of great supernatural power, desiring the Dharma and pure in intention, took flowers, incense, and other offerings and entered the monastery of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin in order to worship the Blessed One.
Then, not seeing the Blessed One, he asked him:
"Where is the Blessed One going? Where does he dwell?"
"Alas! The Blessed One has not been reached by me, one of such meager fortune."
Sunanda also entered for alms.
Then that merchant, having smeared the ground with cow dung and fashioned it into a circular mandala, performed an offering for the sake of the Blessed One;
thereafter, a further thought arose in him.
"By this very method, who will perform worship without having prepared a mandala by smearing it with cow dung?
For what reason, then, would they take pleasure in an empty place?
Therefore, I shall thus fashion a golden mandala."
When this has been done, all the masses of people will attain clarity of mind for the purpose of worshipping the Tathāgata.
Having thought thus, that merchant had a mandala constructed by a laborer according to square proportions and had it built in the middle of the monastery.
Immediately thereafter, that merchant, having had it constructed, was descending the street when he called out to the entire multitude of people and said:
Whosoever among those who desire to worship the Tathāgatas should perform worship in that maṇḍala,
until the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened Vipaśyin, has arrived.
Having heard that, from that time forward, all the people of Bandhumatī, upon seeing him, were filled with faith and performed worship for the sake of the Blessed One.
Then, at another time, the merchant, having worshipped the mandala, made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit, may I become a forest-dwelling bodhisattva;
when the final teaching has arrived, may I receive the prophecy of perfect enlightenment"—thus he made this aspiration.
Then, having fixed his mind with serene faith upon the Blessed Buddha and passing away, he was reborn in the womb of the queen of King Kauravya.
Then, after the passing of nine months, a son was born who was handsome, gracious, and beautiful to behold;
as soon as he was born, the entire city was illuminated by his radiance.
Just as the moon rises with cool rays, so too did he become manifest with radiance.
When he was born, they held a birth festival and established his name,
asking, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
The ministers said:
"Since his radiance has issued forth, let the boy be named Candraprabha"—thus it was established.

Then he was raised and nurtured by a group of nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions, both refined and highly refined; he grew quickly like a lotus in a pond. When the boy Candraprabha had become grown, [he was brought before his father].

And that Bhadra, being of noble and virtuous intent and naturally intelligent, became skilled in mastering all the sciences and treatises; he was accomplished in the knowledge of arts, in the coloring of gems, in instrumental music, in the theory of song, in the science of music, and in the art of archery and other disciplines.
With that prosperity, he gladdened his kinsmen, friends, dependents, the destitute, those worthy of honor, guests, and teachers, just as a great cloud rains down upon the lands. (Dak 11.4)
(Dak: 118) At another time, surrounded by his companions and attendants, he wandered all around the city to display his skill and curiosity regarding statecraft;
as he looked at the people, he saw some who were elderly, hunchbacked, deaf, deprived of their senses, and afflicted by diseases.
He sees some who have roared with the pride and arrogance born of the intoxication of beautiful forms and youth.
Having seen them, this thought occurred to him:
In this saṃsāra, everything is thus devoid of purpose:

this body is agitated by impurity and evil, a locus of disease and sorrow, overwhelmed by fear, fashioned by illusion, and tormented day and night by the suffering of the ocean of saṃsāra, which resembles the Avīci hell;
there is no means to ward off old age and death.
Therefore, thinking, "I shall seek the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra," he entered Rājagṛha and, remaining silent, reflected.
Through passion, greed is born; through greed, sorrow is born.
Through sorrow, one withers the body, and therein death is encountered.
Therefore, I do not see any happiness for human beings at any time;
such is this cycle of suffering, wherein the perception of "unhappiness" is established.
In such a thing as this, which is devoid of essence, who could extract any essence?
Then that Candraprabha made a request to his father, the king.
"Father, listen to my wish.
Born as I am into your pure lineage, I desire to give gifts to certain mendicants—whether they be ascetics, brahmins, or wanderers.
Father, listen to my intention."

Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one [into the next life] and is not shared with thieves or others; it is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind.

Giving is the removal of the fatigue of the journey through saṃsāra; giving is a comfortable vehicle; and a true friend is one whose countenance is bright with many comforts and who is constant to the end. (Dak 11.7)
Whether it be the arising of wealth, splendor, the quality of authoritative knowledge, residence in the city of the thirty-three gods, or the excellence of physical beauty—
whatever one desires, all that one attains through giving.
Thus, when the benefits have been thus enumerated, who would not give gifts? Dak_11.8 //
Therefore, I make this request.
Then Janaka, smiling, said to him:
Oh, how difficult it is for one of pure mind to overcome;
even a child finds only giving to be pleasing.
He spoke again:
"Son Candraprabha, what are you saying?

Surely in your realm there are houses of food and houses of drink, completely filled with gold, silver, jewels, and pearls; all of that is at your disposal. Give as you wish, according to your intention."
He said: "Father, well said; may it be auspicious."
Having spoken thus and bowed his head to his father’s words,
he gave gifts to ascetics, brahmins, and mendicants, and performed meritorious deeds.

(Dak: 120) Then, having reflected upon the worthlessness of cyclic existence and its many faults, the mind of that youth Candraprabha took no pleasure in dwelling within a household; he thought, "I wish to go to a forest retreat."
This thought occurred to him:
"This is improper; how could I go without informing my mother and father?
Therefore, having first informed my parents, I shall depart for the forest retreat. Having announced this, he approached his father, and having approached him, he spoke to his parents.
"Father, grant me your permission; considering the household life to be a web of many evils, I wish to become a forest-dweller. Therefore, give me your leave."
Thus addressed, his parents, their faces bathed in tears and their throats choked with emotion, took a deep breath and spoke to him.
It does not behove you to reopen, with supreme sorrow, this wound of the arrow of grief that has not yet healed within our hearts for our son.
Likewise, you understand what is appropriate: the attachment to home or the path of welfare found in the happiness of dwelling in the forest.
Why do you wish to go alone to the forest, abandoning us, who are without a protector, here in our home?
Having heard that, he said:
Let Your Majesty behold.
In a home that is the abode of negligence, intoxication, lust, greed, and hatred,
what room can there be for the acceptance of Dharma, which is the opposite of those?
(Dak:

121) When will the householder—who is dragged away by many evil deeds, who is distracted by the acquisition and preservation of possessions, and whose mind is unpeaceful due to the onset of calamities—ever find the path of tranquility? *Daśakumāracarita* 11.11.
Having thus reflected and reached a firm resolution regarding the affectionate efforts of his friends,
he cast aside their despondency with words sweet with persuasion and departed for the forest of asceticism.
Having produced immeasurable meditative absorptions there, he ascended to heaven.

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time and on that occasion was the merchant was this very Bodhisattva Candraprabha. Having had a golden mandala constructed for the monastery of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, through the ripening of that karma, he experienced sovereignty in the Kauravya clan; then, having become a Bodhisattva, he attained the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the six perfections."
I too have prophesied his attainment of perfect enlightenment; it has come to pass exactly according to the vow he made, and not otherwise.
The great fruit and benefit of the Tathāgata’s maṇḍala are the fruit and benefit [of this practice].
Listen again!
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Whoever constructs a maṇḍala in this supreme abode of the Sugata.
Those who [take refuge] in the Buddha, who is honored by the three worlds, suddenly attain sovereignty over people, long life, and are liberated from the fears of various diseases.
Having prepared them, they become mandalas together with flowers. // Dak_11.14 //
Endowed with divine pleasures and all the finest enjoyments, mortals become possessed of a most beautiful complexion surpassing gold;
they have lotus-like faces, well-proportioned limbs, and large eyes.
Having adorned the earth with various kinds of flowers for the Gaṇa.
One should train in this way; for one whose actions are thus perfected, even with respect to the Buddhas and all phenomena, a great fruit is obtained.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Story of Maṇḍala, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XII. Discourse on Food.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, for the sake of generating wholesome roots in sentient beings, spoke again to the Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear:
what is the fruit of the gift of food? Tell me all that, O Lord of Speakers; how is it that the Sugata’s meal [yields such a result]? (Dak_12.1)
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Listen, Maitreya, at one time I was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, together with the community of śrāvakas."
At that time, there lived in that place a certain merchant-householder who was wealthy,

possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive property and an accumulation of wealth equal to that of Vaiśravaṇa, rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa himself; he was devoted to the heretics, but having been won over by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, he was introduced to the Teaching and became exceedingly devoted to the Blessed One.
That householder was noble and possessed great resolve; he said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Be my companions;
I wish to perform an offering to the Blessed One."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana consented to that householder by remaining silent.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, taking that householder with him, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One in this way.

"Venerable sir, this householder desires to feed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples; may the Blessed One, out of compassion, grant him his consent. The Blessed One gave his consent to that householder by remaining silent.

Then that householder, understanding the Blessed One’s acceptance by his silence, took food of a hundred flavors and, in the presence of the Blessed One, offered flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
and the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana requested Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Please provide an offering for this householder."
Then, at that very moment, Śakra, the lord of the gods, transformed the entire bamboo grove into a sandalwood grove.

Thousands of nāgas, resembling Airāvata and Supratiṣṭhita, fanned him with yak-tail whisks; and many thousands of gathered gandharvas, headed by Supriya, Pañcaśikha, and Tumburu, played various kinds of musical instruments and offered divine ambrosial food.
Then that householder, having attended upon the Blessed One with divine and human requisites, prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet with his whole body and began to make a formal aspiration.
"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this relinquishing of gifts, may I become a Buddha in a world that is blind, leaderless, and without a guide."
Then the Blessed One, having understood the succession of causes and the succession of karmic actions of that householder, manifested a smile.
At that time, blue, yellow, red, and white rays of light issued forth from the Blessed One’s mouth;
having issued forth,
they illuminated everything from below up to the peak of existence.
Then those rays of light, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished into the Blessed One’s uṣṇīṣa.
Then the venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the Blessed One.
A manifold array of light, variegated with thousands of colors, issued forth from within his mouth,
by which the directions were illuminated on all sides, just like the rising sun.
(Dak: 126) Free from rebirth, having abandoned both dejection and pride, the Buddhas are the supreme cause for the world.
These Jinas, who have conquered their enemies, do not display a smile as white as a conch shell or a jasmine flower without a reason. Dak_12.3 //

O Hero, O Lord of Jinas, having yourself realized that at this very moment through your wisdom, dispel with your firm, supreme, and auspicious words, O Bull among Sages, the doubt that has arisen in those listeners who long to hear it.
The Fully Awakened Ones, the Protectors, who possess the steadfastness of the king of mountains amidst the salt waters, do not display a smile without cause;
those multitudes of people desire to hear the purpose for which the Wise Ones display a smile.
The Blessed One said:

"It is so, Ānanda, it is so. Ānanda, it is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones manifest a smile. Look, Ānanda, how this householder has performed such an act of veneration for me.
Thus, Ānanda, by this root of merit, this production of the thought of awakening, and this relinquishment of gifts, this householder [will attain] for the Blessed One..."
And having realized enlightenment, which was fully accomplished over three incalculable eons, and having perfected the six perfections imbued with compassion,
he will become the Perfectly Awakened One named Divyānnada.
This serene clarity of mind toward me is his gift of merit.
(Dak: 127) And when King Bimbisāra and the attendants of Magadha heard this account, they were struck with great wonder.
The monks, having become filled with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is the dispeller of all doubts.
Behold, Blessed One, how this householder has honored the Blessed One together with the community of disciples with both divine and human miraculous powers!
The Blessed One said:
The Tathāgata himself performed and accumulated these actions; who else would experience them?
For monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated—whether wholesome or unwholesome—do not ripen [upon others].
They never perish at any time.

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there arose in the world a Perfectly Enlightened One named Pūrṇa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Then the Perfectly Awakened One named Pūrṇa, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at a certain royal capital.
The Kṣatriya king heard that the Perfectly Awakened One Pūrṇa, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, had arrived within his own realm;
and having heard this, endowed with great royal splendor and great royal majesty, he went toward Pūrṇa.
He approached the Perfectly Enlightened One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One Pūrṇa and sat down to one side.
As the Kṣatriya king sat to one side, the Perfectly Enlightened One Pūrṇa exhorted him with the qualities that bring about awakening.
Then the Kṣatriya king, having conceived a serene faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One,

attended upon the Perfectly Awakened One, Pūrṇa, together with the community of disciples, for three months with robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick; he gave various kinds of food, drink, and edibles to the Blessed One and his Saṅgha.
