Having had a jeweled image of the Blessed One fashioned, he caused the Buddha’s joy;
therein, many hundreds of thousands of living beings attained great faith.
With that as their cause and that as their condition, they have attained final nirvana.
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.

Because I performed such offerings and provided food for the Perfectly Awakened One Pūrṇa, I experienced infinite happiness throughout saṃsāra. And by that very same cause, such honor has been paid to me, the Tathāgata, by the merchant, by Śakra, and by the inhabitants of the divine realms."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor and revere the Teacher."
The great benefits of giving food and providing a meal.
And listen again!

In the city of the gods, the deities and the lords of the immortals consume that divine nectar, which is held in the lotus-petal-like hands of their beloveds, radiant with excellent color and fragrance, pleasant to the touch and delicious,
and served in vessels of shining gold.
That is the fruit resulting from the gift of food offered toward the Noble Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha.

The Sugata, having conquered the enemy Smara along with his servants through loving-kindness upon the adamantine seat, and having likewise subdued the enemies that are the afflictions, the internal objects of sense which are difficult to restrain, the wicked ones,
as well as the enemy of the aggregates and Death itself by force;
He too has attained mastery over the enjoyment of the finest of all flavors through the power of giving food.

Through the gift of food, the wise person attains a life span, strength, complexion, and noble form, endowed with all limbs complete and possessed of glorious happiness and peerless eloquence. (Dak 12.8)

Those lords of men who, having conquered enemies endowed with strength and valor and having attained royal fortune, enjoy delicious foods—it is because of their previous giving of food that they have become bipeds. (Dak_12.9)

The gift of food is the most excellent; indeed, there is nothing superior to the gift of food. There is no suffering greater than that caused by hunger; therefore, food is of the highest importance. (Dak 12.10)
And he who is deprived of food possesses neither strength nor vigor; in his exertion toward purposeful action, no such exertion exists. (Dak 12.11)
Furthermore, for one who neglects the observances, the worship of the deities, and other duties, sexual pleasure and play perish;
food consumed at the wrong time is lost, and his knowledge of the sacred narratives declines. (Dakṣa 12.12)
For those who are deprived of food, all religious merit languishes;
therefore, one should diligently accumulate the gift of food above all else.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Story of the Meal, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XIII. Discourse on the Drink.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:
Furthermore, I wish to hear the fruit of the gift of drinking water;
tell me all of that, O Lord of Orators, who triumphs over all the worlds. (Dak_13.1)
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Maitreya, for I shall tell you the fruit of the gift of a drinking vessel;
do so with a one-pointed mind, surely out of a desire for the welfare of the world. (Dak_13.2)

Those who joyfully offer to the Saṅgha a refreshing drink that cuts through craving—one endowed with a pleasant taste and flavor, exceptionally potent, delightful with its fragrance, and dear to the heart—having given this auspicious beverage, they cast off their longing for the fears of existence; through wisdom, they certainly reach the further shore of the ocean of becoming. (Dak_13.3)
As it is heard in tradition:

Monks, in the past, in a former age, during this very Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Leader of the World named Kāśyapa, a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.
The Blessed One was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
In that place, eight certain monks who had set out on a journey to see the Blessed One were scorched by the rays of the sun; afflicted by thirst, they approached a well.
There, a certain young woman arrived having filled a water-jar.
Then, monks, they said to her:
"Sister, please give me some water."
Then, envy arose within her;
having seized the requisites, she said to the monks:
"O monks, even if you were to die, I would still not give you even a drink of water,
for my jar would become depleted."
Then those monks, afflicted by thirst and having lost all hope, departed.
Then, in the territory of Magadha, there was a very wealthy caravan leader named Siṃhaketu; his daughter, having taken a water jar, went out from the door of her house to fetch water.
Then they said:
"O noble girl, we are extremely thirsty;
give us some water to drink."
Then that girl, whose disposition was characterized by the quality of supreme cleverness, spoke to those monks.
"Venerable ones, monks, enter and stay here;
I myself will bring the cold water back very quickly."
Having spoken thus, the girl departed; having departed, she quickly took her water-jar, entered her own dwelling, and said to her father:
"Father, the monks are standing at our gateways;
having arrived at this present time, they are afflicted by fatigue and thirst.
Grant them jaggery, sugar, and black pepper, distributed according to their respective needs."
I give this drink, having partaken of it myself.
Then that caravan leader, Siṃhaketu, having heard his daughter’s words, granted her request.
Out of supreme joy and the arising of faith, that girl immediately prepared a drink with cold water and a mixture of sugar and other ingredients, and gave it to them.
Then the monks collected it and drank it; having drunk it, they said to that girl:
"O auspicious girl, may there be well-being!
May there always be well-being for you, O auspicious one; may that mind which is your desire be fulfilled. May you always possess auspiciousness and spiritual enthusiasm toward the Buddha. (Dak_13.4)
Then, having heard for the first time the name of the Buddha and the description of the Buddha, that girl, filled with serene faith, spoke to those monks.
"Venerable ones, where is the Blessed One, what is he like, and how is he?
I do not know the name of the Buddha; tell me his specific qualities. (Dak_13.5)
The monks said:
For the Blessed One Kāśyapa, O maiden, possesses great power; having taught the Dharma to all sentient beings,
he dwells here in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
Then that girl said to those monks:
"O monks, faith has arisen in me toward Buddha Kāśyapa;
I shall certainly pay him honor.
In my name, you should offer salutations to the Blessed One Kāśyapa and inquire after his freedom from illness."
Then the monks, having said, "We too shall speak in this very same way," departed.
Then eight monks, having approached the Blessed One at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipatana and having bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
Seated there, they inquired after that girl’s freedom from illness and her well-being.
Then the Blessed One Kāśyapa had an assembly hall constructed.
Then this thought occurred to that girl:
"What if I were to satisfy eight monks with offerings of drink;
by that, my mind would be truly satisfied."
In that way, I shall provide the Blessed One Kāśyapa and the Saṅgha with drink.
Then that girl, having informed her father, prepared herself to honor the Blessed One.
Then Siṃhaketu, the caravan leader, in order to increase that girl’s faith, gave her whatever she desired.
Then that young woman invited the Blessed One Kāśyapa, together with his community of disciples, for a meal at her home on the following day.
And the Blessed One consented for the sake of favoring her.
Then that girl gathered a great quantity of perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having prepared food, drink, and other provisions, she announced the time to the Blessed One by means of a messenger.
"It is time, Venerable Sir; everything has been prepared. Now, Blessed One, please do as you deem fit."

(Dak: 135) Then the Blessed One Kāśyapa, surrounded by a multitude of monks and preceded by the community of monks, approached the residence of the caravan leader Siṃhaketu; having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.

Then that girl, perceiving that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was comfortably seated, offered them water for their feet and personally gratified them with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Furthermore, sugar drinks, molasses drinks, medicinal drinks, milk drinks, and sweet juice drinks were prepared according to their own wishes and offered to them.
Then, in order to increase her faith, the Tathāgata drank it with ease, even though he was free from thirst.
For Tathāgatas never experience thirst, nor hunger, nor fatigue, nor sloth and torpor, nor the sensations of cold or heat;
nor does impurity adhere to their bodies.

He walks upon the earth with feet unstained by dust; nevertheless, he washes his feet and even bathes for the sake of conforming to worldly custom and as a cause for sentient beings to attain their fruits.
Whatever is given, he accepts it all, and each such gift is received by the Tathāgatas.

Then, seeing that the Tathāgata had drunk [the milk] with ease, the girl was filled with supreme faith; she bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet as if cutting them from their very roots and made this aspiration:
By this root of merit, wherever I may be reborn, in each and every birth may I remember my past lives;
and recollecting them, may I be filled with serene faith toward the Buddha, the Blessed One, when he is honored.
"I shall perform worship and honor for the Tathāgata."
Then that girl, having developed serene faith in the Buddhas, passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

Surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, she was seated comfortably in a celestial palace, which resounded with various musical performances and was devoid of men. Immediately upon being reborn, whether as a woman or a man, three thoughts arise:
"From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma?"

She saw that she had passed away from among humans and was reborn here; moreover, because she had performed acts of veneration toward the Blessed One Kāśyapa, she was reborn among the gods by virtue of that root of merit.
Then, this thought occurred to that daughter of the gods who was the giver of the drink:
"It would not be fitting for me that, having completed my period of probation, I should approach the Blessed One Kāśyapa for an audience."
Knowledge and vision proceed.
The Blessed One Kāśyapa, having performed the work of a Buddha, passed into nirvāṇa.
A great stupa for his relics exists there.
Then this thought occurred to her:
"Alas, I am so unfortunate! Where shall I show myself to the Blessed One Kāśyapa?"
Then she remembers: "I have heard that those who worship even a relic of the Tathāgatas the size of a mustard seed will obtain the fruit of purification."
The evil of an evil-minded person comes to an end.
Having spoken thus, that goddess who had provided the drink, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred asura maidens, came at night when all was quiet, taking various *māndārava* flowers,
*pārijāta* blossoms, perfumes, garlands, incense, and other offerings, and arrived at the place where the reliquary stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa stood.
He strews it with māndārava flowers.
Having scattered [the flowers] and circumambulated [him], she went to her own abode.
Then, that celestial maiden who had given her drink was no longer afflicted by thirst;

for when she was a human being, she had offered the eightfold water to the eight [Buddhas]. By this root of merit, monks, humans should give gifts of drink, they should construct wells and the like, and they should build tanks, ponds, wells, and lotus-pools.
The monks said:
"I am awakened, O Sugata; I am awakened, O Blessed One.
Then another woman, who had been stingy toward the monks and did not give them water, asked: "Where has that woman gone, and what fruit has she attained?"
The Blessed One said:

What need is there to say, monks, that this girl, having practiced, cultivated, and frequently indulged in that stinginess, after her death was reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*s)? She has the appearance of a charred pillar, covered with her own hair and body-hair, with a mouth like the eye of a needle.

With a belly as high as a mountain and filled with a framework of bones, she is ablaze, burning, and become a single mass of flame; wailing with a cry of distress, tormented by thirst, she experiences suffering that is sharp, harsh, and bitter.
Experiencing an unpleasant feeling.
Then, wherever she went to drink water out of thirst, the rivers and wells dried up at the mere sight of her.
When the god rains, then upon her falls a rain of glowing embers accompanied by sparks.
He experiences such painful, intense, harsh, bitter, and disagreeable sensations.
Therefore, monks, you should exert yourselves for the sake of abandoning stinginess.
The gift of a drink brings great merit and great benefits;
listen further, O monks!
The pure, shimmering interior of a blue lotus, red as a ruby, desirable and placed within a golden vessel, filled with honey mixed with frost—
this is drunk when offered by a beloved woman whose eyes are slightly copper-hued.
Accompanied by the sound of music, that is the fruit of giving drink to the best of men.

Indeed, the gods, together with divine maidens whose chest-areas are filled by the weight of their jar-like breasts, [revel] in vessels fashioned from the finest lapis lazuli and sapphire, as well as from gold.
Those addicted to joy drink together sweet honey or Mādhava wine;
the wise declare that this is the delightful fruit of giving drinks to one who possesses a multitude of virtues.
That drink which is endowed with qualities such as color and fragrance, prepared to destroy thirst,
and expert at pacifying phlegm, humors, and severe wind— consisting of powdered long pepper and sugar-candy,
refined in summer within a vessel resembling moonbeams by being mixed with snow; that [is the drink].
Having given [a drink] to the Saṅgha with great devotion, one who has gone to the world of the gods obtains divine drink.
He who respectfully offers a drink as sweet as honey and sublime to a distinguished assembly,
shall for a long time drink the finest beverage, served by excellent women, both in heaven and throughout the entire world.
Those people on earth who, with minds clear through faith, offer excellent drinks to the Saṅgha at the proper time,
dwell upon the slopes and in the caves of the mountain of saṃsāra, and they constantly obtain sweet, excellent drink.
Those who joyfully offer to the Saṅgha this refreshing drink— which severs craving,
is endowed with a pleasant taste and flavor, is exceptionally potent, delightful with its fragrance, and dear— [attain great merit].

Having quenched their thirst for the fear of existence with the firebrand of craving, they cross to the further shore of the ocean of becoming by means of wisdom, having surely given the drink of virtue.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Story of Pāna, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XIV. Discourse on Clothing.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"I wish to hear those words of yours, O Protector, which are like nectar;
and tell me, O Great Lord, the auspicious account of the garments. (Dak_14.1)
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Maitreya, I shall describe the gift of clothing;
by the gift of a *kaṭhina* cloth, one is born with clothing. (Dak_14.2)
At one time, I was dwelling at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove together with the community of disciples.
In that great and excellent city of Kapilavastu, there lived among the Śākyas a certain Śākyan named Rohiṇa,
who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and vast enjoyments, with extensive and wide-ranging possessions; he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled Vaiśravaṇa himself.
His wife had neither son nor daughter;
with his cheek resting on his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth, yet I have neither son nor daughter."
Thinking, "After my passing, all my property will inevitably come under the control of the king," he lamented excessively and became extremely distraught.
(Dak: 142) Then, by the power of destiny, after a short time, having passed away from one of the divine hosts, he descended into the womb of that lady of the Prajāpatis.
Thereupon, she informed her husband.
Then this was understood by the Lord himself; then it was said by the Lord:
"O blessed lady, if you give birth to a son, that will be well;
but if it is a daughter, I shall have you expelled along with her."

When eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful, pleasing, and transcended the human form without yet having attained the divine. She was clothed in white celestial garments and remained unsullied by the impurities of the womb.
Eventually, Rohiṇa heard that Prajāpati had given birth to a daughter.
Enraged, he entered;
then a girl dressed in divine garments was brought before him by Prajāpati.
Upon seeing the girl, Rohiṇa the Śākya was struck with great wonder.
"Oh, what a marvel! How is my daughter adorned with such beauty? By what karma was she born already clothed? (Dak 14.3)
Then, having performed the birth ceremony for her, a name was established; because she was clothed in white garments, the girl's name was set as "Śuklā" (The White One).
That girl grew rapidly through the excellence of her various provisions, like a lotus situated in a lake.
And just as the maiden Śuklā grew, so too did those garments grow;
they did not become soiled, nor was her body ever overcome by impurity.
(Dak: 143) When the girl Śuklā had gradually grown up and become a woman, many young men—sons of kings and sons of ministers—came as suitors seeking her hand in marriage.
Then, being harassed by them, her father sat with his cheek resting in his hand, lost in thought.
"If I give to one, others will become my enemies."
Then that girl, seeing her father absorbed in deep anxiety, spoke to him.
"Father, why are you lost in thought?
He then explained the matter to him in detail:
"Listen, daughter, I shall tell you the reason for my preoccupation."
The princes have gathered together with you for the sake of the Dharma.
"Many sons of ministers come to me day after day; therefore, I have become lost in thought: 'To whom indeed shall I give it, O friend? (Dak 14.5)
The girl said: "Father, you should not grieve; I am not one who seeks after desire. And why is that?

Wealth, grain, the body, the home, and all objects of sensual enjoyment are indeed useless, exceedingly fickle, and fragile; like a flash of lightning, they are pleasing to the world for only a moment. Having seen that even what is perceived is ultimately harmful, O Sugata, I shall indeed go forth into the religious life.
(Saṃsāra is impermanent; the treasury is impermanent; friendship, along with sons and wives, is impermanent;
sovereignty and various enjoyments are impermanent. In saṃsāra, everything is indeed impermanent. (Dak: 144) Dak_14.7 //
Therefore, merit alone is indeed a true kinsman of excellent essence; there is nothing other than merit.
Like a lamp in the night amidst thick darkness, it is the bestower of happiness and the dispeller of affliction.
"Therefore, I shall go forth into homelessness in that teaching of the Blessed One;
grant me your permission, father."
Eventually, having obtained permission from her mother and father, she went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.
The very garment with which she was born emerged as a complete set of five robes for her.
By applying herself, striving, and exerting effort, she—

Having understood this very five-factored wheel of saṃsāra to be moving and unstable, and having struck down all conditioned states by means of their nature of falling, collapsing, dispersing, and disintegrating, she realized arhatship through the abandonment of all defilements;
she became an arhatī.

They were free from passion for the three realms; to them, a clod of earth and gold were equal; their minds were like space or the palm of a hand; they were as indifferent to an axe as to sandalwood; they had split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge; they had attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the analytical insights (*pratisaṃvid*); they turned their backs on existence, gain, greed, and honor;
and they became worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.

"Venerable sir, what white deeds were performed by her, such that she was born into a wealthy family, beautiful, handsome, pleasing to behold, dressed in white garments, and having gone forth, realized arhatship?"
The Blessed One said:
Monks, it is by white deeds alone that actions performed and accumulated in previous births—whether auspicious or inauspicious—ripen. Listen to that.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, during this very Fortunate Aeon when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years,
there appeared in the world a Truly Perfectly Awakened One named Kāśyapa— one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world,
an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling in dependence on the city of Vārāṇasī, at Ṛṣipatana in the Deer Park. At that time, a certain wife of a merchant— faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent— went to Ṛṣipatana for some business matter.
Then he beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels.
Seeing from all sides that the Blessed One was auspicious, she prostrated at his feet and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One Kāśyapa taught her the Dharma; having gained faith, she said, "I shall honor the Blessed One together with the community of disciples in my home.
Having said this, she provided the *kaṭhina* robe for the community of monks, and after gradually obtaining permission from her parents, she went forth into the teaching of the Blessed One.
"What do you think, monks? That wife of the merchant was none other than this nun Śuklā.
Because she bestowed a *kaṭhina* robe upon the community of monks, she was born clothed in white garments."
Because he had fully observed the life of celibacy, he realized arhatship in this very life.

The great benefits of the gift of clothing are found both in the worlds of men and in the world of gods; indeed, those who offer garments with devotion obtain whatever kind of clothing they desire. Dak_14.9

Those who offer to the Teacher of the World, together with his supreme retinue, bright garments and garlands fashioned from various colors— blue, yellow, green, crimson, white, and variegated— shall obtain their desired and most excellent robes.

(147) Whoever, with faith and devotion, offers a robe and a garland to the most excellent among all the assemblies of the Saṅgha, obtains the garment of modesty— the finest of cloths— and the saffron robe, which is the antidote to the dregs of the afflictions.
Having offered beautiful garlands fashioned from clusters of excellent, tawny, and variegated flowers, along with robes of blue, yellow, white, red, and other lovely, radiant garments, he—
handsome and charming— bestowed divine, exquisite cloth upon the assembly of the sons of the Sugata.
Adorned with the garment of modesty, he becomes one of sharp intellect and a sovereign over all phenomena.
And again:

Whether in heaven or on earth, they declare that clothing is the most excellent ornament for the body— adorned with necklaces, head-ornaments, anklets, and armlets made of lapis lazuli, gold, and pearls— which serves as the very method of decoration.
Not only that.
Though endowed with beauty, born of noble lineage, and wise; though having exerted effort in the world's various treatises;
and though adorned with a multitude of virtues such as ethical discipline—
A man does not shine in heaven with fine garments without [merit].
Therefore, having observed that clothing is an incomparable ornament, and that it wards off cold, heat, and darkness;
Those who desire to obtain the peerless garment of moral shame (hrī) should repeatedly give gifts of clothing to human beings. Dak_14.15.
Seated upon a lion throne with golden handles for fly-whisks shimmering like moonbeams, and shaded by white parasols,
though his head was adorned with crowns of gold and jewels, he remained.
Even a glorious universal monarch does not shine without clothing. (Dak 14.16)
In the city of Alakā, the dwelling place of the illustrious Lord of Wealth;
on the Bhogavatī river, adorned by the serpent with a thousand tongues;
and upon the peaks of Kailāsa and Meru, in the midst of the assembly of gods.
Even the garments of Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra do not shine without [the proper] clothing.
"Thus, monks, having cast aside dark deeds, one should apply oneself only to bright deeds; in this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what was said.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Story of the Garment, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XV. The Discourse on the Flower.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the fruit of offering flowers;
please speak the discourse on flowers according to the different colors of those blossoms. (Dak. 15.1)
The Blessed One said:
Surpassing Śakra, endowed with excellent enjoyments, their bodies possessing the luster of the lotus and the moon, and possessed of sublime fame,
they constantly prevail over Śakra with impetuous force.
Those who offer worship to the Buddha by scattering beautiful flowers. // Dak.15.2 //
Thus, considering it to possess many virtues and yielding great fruit once again, let men perform worship of the Buddha with various kinds of flowers. (Dak. 15.3)
It is as follows:
Among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, there is a divine maiden named Kusumagandhinī.
Having ascended a flower-palace, she wanders from heaven to heaven, surrounded by a retinue of five hundred divine maidens.
Then, in due course, that celestial maiden, fragrant with the scent of flowers, approached the vicinity of Sudharmā, the assembly hall of Śakra, the lord of the gods.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, saw from afar that celestial maiden adorned with a celestial chariot of various flowers; seeing her whose roots of merit were fully purified, he addressed her in verse:
Oh, how wonderful is the great power of the root of merit belonging to this divine maiden!
(Dak: 150) Then that celestial maiden, Kusumagandhinī, by her splendor and radiance, eclipsed the divine luster of Śakra, the lord of the gods;
she became like the moon shrouded by white clouds in the autumn season.
Then that son of the gods, Sudharma, having seen her, his mind captivated, said:

By what means has her body come to resemble polished gold, and her face the moon? From where has this incomparable splendor of her limbs, this wealth of exquisite beauty surpassing even Śakra, emerged?
And from where comes this peerless, fragrant, and sweet scent of her excellent body, such that one could never be satiated by beholding it?
"Blessed is this woman who has performed wholesome deeds; oh, how she has been reborn in heaven! (Dak. 15.4)
The monks said this to the Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, these multitudes of people desire to hear from you about the birth, origin, and name of this celestial maiden Kusumagandhinī."
The Blessed One said:
Long ago, monks, there was a delightful city named Malayavatī; it was filled with various festivals,

crowded with many people, inhabited by wise men, teeming with those of great supernatural power, thronged with many women adorned with beauty and youth— a city endowed with auspicious marks and surrounded by a wall of trees.
In that city lived a merchant named Ketuvikrama, who was exceedingly wealthy, possessed of great enjoyments, extensive property, and abundant riches;
he had a single courtesan.

That female attendant, having gathered the flowers of that garden every day and returned, would at the proper time place a single handful of flowers upon the stūpa of the hair and nails of the Tathāgata on the road;
then, having arrived, she would offer them for the worship of the deity Ketuvikrama.
In this manner, that female attendant was appointed to that task every day.
By that, she becomes one who wanders through the garden.
In the time immediately following that, as they reached the number of one hundred thousand,
the deity of the shrine became pleased, and she attained a state of serene faith.
The fruit was obtained right here:
she became that very servant girl, who turned out to be supremely beautiful and possessed a virtuous nature;
furthermore, her storehouse became filled with an abundance of wealth and grain, as well as various ornaments.
Then happiness is experienced.
Then Ketuvikrama, having attained the utmost wonder, thought: "How is it that my wife's body has become so well-formed? What is the cause? What is the reason?"
In the same way, other people were also addressed;
some said, "Alas, sir! How is it that this servant girl has become possessed of various fine garments?"
In the same way, other people, upon seeing her, were struck with wonder.
Then, having lived a short life and passed away,
she was reborn in the womb of the wife of a certain merchant named Dharmaśīla in the great city of Śrāvastī.
Then, after the lapse of ten months, a girl was born who was handsome, pleasing, and most beautiful; in due course, she grew up to be a young woman.
(Dak: 152) At that time, I myself was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with the community of disciples.
Now, at that very time, a festival called Sālaprabhañjikā had arrived in Śrāvastī.
There, having gathered many hundreds of thousands of living beings, they took *sāla* flowers and played, enjoyed themselves, and amused one another.
Then that merchant’s daughter, taking *sāla* flowers, entered Śrāvastī;
and the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was departing from Śrāvastī after wandering for alms.

He beheld the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns; like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides.
Having seen him, and being filled once more with serene faith, he scattered *sāla* flowers over him.
Then, having circumambulated [him], she turned back,
thinking, "I shall bring yet other things for the sake of the household."
When she had climbed the sāla tree and fallen down, having rendered service to the Blessed One, she passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Adorned with celestial palaces of *sāla* flowers, she wanders from heaven to heaven, taking her delight.
In the same way, monks, as for that girl by whom the Arhat was strewn with *sāla* flowers on the path—
for this reason, monks, one should perform services for and show honor to the Tathāgatas.
"Such a fruit as this is obtained.
Then, having heard the words of the Blessed One, Ānanda, filled with serene faith, addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, what is the fruit of the hundred-thousand-fold flower?
O mighty-armed Supreme Lord, you who desire to hear it, please tell me."
The Blessed One said:
I shall explain in brief for the benefit of the world;
listen attentively, Ānanda, to the sequence of the hundred thousand flowers. (Dak. 15.6)
The sin of a hundred murders of Brahmins, indeed those committed over a hundred lifetimes, the climbing of the *māghya* flowers pacifies; of this there is no doubt.
Wherever men grow the black Aparājitā, it removes all sins and cuts down all terrible enemies. (Dak. 15.8)
There shall be the destruction of various obstacles, as well as the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
having attained the happiness of a sovereign, one reaches the excellent station of the king of the gods.
Indeed, white Aparājitā flowers will bloom, and men will grow peaceful in nature, wealthy, and masters of various scriptures. (Dak. 15.10)
Endowed with fortitude and heroism, and possessed of various forms of wisdom, those who attain the station of a king go to heaven. (Dak. 15.11)
Those men who grow upon a golden jasmine flower shall become wealthy and possessed of enjoyments, equal to Kubera in their riches.
The most excellent men ascend the supreme *karavīra* flower;
having attained mastery over all worlds, they increase the delight of the gods. (Dak. 15.13)
Those people who grow the *damanaka* flower with great faith will always possess fragrant bodies and attain a form that is never satiated. (Dak. 15.14)
If the *kokilākṣa* plant sprouts, one becomes possessed of people and wealth;
born into a family of those possessing knowledge, he is honored by all the world. (Dak. 15.15)
Indeed, those men who with faith [plant] a campaka flower from Rohaṇa obtain fame and renown in the worlds, as well as all prosperity. (Dak. 15.16)
They will be beautiful and handsome, possessing bodies like those of the god Kandarpa,
endowed with fragrant bodies, and they shall attain royal splendor.
They produce jasmine flowers and are born into noble families; indeed, their bodies possess a most exquisite fragrance, and in wealth they are equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). Dak. 15.18.
Just as a certain lotus flower grows forth with clarity,
so too does one attain the wisdom of a Buddha and is born upon the lotus seat.
With *madhūka* flowers one obtains honey; likewise, with *kusumbha* flowers one obtains clothing.
With *kauśika* flowers one obtains clothing, and with *kiṃśuka* flowers one obtains red garments. (Dakṣa 15.20)
The person who grows a flower of the *pārijāta* tree attains infinite happiness and shall possess a fragrant body. (Dak. 15.21)
By planting the bandhūka flower, which destroys all sins and misfortunes, and by planting the ketaka flower, men shall become renowned;
it is auspicious in every respect and endowed with fragrance and happiness. (Dak. 15.22)
White water-lilies grow there, and faces with countenances like the moon arise in the abode of the Thirty-three Gods, gentle and equal in splendor to the moonlight. (Dak. 15.23)
Those who, with faith, cause blue lotus flowers to grow in his mouth shall possess the fragrance of a blue lotus and become a king of great supernatural power.
Aśoka flowers bloom and his body becomes peerless;
he is born as a sovereign king, completely liberated from all diseases. (Dak. 15.25)
O supreme men, one should take *kusuma*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and *rohaṇa*, which destroy all diseases, sorrows, and most terrible ailments. (Dak. 15.26)
Men who are leaders of men, growing like the flowers of the Javā plant, become enchanters of all the worlds and bring the worlds under their control. (Dak. 15.27)
Men of pure mind who cultivate *arkapuṣpa* plants shall become endowed with a thousand rays [of splendor], possessed of progeny, and wealthy. (Dak. 15.28)
One who, with a very serene mind, ascends upon a white water-lily flower, destroys all diseases and always carries prosperity. (Dak. 15.29)
By worshipping here with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, one shall become happy in the next world;
likewise, with *mālatī* flowers, there is the destruction of great sins. (Dak. 15.30)
By diligently gathering bilva leaves from their place of growth, one attains auspiciousness everywhere, as does the recitation of a thousand *yajus* verses. (Dakṣa 15.31)
One who plants *dhūrtapuṣpa* flowers fashioned like gold attains the fruit of enjoyment, endowed with wealth and happiness. (Dak. 15.32)

By worshipping with red lotuses, one destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin; and those men who, with devoted minds, worship with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and *kunda* flowers, are instantly liberated from the sins accumulated over a hundred lifetimes. (Dak. 15.33)
Tagara flowers grow there, bringing happiness in the next world;
the ancestors attain satisfaction, especially through the performance of śrāddha rites. (Dak. 15.34)
Men who perform those [rites] will always be prosperous;
they shall possess an abundance of wealth and grain, and their desired aims will bear fruit. (Dak. 15.35)
The jasmine flowers grow again, and Māra cannot disturb them;
with the growth of these fragrant blossoms, the fame of their sweet scent is proclaimed. (Dak. 15.36)
The Blessed One said:

I shall explain in brief the specific characteristics of the *lakṣapuṣpa* flowers, including their growth, their fruitfulness or lack thereof, and all qualities such as being high or low. (Dak. 15.37)
Indeed, the *māghya* flower is preeminent, especially within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*);
thereafter is the black *aparājitā*, then the golden *yūthikā* flower, and finally the *karavīra*.
After that, *damanaka* flowers, and whatever flowers are found everywhere, as well as those specifically praised by the Victors for the Buddhas at all times. (Dak. 15.39)
Campaka and jasmine flowers, as well as pārijāta, ketakī, and fresh garlands, along with lotus, kumuda, and utpala. (Dak. 15.40)
Aśoka flowers, arka flowers, kahlāra, nāgapuṣpa, bilva leaves, dhattūra, and likewise javā flowers. (Dak. 15.41)
The flowers of bhrṅgarāja, then lakṣmīpuṣpa in sequence, as well as tamāra, nirgranthī, yūthī, mallikā, and mādhavī. (Dak. 15.42)
The *vanamālā*, *kunda*, and *bandhūka* do not wither, nor does the *kuvalaka*; likewise, the *saireyaka*, *kroraṇa*, and the *madhurīkusumāvatī*. (Dak. 15.43)
In this manner, there were various kinds of flowers of many species, arranged in distinct and excellent sequences for each of the others. (Dak. 15.44)
I have not spoken anything else regarding the common flower;
indeed, all matters concerning flowers have been explained by the Lords of Jinas from every perspective.
Because of the offering of all kinds of flowers and so forth at a caitya, the fruit is supreme;
therefore, the Jinas have described the fruits of each individual type of flower separately. Dak. 15.46.
Ānanda said:
O Protector, O bull among speakers, I have heard of the [merit] of stūpas through the offering of a hundred thousand special flowers; tell me likewise of other Tathāgatas. (Dak. 15.47)
The Blessed One said:
And at that time, there was the presence of the flowers and the caityas as previously described; O Ānanda, listen fully as I shall explain it from every aspect. (Dak. 15.48)
Toward the Tathāgatas, who are beyond leading astray, and especially toward the deity, one should offer the previously mentioned flowers as appropriate and according to one's desire;
likewise, the deity [is honored] by means of the distinction of colors of the flowers. (Dak. 15.49)
In this way, Ānanda, it should be understood that a man who causes flowers to grow obtains the previously mentioned fruit constantly; of this there is no doubt. (Dak. 15.50)
For it is said that from the climbing of flowers there is great merit and a corresponding fruit;
likewise, the fruit is the same whether one offers them to the Buddhas, to their images, to stupas, or to other deities.
And again:

Those who scatter offerings of exquisite flowers before the Buddha constantly become superior even to Śakra, endowed with preeminent enjoyments, possessing bodies as radiant as the lotus and the moon, and graced with supreme fame; having swiftly triumphed over the Śakras, they remain so forever.
With the fragrance of their bodies equal to a cluster of blue lotuses, their pure and far-reaching beautiful eyes renowned for their fame,
these beings who have become human walk upon the earth like jewels; having offered sublime incense of noble scent to the Jina,
their limbs are adorned with beryl, pearls, and gems, and their entire bodies are draped in silken garments.
The best of men are attended by all people because of their offering of fragrant substances to the Buddha.
In this way, monks, that stūpa also obtained such a fruit.
Therefore, monks, the Tathāgatas’ stūpas and images should be honored with flowers.
"Monks, you should train yourselves thus."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Story of Puṣpa, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XVI. Discourse on Prostration.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having bowed down to the Blessed One, spoke as follows:
I wish to hear, O Lord, Blessed One, Deliverer from Existence:
tell me, O Master, the fruit of those who pay homage to the Tathāgata. Dak_16.1
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Maitreya, that you have asked me this!
Now, indeed, I shall speak of the fruit of bowing to the Buddha."

The merit of bowing to the Buddha is great: those who, with single-minded devotion, prostrate themselves as a cause for crossing the ocean of existence, shall attain happiness and beautiful forms. (Dak 16.3)

In the past, Maitreya, in a time long gone, incalculable eons ago, the Perfectly Awakened One named Padmottara, while wandering on a tour through the countryside together with Dīpaṃkara, arrived at a certain great kingdom.
There, standing in the marketplace of that great city, he taught the Dharma to the people.
At that time, a preeminent brahmin from the southern region named Puṣkaraśālin, surrounded by a retinue of thirty-two disciples, having heard the praises of the Buddha’s qualities,
came to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa for the purpose of hearing the Dharma.

Then they beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty minor characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, and possessing a splendor exceeding that of a thousand suns;
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect. And having seen him, faith arose within them toward the Blessed One.
Having circumambulated the Blessed One three times and bowed at his feet, they sat down to one side;
yet another did not incline his mind toward the Blessed One even mentally,
nor did he have any clarity of mind regarding the Buddha, the Blessed One.
With some remnants of evil karma remaining, his mind turbid and crooked as he entered the families of the Buddhas, he remained silent.
Others remained with hearts full of serene faith toward the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having understood that their minds were intent upon taking up the life of renunciation, the Blessed One spoke thus:
"O Brahmin, best of the twice-born, tell me for what purpose you have come here with your companions."
The Brahmin said:
“Blessed One, I wish to hear the supreme Dharma of the Buddhas;
for the Buddha speaks that which is not false, he is a speaker of truth, a Tathāgata. (Dak_16.4)
Neither stained by passion, nor stained by hatred, nor stained by delusion, he is like a pure gold coin;
among all sacred waters, he is like the water of the Ganges, having become purified and free from all impurities.
Grant me the opportunity for the Dharma, for we are deluded and lack liberated knowledge.
O Sage, O Victor, bestow upon me the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, so that by means of it alone I may liberate all sentient beings.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of the twice-born! Excellent, excellent is this well-spoken [verse].
O knower of right and wrong conduct, knower of the Dharma, may you maintain your moral discipline for so long."
Through ethical discipline one attains the divine; through it, excellent gain comes forth;
together with fame and prosperity—O best of the twice-born, uphold ethical discipline! (Dak 16.8)
But what is ethical discipline?
Non-malice toward all living beings in action, thought, and speech, as well as benevolence and knowledge— this, O best of the twice-born, is moral conduct (śīla). Dak_16.9.
There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods.
Through patience, one dwells in heaven; such a person goes to heaven eternally.
Having attained great fortune, he becomes one who goes to liberation.
O best of the twice-born, those who with effort meditate upon the Supreme Self with devotion and contemplation of the heart attain the supreme goal. (Dakṣa 16.12)
Having dispelled the darkness of delusion by means of the radiance of the sun of wisdom,
one attains the state of Buddhahood and shall become one who constantly proceeds toward liberation.
Through wisdom one attains merit; through wisdom, one is endowed with the Dharma.
Having fully realized infinite knowledge, one proceeds toward the wisdom of a Buddha.
Those men of pure mind who perform acts of benefit for others, having understood the happiness and suffering of others, attain happiness at all times. (Dak_16.15)
One should treat one's own suffering and the suffering of others as equal;
having lightened one's own suffering, one should regard the suffering of others as more significant.
He trembled at the suffering of others, like the king of mountains during an earthquake.
One should teach with a virtuous mind what is the work of Dharma or what is a good deed, so that when the time has entered upon evil paths, one's own mind may turn back from them. (Dak 16.17)
Certain humans, as well as living beings such as birds, insects, and so forth, should protect themselves equally from suffering by means of cutting off their own pain. (Dak_16.18)
One should know that helping others is the supreme path; one devoted to it becomes a partaker of merit.
Through that merit of helping others, happiness is attained;
by means of happiness, dharma is accomplished, and through dharma, liberation is achieved.
Whatever task arises, one should undertake that very task;
O you who are intent on the wisdom of enlightenment, know it to be for the benefit of others. (Dak 16.20)
Having heard this, the brahmin spoke thus to the Blessed One.
Some humans, as well as living beings such as birds, insects, and the like—who on this earth experiences their own suffering and their own happiness as equal? (Dak 16.21)
The Blessed One said:

Long ago, O Brahmin, there was a certain country named Śālavatī, which was exceedingly vast, enchanting, filled with all people, prosperous, flourishing, well-supplied with food, and beautiful to behold; it was free from disturbances, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, buffalo, and crops. In that country, there was a king named Sarvadada.

And that king was compassionate in disposition, a giver of all things, naturally inclined toward unattached renunciation, wise, virtuous, well-behaved, honest, and straightforward; he was free from passion, hatred, and delusion, humble, possessed of speech that was gentle, sweet, and affectionate, fond of guests and beggars, and pleasing to behold for all people.
Therefore, the fame of that King Yaśas became renowned throughout all worlds; he was like a wish-fulfilling gem for those who sought his help, fulfilling their hopes and intentions.
Having seen that the entire kingdom, the enjoyment of sensory objects, and cyclic existence are devoid of essence, his mind finds no delight in remaining here.
Having abandoned the entire splendor of his kingdom like a garland whose flowers have been worn out, soiled by use, and withered, he adorned a certain secluded hermitage.
As if being summoned by the branch-hands of the leafy trees,
which were beautiful with the ornaments of their own flowers,
that lord of kings approached the peaceful forest edge and attained nectar through the pleasures of royalty.
Never before attained. // 22 //
Like a seer in person, he enters into meditative absorption and dwells in happiness.

(Dak: 165) Then, having witnessed the extraordinary power of his asceticism, Sureśvara, the lord of the gods, descended from the realm of the gods— which was agitated by fear and dread arising from the destruction of that [ascetic’s] power— assuming the form of a bird, and taking up bow and arrows.
While he was swiftly pursuing a certain pigeon for the sake of striking it with an arrow,
the bird fell into the lap of the king who resided in the penance grove.
Then that king, his heart filled with compassion upon seeing him,
the lord of the earth, took him onto his own lap with supreme joy.
That pigeon, agitated by the fear of his enemy, stood with his heart trembling as if his life were at its end.
Immediately thereafter, Śakra, the lord of the gods, having assumed the form of a Niṣāda, approached him and, as if exhausted by great fatigue, heaving heavy sighs, questioned him.
"Give me the pigeon; I have come with great speed for food.
Today no food has been obtained; how shall I live without food? (Dak 16.23)
O ascetic!
The king said:
"How can I abandon you, O noble one, who have come to me for refuge?
And how is it that you do not recognize the happiness and suffering of all beings? (Dak 16.24)
How can I give over to you for food the pigeon that has come to me for refuge?
This is improper and unrighteous.
The Niṣāda said:
"If you do not release this pigeon,
give me the meat for my food;
otherwise, I shall die right here after uttering a curse."
When this had been said, the king spoke to the Niṣāda.
I shall fulfill your intention exactly as it is, for you who have come to me for refuge for the sake of protection.
The Niṣāda said:
"Excellent, O Lord of the Earth!
It is even so. Having weighed this pigeon on a scale, he said: 'Whatever flesh there is of this pigeon, give me an equal amount of flesh from another.'"
The king said:
For how could I harm another’s self, and how indeed, O friend, could I give it to him?
My own self and the other’s self, as well as pleasure and pain, are all equal. (Dak 16.25)
Having harmed another living being, what dharma or ascetic vow could there be?
And how can there be benefit for others by harming another within oneself? (Dak 16.26)
Therefore, I shall certainly give the flesh of my own body;
for how could there be any benefit from one who is sustained by a single [mouthful] and nourished by a single [hand]? (Dak_16.27)
Then the Niṣāda, having closely observed the firmness of his pure intention regarding the construction of the balance, sat down before him and said this to him:
"I am afflicted by hunger, emaciation, and thirst; what is the use of such long delay, O Lord?
Therefore, give this to me quickly; if you do not give it, I shall depart."
Having heard this, the king then placed the pigeon on one side and, having cut the flesh from his own body, he put it into the scale.
Then Śakra, in the form of a Niṣāda, by means of his supernatural power, made the pigeon heavier.
(Dak:
167) Then, with each successive addition, the pigeon became increasingly heavy;

nevertheless, through the sovereign’s power of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) in protecting his beloved pet bird, and by virtue of his unswerving mental affection, the king placed it on the scale even after reducing it to mere bones.
Then Śakra, having assumed the form of a Niṣāda, saw him and,
his mind being won over, said:

Excellent, excellent, O Great-souled One! You are of such a noble nature; for the sake of another, you have performed this difficult deed even without regard for your own life—what was it that you desired to do such a thing?
He said:
Having attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, I have no doubt whatsoever that I shall deliver all sentient beings.
Having heard this, that Niṣāda beheld his own body and spoke to him.
"O King, I wander about for the purpose of examining your mind. My good sir, let it be as you intend;
let your body be as it was before."
Having spoken thus and bestowed his blessing in the guise of Śakra, saying "So be it," he departed for his own abode.
At that time, I was that king; it should be seen that I was no other.
I conducted myself with an even mind toward all beings, including animals and birds.
Having now enjoyed great happiness within saṃsāra, I have become a Tathāgata and taught the Dharma to sentient beings.
(Dak: 168) Then those thirty-two brahmin disciples, headed by Puṣkara and Śāli, having heard the words of the Tathāgata, were filled with joy and gladness and said to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, we shall go forth in your teaching; please grant us your favor."
Then the Blessed One, having understood their disposition and their fundamental nature, spoke to them thus:
"If you so desire, please sit down."
And as soon as he said to them, "Come, monks," whatever sectarian marks they bore all vanished at that very moment.
The three robes and the alms bowl appeared.

Then their hair fell away, and just as the deportment of a monk ordained for hundreds of incalculable years is perfectly restrained, so too did that become their going forth, their full ordination, and their status as monks.
Because of a single thought of stinginess toward the Tathāgatas, a monk's robe and alms bowl did not reappear.
Then, monks, at that time, they prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and made this request:
In the presence of the Tathāgata, he conceived the perception of him as a Teacher, as well as love, serene confidence, and reverence.
Then, as his single robe was no longer visible, overcome once again by that sense of shame, he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and made this request.
"How is it, Blessed One, that a robe has not been produced for me alone?"
The Blessed One said:
"In the past, at the time of paying homage to the Tathāgatas, it was due to the fault of stinginess."
When this had been said, he sighed, offered a request for forgiveness, and bowed down before the Tathāgata.
Then, through the power of the Blessed One, a robe appeared.
At that very moment, it became soiled.
Seeing him, the monk, his mind bowed down with shame, spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, by what karma has my single robe not appeared, and once it had appeared, why did it become soiled?
What is the cause, what is the condition?"
The Blessed One said:

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, incalculable eons ago, the Perfectly Awakened One named Padmottara— having previously been Dīpaṃkara— while wandering on a tour through the countryside together with his Saṅgha,
arrived at a certain great kingdom.
There, standing in the middle of the street in that great city, he taught the Dharma.
Then all the citizens approached that place and heard the discourse on the Dharma.
Then a very learned brahmin named Somakaumudī, having heard that news together with his circles of disciples,
approached the place where the Perfectly Awakened One Padmottara was; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he stood before him and listened to the Dharma.
Then, having conceived faith, they all took up the going-forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Tathāgata.
With a sense of the Teacher, love, and reverence born toward the Tathāgata, they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Blessed One.
At that time, you were a disciple of the brahmin Somakaumudi.
At the moment of prostrating before the Tathāgata, you alone cultivated a mind of stinginess, thinking:
"If I do not perform this salutation to the ascetic, what will become of me?"
Due to that act of stinginess,
after undergoing births censurable by the world for many hundreds of thousands of years,
he was reborn as a great venomous serpent.
Even today, it is said that your skeletal remains of a venomous serpent remain in a cave of Mount Kālañjara, standing like a mountain of immense height and proportions.
Then, after the passing of a hundred years, he was born into a poor family; subsequently, he became a heretic, a wearer of matted hair, and a mendicant.

At that time, in the city of Pāṭaliputra, a certain householder prepared food endowed with the finest flavors for the sake of feeding the *tīrthikas*; having invited the *tīrthikas*, he fed them according to his own intention, saying:
"You have eaten twelve *prasthas* of milk-rice."
Nevertheless, his belly did not become full.
At that time, all people consider him to be a ghost beggar.
Immediately after that, sighing with shame, you thought to yourself:
Thinking, "Fie on this life," he departed from that place;
then, passing away from that very birth, he attained a human birth.
Then that brahmin, seeing him approaching together with his groups of disciples, [thought], "They have come here having met together."

Having experienced such suffering due to the sin committed through stinginess regarding prostration to the Tathāgata, even now, because of the remainder of that sin, he does not perform prostration; for that very reason, his robes and other requisites do not appear, and they have become soiled.
(Dak: 171) Then that monk, having said, "O Blessed One, may you likewise accept my transgression as a fault," prostrated at the feet of Gautama and stood there.
Then, through the power of the Blessed One, he was liberated from that evil;
and having cast off his soiled robe, it became as it was before.
"Thus, monks, you must not address the Tathāgata by name or by the title 'Venerable'."
"O monks, because he has now conceived a serene faith in my presence, by this root of merit he has attained arhatship."
Again, having addressed the monks, he spoke thus:

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, while serving as a disciple of the brahmin Somakaumudi, experienced such suffering due to the fault of stinginess at the moment of prostrating before the Tathāgata Padmottara—[was he anyone else?]"
Thus, I am the Brahmin Somakaumudi, and you are my disciples.
Even now, you have become my disciples.
And by virtue of the merit acquired through attending upon many Tathāgatas, I have experienced infinite happiness within saṃsāra and attained the state of a Tathāgata.
Therefore, monks, you should rejoice in the Tathāgata, serve the Tathāgata, proclaim the qualities and benefits of the Tathāgata, and bow down before the Tathāgata.
Listen to the great fruits and benefits of bowing down to the Tathāgatas.

The fact that a universal monarch is saluted with great devotion by the foremost of kings— who join their palms, whose cheeks are as beautiful as earrings, and who bow their noble heads— is said by those who know the truth to result from his prostration before the Buddha.

Those who, as soon as they are born, attain lordship and always take birth in an excellent family, travel about on elephants, horses, and vehicles, having paid homage to those even more excellent than themselves. (Dak_16.30)
It spreads renown, bestows excellence, increases splendor,
removes all misfortune, and indeed dispels every enemy;
it makes the lineage of men in this world certain of a happy rebirth.
And the salutation to the Lord of Sages inevitably bears fruit for one's welfare in the end. (Dak_16.31)

When a king becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), endowed with power and fame, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks—indeed, he arises as the preeminent among rulers—that is said to be the fruit of bowing to the Buddha. (Dak_16.32)
Having thus considered the body to possess many virtues yet to be fragile, what wise person would perform any other physical action than bowing to the Buddha? (Dak_16.33)
Who, seeing him from afar and fearing rebirth, would not pay him homage—
he by whose cause the mere act of a single prostration led one to reach the further shore of existence?
"In this way you should train: having cast aside black deeds, one should apply oneself solely to white deeds; thus, monks, you should train."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; and the monks rejoiced in what was spoken by him.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Story of the Prostration, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XVII. The Story of Giving the Burning Ember.
Then indeed the Blessed One—the compassionate one for the world, the knower of the world, the teacher of the world, the omniscient one—dwelt in the bliss of meditative absorption.
At that time, great calamities arose in the city of Vaiśālī.
Then all the citizens there, excessively lustful for sensual pleasures, indulged in whatever delights they desired and engaged in sinful conduct. (Dak_17.1)
Then, even a kṣatriya who is thus deluded by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, infatuated with a circle of women, and disrespectful toward ethics and dharma; Dak_17.2 //
Having seen the beautiful Sundarī, though she was unapproachable, he was infatuated;
having even forcibly drawn her toward him, he enjoyed her at his pleasure with delight.
Likewise, all those citizens, their intentions utterly corrupted, rejected the true Dharma and lived as pursuers of sensual pleasures. (Dak_17.4)
Having abandoned the boundaries of their own family dharma and acting according to their own whims,
they disregarded truth and righteousness, wandering like elephants in rut.
Likewise, groups of women, their minds agitated by the affliction of desire, abandon the dharma of their own families and act according to their whims. (Dak 17.6)
At that time, many wicked men—thieves, rogues, and the bold—who held no regard for the Dharma, would revile virtuous people and act [accordingly]. (Dak 17.7)
At that very moment, through the proliferation of evil, the Kali age spread everywhere;
the true Dharma grew weak and perished like something base.
Then, when the progression of the Kali age had become powerful there,
all the lords of the world, having seen it, turned their backs on the wicked.
In this way, the other gods as well, turning their backs on providing refuge everywhere,
did not even desire to grant them a vision of themselves.
Not even one among them was able to protect them in any way whatsoever;
thus, a great calamity broke out here on all sides.
Their souls struck down by all manner of afflictions, they engaged in mutual conflict;
and due to their particular sins, calamities manifested.
Then darkness appeared, shrouded by clouds;
a great, untimely wind and thunder roared amidst the clouds,
and flashes of lightning issued forth.
The ten directions became agitated, and a blinding darkness appeared;
the sun and moon did not shine,
and a wind and rainstorm blew forth.
The earth became flooded with water as if at the time of universal dissolution; it was no longer firm, being possessed by certain beings.
Then the entire multitude of people became terrified and agitated in mind;
whatever brahmins and householders there were who paid homage to Brahmā,
some who paid homage to Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, Śakra, Māṇibhadra, Hārītī, the moon, the sun, the planets, and the constellations, all began to offer prayers.
Some offer sacrifices to rivers, lakes, ponds, tanks, wells, and so forth;
nevertheless, there is no protection whatsoever.
(Dak: 176) Then, some who were devoted to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha paid homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
O Blessed One, you are the all-seeing one!
How may we be completely liberated from such a calamity, from this place of fear?
O Blessed One, Protector, be our savior from such a disaster!
Having spoken thus and paid homage to the Buddha, he remained absorbed in reflection.
In this interval, there is nothing whatsoever unknown or unperceived by the Blessed Buddhas.

Indeed, it is the natural law (dharmatā) of the Blessed Buddhas— those who are greatly compassionate, who act for the benefit of the world, and who maintain a single mode of protection— that [they perceive all things].

Those who dwell in calm abiding and insight, who are skilled in the three bases of training, who have crossed over the four floods, who are well-established on the soles of their feet through the four bases of psychic power, and who have long practiced familiarity with the four means of attraction;
who have abandoned the five factors, who have transcended the five destinies,
who are endowed with the six factors, who have fulfilled the six perfections,
and who are richly adorned with the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment;

For those who see the eightfold path, who are skilled in the nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling, who possess the power of the ten strengths, whose fame fills the ten directions, and who are superior to the thousand lords of the Vaśavartin gods— having surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye for three nights and three days, their vision of knowledge proceeds.

"Who is declining? Who is prospering? Who has fallen into hardship? Who has fallen into distress? Who has fallen into calamity? Who has fallen into both hardship and calamity? For whom, sunk in the mire of suffering, shall I provide a hand to lift them up? Whom shall I rescue?"
(Dak: 177) Then, at that very moment, having risen and returned,
he addressed the community of monks headed by the venerable Ānanda.
"O monks, go to the city of Vaiśālī at my command and by my word; having gone to the city of Vaiśālī, sit in the middle of the street and recite this verse.
Then all obstructing spirits and grahas will surely be silenced, and all calamities and wicked beings will flee.
It is as follows:"
And these verses:
"Disperse, disperse, you wicked beings! Release, release! Do not remain! May this calamity be stilled!"
Having addressed the community of monks in this way, he dismissed them.
Then those monks, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and having received the words of the Blessed One upon their heads,
kept this dhāraṇī for dispelling obstacles in their hearts.

At that very moment, by means of their supernatural power, the community of five hundred monks led by Ānanda arrived at that region from the sky like royal swans with crimson wings descending from the heavens.
Then the community of monks, headed by Ānanda, went to the city of Vaiśālī and, standing in the middle of the street, began to recite this verse with one mind and one voice in the Brahma-like tone:
And these are the verses: (Dak: 178)
Disperse, disperse! The Buddha, who has compassion for the world, commands: release, release! Do not remain!
May the plague be pacified!
Depart, depart!
The Buddha, the supreme teacher of gods and men, now enters from Mahādeva.
The gods together with Indra, along with Brahmā and Prajāpati, and the four world-protectors shall enter, as will many thousands of deities.
The lords of the asuras and many hundreds of thousands of asuras shall dwell there.
And many thousands of spirits, being devoted to the Blessed One, shall manifest for the sake of all sentient beings.
And may they not cause me harm.
Go forth, go forth!
Flee quickly!
If you do not depart with evil intent, you shall perish!
Those who possess minds of loving-kindness, who do not desire to commit offenses, and who wish to follow the protection—let them stay and enter.

Thus does the Buddha, who has compassion for the world, give this command: he whose resolute intention is the welfare of all beings, who dwells in loving-kindness, dwells in compassion, dwells in sympathetic joy, and dwells in equanimity.
These mantra-words are perfected; they are the perfected verses spoken by the Victors for the benefit of all deities and beings who desire welfare.
Through this supreme knowledge, and likewise through the nature of reality (dharmatā), may all the calamities of the worlds be pacified today; may you possess health.

When this was spoken, the hosts of all beings were terrified; with agitated minds, they fled in the ten directions and perished. Those wicked beings, whose hearts were intent on harm and whose minds were provoked to anger, became completely stilled.
And at that time, the sky became filled with clouds, lightning, wind, and rain, yet it was subsequently calmed.
And they became beautifully adorned with fruits and flowers, possessing divine flavor and sweetness.

Thus, through the power of the Buddha, all calamities and famines in that city were pacified; all seasons flourished according to their intended purpose, rain fell at the proper time, and the winds blew at the proper time.
Then all the assemblies of people, filled with great joy, invited all the communities of monks to take up residence and partake of meals.
Then, monks, at the end of the rainy season, at the end of autumn, and at the end of the four months, when the cold season had arrived, Ānanda and the others spoke thus to the multitude of people:
Four months have passed while we have remained here; let us go into the presence of our teacher.
When this had been said, the entire assembly of people, having perceived that it was time for the community of monks to depart, honored, worshiped, and revered them, and then dismissed them.
Then those monks, walking on foot from city to city with steadfastness, arrived at a certain district in another country.
(Dak: 180) Now, in that country, there was a man who was exceedingly wealthy, abundant in gold and bullion, possessing great enjoyments, vast possessions, and great generosity;
he had a large retinue, was pure in intention, righteous in nature, and helpful to others, taking delight in supporting ascetics, brahmins, and mendicants.
The merchant named Śuddhacetas, who had been seen by Mahākāruṇya as one who delivers those suffering from their suffering, dwelt in the play of happiness surrounded by thirty-two women.
Renunciation at the proper time; enjoyment at the proper time.

Seeing those monks assembled there and perceiving that they had come afflicted by the cold, the merchant was overcome with great compassion; he respectfully led them to his fire-hall, kindled a blazing fire, and gave it to them.
That merchant had many fire-halls constructed, and by means of the heat from those fires, groups of five hundred monks were satisfied.
Thereafter, food was offered;
those monks did not eat that food.
Seeing this, the merchant said to them:
"Monks, by whom has the food given by me not been consumed?"
The monks said:
"O monks, that which is not to be eaten out of season is that which occurs at the time of sunset and during the night; this is what the Buddha has declared."
Then that merchant, having said "So be it," entered his house.
Then, at the end of the night, during the morning hours, he honored them by providing alms-food and other offerings according to their respective needs.
(Dak: 181) Then those monks, having taken him and given him their pure blessings, announced, "We shall go," and departed from that place.
Having departed, they approached the Blessed One at Vulture Peak; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then the monk Ānanda, rising from his seat, stood before the Blessed One and spoke as follows.
O Blessed One, Omniscient One, just as you commanded, so indeed were all calamities in the city of Vaiśālī completely pacified.
Thinking it was through your power, we have come here.
The Blessed One said:
Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! Excellent, excellent, monks! In this way, one should exert oneself for the sake of others.
Then Ānanda spoke again to the Blessed One.
"Lord, when you had departed from the city of Vaiśālī, we arrived at a certain district in another country.
We went to that city;
there, a certain wealthy merchant, seeing us arrive weary from the cold wind and fatigue, respectfully called out to us."
Having first brought the fire into the fire-hall and kindled it, he gives [the gift];
for there are many fire-halls.
This man was a merchant of supreme righteousness;
whenever any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or tīrthikas arrived, he would light a brazier and give it to them all out of faith during the winter and cold seasons.
The Blessed One said:
The great fruits and benefits of the *ujjvālikā* are like nectar at the onset of the cool season; therefore, monks, listen as I speak of these great fruits and benefits of the *ujjvālikā*.

That the lords of the earth, in the winter season, sport within inner chambers embraced by the pair of arms of their most beloved wives— wearing soft, magnificent garments made from the wool of various deer species, and provided with an abundance of food and drink of diverse flavors and excellences— is the exceedingly sweet fruit of the *ujjvālikā* offering dedicated to the community of monks.

Having given to the most excellent of great sages a blazing torch— enveloped by a spreading fire with waves of flames, making a terrifying sound, and destroying the cold of winter— one becomes possessed of radiant splendor in the worlds of gods and men.
Accompanied by Gandharvas, Asuras, and Kinnaras, with radiant faces resembling the flash of lightning or the autumnal moon,
these gods wander through heaven with glowing bodies, sporting and embraced by their beloveds.
Having given that with faith to the community of noble ones during the cold season, along with a warming lamp, [one attains great merit].

Those who, having conquered their enemies, rule the earth on all sides with elephants and horses—their faces radiant and their bodies adorned with gold—reap nothing but the fruit of the blazing funeral pyre. (Dak 17.18)

If those people, desiring to obtain such a fruit, should provide glowing embers—having established fire-houses during the cold of winter—for the community of noble monks and others, constantly; Dak_17.19.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Story of the Gift of the Burning Torch, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XVIII. The Discourse on the Lamp.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“Blessed One, I wish to hear what the fruit of offering a lamp is;
whether at a stūpa or before an image of the Buddha, please speak for the sake of the world’s welfare. (Dak_18.1)
The Blessed One, having remained silent for a moment and having surveyed the assembly, addressed Maitreya and spoke thus:
Listen, Maitreya, I shall speak for the sake of the welfare of the world; having heard this auspicious narrative that I have heard, joy will arise. (Dak_18.2)

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one kalpas ago, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.

When the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin had completed all the works of a Buddha and passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted, King Bandhumat performed the funeral rites for his body and erected a stupa made of the four jewels, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
Where many hundreds of thousands of living beings, having passed away, become intent upon heaven and liberation.
A great festival was held at that stūpa;
faithful brahmins and householders performed worship with various perfumes, garlands, ointments, umbrellas, banners, and flags.
(Dak: 185) Then, at another time, in this city, there was a certain man who was deprived of hands and feet, whose body was afflicted with leprosy, and who was unable to go anywhere.
Having heard that very report, this thought occurred to him:
"O brahmins and householders, you are honoring this stūpa;
likewise, I too would honor it in this way. But being devoid of feet and hands and unable to move, how could I go?"
Having said this, an understanding arose in him.

Tonight, having generated the strength, power, and vigor of my own body, I shall cause him to go forth from his home; and once he has gone forth, if he is capable, let him perform the circumambulation.
Having spoken thus, at night, while the moon and its moonlight were shining brightly, he generated the power of a *kāyasthāma* and arrived near the stūpa through the exertion of his strength.
His body tormented by the affliction of lethargy and drowsiness, he sighed and collapsed upon the ground.
Then that man, having paid homage to this stūpa, began to circumambulate it himself by turning his body;
thereafter, throughout that very night, he performed one hundred and eight complete circumambulations.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, at that very moment the toes of this man became properly formed;
likewise, his sprout-like hands were restored,
and the leprosy on his body was cured.
Having destroyed his previous karmic obscurations through this root of merit from his difficult vow, he became one of pure body.

(Dak: 186) Then that man, having become filled with faith, once again performed a prostration with eight limbs before the stūpa; then at dawn, his heart gladdened and his face beaming with a smile, he returned to his own home.
Then, seeing that he had arrived at his own home, his wife and the rest of the household members, their minds filled with devotion, spoke.
"Oh! Where have you gone?

How is it that your body has been liberated from misdeeds and has become healthy? Oh, what a marvel of supreme fortune! You have attained a state exactly like a rebirth. Without being touched by physicians or medicines, by whom was this leprosy cast off?"
He said:
What can be accomplished by physicians and medicines for the pacification of a great disease?
But by merit performed toward the Buddhas, one is released from evil. (Dak_18.3)
Then that man indeed performed one hundred thousand circumambulations around that stūpa;
having done so, he reflected:
"What if I were to honor and worship the stupa of the Blessed One with such offerings? Surely no worship could ever equal that which is performed by the sacrifice of one's own body."
"It has been accepted."
Thereafter, every month on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the bright fortnight, he observed the upoṣadha vow for one year and performed worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, beginning from the full moon of Kārttika until the full moon of Āśvina, he observed fasts and began to illuminate his own true nature.
Then, from the sky, a voice was uttered, pronouncing these words:
Thus, do not perform such an abandonment of your own body, which is a great hardship, a supreme hardship;
for you are not the equal of the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana.
Therefore, it is not easy for you to accomplish this.
He asked, "How is that?"
Again, from the sky, he spoke thus:
In the past, there appeared in the world the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candravimalasūryaprabhāsaśrī.
The lifespan of that Blessed One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was four million two hundred thousand kalpas;
the lifespan of those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and Śrāvakas was exactly the same.

For the purpose of honoring him, at that moment, the Bodhisattva named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana entered the samādhi called "Appearance of the Forms of All Beings. Immediately upon entering that samādhi,
by its power, a great rain of flowers— of mandārava and mahāmandārava blossoms— fell from the sky above.
