A cloud of black sandalwood, following the wind, was formed and rained down a shower of the finest uragasāra sandalwood;
such was the Bodhisattva named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana who pervaded this Sahā world-system with his fragrance.
(Dak: 188) Then indeed, the bodhisattva named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, mindful and clearly comprehending, arose from that samādhi.
Having arisen, he reflected thus:
The worship of the Blessed One through the display of the miracle of supernatural power is not performed in such a way as it is by the relinquishing of one's own body.
Then, at that time, the bodhisattva named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having mixed agallochum, turushka, and kunduruka, drank campaka oil.
For twelve years, he continuously and constantly consumed incense and drank fragrant oil.

Then, at the end of those twelve years, having wrapped his own body in divine garments and saturated it with fragrant oil, he set his body ablaze as an act of worship for the Tathāgata and for the sake of honoring this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Then, indeed, by those flames of light emitted from the lamps on the body of that bodhisattva, world-systems as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges rivers were pervaded.
In those world-systems, Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of eighty Ganges rivers gave their approval, saying, "Excellent!"
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! The arousal of vigor by Bodhisattvas is a most difficult task; such is the worship of the Tathāgata, the worship of the Dharma.

Noble son, the offering of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, parasols, banners, and flags is not the supreme gift; likewise, the gift consisting of the renunciation of one's kingdom, beloved sons, wife, and so forth, is not [the supreme gift]."
Furthermore, noble son, this is the most distinguished and supreme form of worship; beyond it, there is nothing else.
Having spoken these words, those Buddhas became silent.
At that time, after the lapse of twelve thousand years, the body of the Bodhisattva named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, which had been blazing with light, became completely extinguished.

Then, having passed away from there, he was reborn by spontaneous birth in the house of King Vimaladatta within the teaching of that perfectly enlightened Buddha; endowed with all the qualities of the primary marks, he appeared sitting cross-legged upon the king's lap.
It is not easy for you to undertake such an exertion of vigor.
Therefore, reflecting with a mind appropriate to your own person, prepare your own body, wrap it in a divine cloth,
kindle it with the great lamp named Mahādīpa, which measures ninety-six finger-breadths in length, and likewise kindle a garland of lamps.
In this manner, it was uttered from space and spoken by him.
Who are you, sir?
He said: "O Blessed One, I am your own essential nature; I should not be seen as anyone else."
Once again, filled with joy, he said:
"Blessed One, how could I fail to honor my own vow?

By this sacrifice of my body and by setting it ablaze, I have done what neither mother, nor father, nor other deities could ever do; rather, through your power, even this very day my karmic obstructions have been brought to an end."
(Ah! This field consists of virtues and is free from all defects;
the seed was sown this very day, and this very day its fruit has been obtained. (Dak_18.4)
Therefore, Blessed One, disregarding my own life, I desire to illuminate my own person.
Once again, a voice issued forth from the sky.
"Excellent, excellent, O bull among men! You are firm in your vow; act exactly as you have seen.
When this is done, let your fame endure for as long as cyclic existence lasts.
When it is thus accomplished, even Māra will not be able to cause anyone's mind to waver."
When this was said, he looked toward the sky;
he saw the form of a Buddha,
which vanished in an instant.
Then that man, filled with joy and gladness, looked toward the sky and stood with his palms joined in reverence, bowing down.

Then that man, having ascertained the truth itself, wrapped it with his own body in a divine white cloth, smeared it with fragrant substances the size of his own limbs, and saying "Great Lamp," he lit a lamp at the reliquary stupa of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin;
they also fashioned a garland of lamps.
He honored [the Blessed One] continuously for the entire month of Kārttika.

Then, by virtue of that root of merit and through the power of his aspiration, that man was reborn in the world-system Dīpārcis as a Pratyekabuddha named Dīparāja, having attained the five superknowledges.

Then that Pratyekabuddha, realizing that cyclic existence is essence-less, performed a miraculous feat like a flash of lightning; having ascended into the air to the height of seven palm trees, he entered the fire-element and passed into final nirvana like a falling meteor.
Whatever bile, phlegm, flesh, bone, sinew, and blood he had, all that was completely purified by his splendor, and he became one whose body was pure.
Having thus attained infinite happiness within saṃsāra, he proceeded to the stage of nirvāṇa.
Monks, by the gift of a lamp, one obtains great merit and great benefits, resulting in manifold karmic maturations.
Listen again in detail.
Even an object that is obscured by mountains, situated in an extremely remote land, exceedingly subtle, or shrouded by masses of intense darkness—
whatever is seen by him with unobstructed vision stands as if it were right at the tip of his hand, throughout all directions.
He beheld the fruit of giving a lamp of great brilliance to the Sugata.
Those people who see the visible world—whether distant, subtle, or situated [before them]—the Sages have declared that to be the fruit of the Garland of Lamps for the Victor. (Dak_18.6)
That kings with bodies like the moon and eyes like long blue lotuses are seen;
that gods, resembling fine gold, illuminate the world of the gods with their own radiance;
and that a universal monarch (cakravartin) proceeds while illuminating the earth with hundreds of rays from his jewels.
All that comes to embodied beings through the gift of a lamp to the Lord Buddha. (Dak 18.7)
Whatever mortals shine in the world with lotus-like eyes, beautiful brows, and golden complexions;
whatever Śakra, the king of gods, shines seated upon his celestial throne with his thousand eyes;
and whatever Brahmā, free from desire and honored by the foremost of the gods, shines in his divine palatial chariot—[all these arise from that source].
Having offered that garland of lamps at the stūpa of the Teacher, it brings forth excellent fruit for human beings.
Having thus recognized the many virtues resulting from the power of giving a lamp,
one who would offer even a single one obtains all that fruit through this endeavor.
He becomes handsome and pleasing to the eyes; he becomes one who is to be gazed upon by both women and men.
In the same way, monks, human beings should always perform their ritual actions with lamps at the time of worship.
During the worship of the deities, while eating, and by properly washing the feet;
likewise upon entering a temple of the gods and during times of sleep. (Dakṣa 18.10)
All action performed by one endowed with the ornament of ethical discipline is praised; furthermore, one should perform both internal purification and external, worldly purification. (Dak 18.11)
Whoever in this world performs that which is pure, both mundane and supramundane, shall be renowned in this world and experience supreme happiness in the next world. (Dak_18.12)
Monks, you should train yourselves thus; this is the instruction for the world.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the Story of Dīpa, within the Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
XIX. Discourse on Monasteries.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Blessed One, I wish to hear what the fruit is of the gift of a monastery.”
To some most noble Ārya, and to the Sugata, [I offer] a house and so forth.
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Maitreya, as I shall show you the fruits and benefits for those who cause monasteries and palaces to be built for the dwelling of the Tathāgatas, the perfectly awakened ones.
Then, at that time, through the power of the Tathāgata, all the people of the city of Rājagṛha became desirous of seeing the Blessed One.
When that had come to pass, all the multitudes of people from Magadha gathered on Vulture Peak.

In that assembly, the gods, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas who were present, as well as the entire congregation whose minds were noble and disciplined by the Buddha, paid homage to the Buddha with palms joined.
They remained there, reflecting, "What kind of miraculous feat will the Blessed One display today?"
Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

Now, King Ajātaśatru, instigated by Devadatta, has deprived his father— the righteous Dharmarāja— of life and established himself in the kingdom. Consequently, those who lacked faith have become powerful, while those who possessed faith have become weak.
(Dak: 195) Meanwhile, a certain senior minister, who was faithless and hostile toward the teaching of the Blessed One,
began to perform a sacrifice for Ajātaśatru among the brahmins.
There, many hundreds of thousands of brahmins had assembled; they made a formal agreement among themselves.
"No one should approach the ascetic Gautama for the sake of seeing him. Do not offer him honor or respect if he comes here;
do not give him almsfood."
Then those selected brahmins, all together and rejoicing, proceeded in the middle of the street to entreat Śakra according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas, saying:
"Come, come, O Lord of the Gods!"
Now, immediately thereafter, there is nothing whatsoever unknown, unseen, or unrecognized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
the Blessed One beheld with his Buddha-eye.

"These brahmins have previously planted roots of merit and have grasped the path to liberation; they are seekers of conduct, facing toward nirvāṇa and turned away from saṃsāra due to their association with non-virtuous friends.
Now, however, they harbor hatred toward my teaching. What if I were to apply myself with zeal for the sake of their discipline, so that it may lead to their welfare?"
"What if I were to summon Śakra, the lord of the gods, surrounded by his host of Maruts, so that by the sight of him their roots of merit might increase?"
"O Śakra, Lord of the Devas, accompanied by the host of Maruts, take a pillar made of gośīrṣa sandalwood and come!"
(Dak: 196) At the very moment that thought arose, Śakra, the lord of the gods, surrounded by a host of Maruts, arrived at the place where Viśvakarman and the four Great Kings,
accompanied by many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and kumbhāṇḍas, were carrying a pillar made of gośīrṣa sandalwood.
Uttering loud cries of "Hāhā! and "Kilakilā!
and shouts of exultation, they constructed a monastery made of gośīrṣa sandalwood for the sake of the Blessed One.

Then, in that monastery, Śakra, the lord of the gods, honored and revered the Blessed One together with the community of disciples with divine food, bedding, seats, and divine perfumes, garlands, ointments, flowers, and incense.
Honored and worshiped.
Then this sound spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha in every direction.
On Vulture Peak, Śakra, the lord of the gods, together with the host of Maruts, having constructed a dwelling for the Blessed One, was honored and worshiped by all the hosts of gods.
Having heard this, many thousands of living beings assembled.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the brahmins had been won over, broke all their agreements and approached the Blessed One on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; having approached,
they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then those brahmins, having seen that divine majesty of the Blessed One, were struck with supreme wonder and fell into this reflection:

"Surely the Buddha, the Blessed One, is preeminent in the world, since he is indeed honored by the gods together with Indra"—with their minds thus won over, they sat down once more before the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One gave such a teaching of the Dharma that penetrates the four noble truths;
having heard it, sixty thousand brahmins shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rises with twenty peaks, with the vajra of knowledge, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
And faith in the Blessed One was attained by many hundreds of thousands of living beings.
Then, monks, those humans and hosts of gods who had conceived an exceedingly deep faith in that monastery did not venture to leave that monastery or set their minds on going elsewhere.
Then the Blessed One, having caused that palace to disappear, delivered a discourse on the Dharma concerning impermanence.
Such is the impermanence of saṃsāra; therefore, saṃsāra is empty, the five aggregates alone are empty, and all is impermanence.
Having heard which, many brahmins attained the vision of the Noble Truths regarding the Blessed One.
And by many hundreds of thousands of living beings, both humans and others, the fruit of stream-entry was attained;
by some, the fruit of once-returning;
and by some, the fruit of non-returning.
Some, having gone forth, realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions;
some resolved their minds upon the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; and some upon the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Some [were established] in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and that entire assembly was established as leaning toward the Buddha, inclined toward the Dharma, and directed toward the Saṅgha.
Then those monks, their minds captivated by the sight of the divine worship offered to the Blessed One, questioned the Blessed One.
"In what place were these roots of merit performed by the Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said:

Monks, these deeds were performed and accumulated by the Tathāgata himself in previous births; their conditions have been fulfilled, their causes have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable—that by which such worship as this has come to the Tathāgata.
"Do you wish to hear it, monks?"
"So be it, Venerable Sir. "Therefore, monks, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak."
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, there appeared in the world a Truly Enlightened One named Surendradamana,
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
While wandering on a journey through the countryside, he arrived at a certain royal capital.
That royal capital was occupied by heretics.
A certain consecrated Kṣatriya king named Surendradamana heard that the Perfectly Awakened One had arrived within his realm.

Having heard this, Mahātya, endowed with great royal majesty and great royal power, approached the place where the Perfectly Awakened One Surendradamana was; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Surendradamana, and sat down to one side.
To the consecrated Kṣatriya king seated in seclusion, the Perfectly Awakened One, Surendradamana, exhorted him with the qualities that bring about enlightenment.

Then that anointed Kṣatriya king, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Perfectly Awakened One Surendradamana, addressed the Perfectly Awakened One Surendradamana as follows:
"May the Blessed One consent to my invitation to dwell for the three months of the rainy season;
I shall attend upon the Blessed One with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
The Blessed One said:
"Great King, is there in your realm any monastery where both visiting and departing monks may take up residence?"
The king said:
"No, Blessed One.
Rather, let it be, Blessed One;
I shall build a monastery where both visiting and departing monks may stay."
They will prepare a dwelling.
Then the king had a monastery built for the sake of the Tathāgata;

it was provided with high walls and arched gateways, adorned with windows, balconies, lattices, crescent-shaped ornaments, and railings; it was furnished with carpets, filled with water reservoirs, surrounded by groves of trees, and endowed with various flowers and fruits.
Having thus completed it, he offered it to the Blessed One together with the community of disciples and entreated the Blessed One to perform a great miracle.

Then the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One Surendradamana, displayed his entreaty to the king and performed various miracles, the playful display of the Buddha-ornament. Upon seeing this, the king, together with his ministers, the merchants, the people of the countryside, and all the city-dwellers, became deeply serene and devoted to the teaching.
"What do you think, monks? He who was the king at that time and on that occasion was I myself.
By me such an offering was made to this Samyaksaṃbuddha Surendradamana.
Through the ripening of that karma, I have experienced infinite happiness throughout saṃsāra."
Now that I am a Tathāgata, this is the splendor of my teaching.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves accordingly.
We shall honor the Tathāgata.
The great benefits of the Tathāgata’s monasteries, palaces, and dwellings are the great fruits and advantages of giving.
Listen again!
On the excellent palace terraces delightful in all seasons, kings take their pleasure with the songs of victorious melodies born from music, accompanied by the women who guard the inner apartments;
and through the gift of monasteries for the community of noble mendicants from the four directions, they enjoy a state free from cold.
By the grace of him who has utterly shattered the mountain of the Kali age with the blow of the vajra of wisdom,

whoever constructs a monastery— rendered beautiful by every requisite— in honor of the Saṅgha, [shall dwell] with beloved women within the Vaijayanta palace, amidst walls and pillars made of the finest jewels.
He alone shall rejoice for a long time in the world of the gods, which is delightful in all seasons.

By giving to the preeminent and virtuous Gaṇa a magnificent house— a principal residence with excellent canopies, variegated lotus-patterned cloths, and walls covered in blue and other colors— one attains Vaijayanta, the jewel of Indra’s palaces.
"The gift of a dwelling has great benefits and great fruits and advantages;
thus, monks, you should train yourselves."
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the Story of the Monastery, within this collection of twenty-two avadānas.
XX. The Gift of Golden Radiance. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One in this way:
O Blessed One, O Lord of Orators, please explain all of this for the awakening of the entire world: what is the fruit arising from the worship of the image of a shrine? (Dak_20.1)
The Blessed One said:
Listen, Ajita; attend well and properly to it, and I shall speak of the even greater merit born from honoring a stūpa.
As it is thus heard in tradition:
Long ago, Maitreya, on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Kapilavastu, in the Nyagrodha Grove, together with a great Saṅgha.

At that time, in that very Kapilavastu, there was a certain Śākya who was wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, with extensive and vast holdings; he was as prosperous as Vaiśravaṇa and rivaled the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and dallied with her.
While he was playing, taking pleasure, and dallying, his wife became pregnant.
After the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; he surpassed human appearance and attained a divine golden hue like that of refined Jāmbūnada gold.
And by this golden-colored radiance, the entire city of Kapilavastu was illuminated. Upon seeing him—
His parents and other beings who had gathered out of curiosity were struck with great wonder and thought, "From where has such a distinguished being as this come?"
When he was born, a birth festival was performed and his name was established;
they deliberated, "What shall be the name of this boy?"
The kinsmen said:
"Since, upon his birth, the entire city of Kapilavastu was illuminated by a golden-colored radiance, let the boy's name be Suvarṇābha."
Then the boy, who was golden-hued, was entrusted to eight nurses:
two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
Reared by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other excellent, refined nourishments, he grew rapidly like a lotus in a pond.

Like a lotus, that wise man was discerning, intelligent, faithful, auspicious, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma.
Then, at another time, while he was sporting outside the monastery, intoxicated by the pride of his physical form,
a great many Śākyas were traveling along that very same road toward the Nyagrodha Grove.
Thereupon, Suvarṇābha saw them and asked, "Where are you gentlemen going?"

They said, "Let us go to the Nyagrodha Grove to see the Buddha, the Blessed One. Upon hearing the name "Buddha"— the word *Suvarṇābha* having heard a name never heard before— all their pores bristled with joy, and a supreme sense of wonder arose.
The thought occurred to him:
"What if I were also to approach the Blessed One for a visit?
He, too, went to the Nyagrodha Grove.

Then that youth Suvarṇābha beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a splendor exceeding a thousand suns, like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious in every respect.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, he prostrated at his feet and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One taught him the Dharma;
having heard that teaching, he became desirous of going forth.

Having obtained permission from his mother and father, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I practice the holy life under the Blessed One."
Then the Blessed One, extending his gold-colored arm which resembled the trunk of an elephant, said this to the boy Suvarṇābha:
"Come, young man; lead the holy life."

When addressed by the Tathāgata with the word "Come," he—shaven-headed and his body wrapped in the saṃghāṭī robe—immediately stood in that very place with his senses perfectly tranquil, in accordance with the Buddha's intention. (Dak: 205) Dak_20.2 //
When he had had his hair and beard shaved for seven days, possessed the deportment of one ordained for twelve years, and stood before the Blessed One with bowl and robe held in his hands,
the Blessed One gave him instructions on mental attention (*manasikāra*).
By applying himself, striving, and exerting himself, he [perceived] this very five-fold wheel of saṃsāra.

Having understood that the course of all conditioned phenomena is both moving and unmoving, and having struck down [all attachment] by means of the nature of decay, falling, dissolution, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.
He became an arhat, free from passion for the fire-element, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, and viewing an axe and sandalwood alike.

Having split open the eggshell of ignorance with knowledge, having attained the superknowledges, the higher faculties, and the analytical insights, and having turned his back on existence, gain, greed, and honor, he became one to be worshipped,
revered, and saluted by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
The monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what meritorious deeds were performed by Suvarṇābha, by which he obtained such a most excellent fruit?"
The Blessed One said:
"Suvarṇābha himself performed those actions; having accumulated their provisions and reached their ripening conditions, they have arrived like a flood and are inevitable.
Suvarṇābha performed and accumulated those actions—who else shall experience them?"

Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external element of earth, nor in the element of water, nor in the element of fire, nor in the element of wind; rather, actions performed— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (Dak_20.3)

Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, a Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vipaśyin arose in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Eventually, after the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin had performed his Buddha-work, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
Then King Bandhumat, having performed the worship of the Blessed One’s remains, erected a stupa made of the four jewels, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
And a festival for the stūpa was prepared.
While that stūpa festival was underway, a certain householder came forth.
From that stūpa, he saw a golden mirror fall;
having had it fashioned into an ear-ornament, he placed it upon that stūpa.
Having performed worship with perfumes, incense, and flowers, he prostrated at its feet and made a solemn vow.
"May I too become a possessor of such qualities;
may I please a Teacher such as this."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the householder, is this very Suvarṇābha. Because he performed acts of service for the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin, such a distinction of physical form as this came to be for him. And because he made a vow, Arhatship has been realized by him in this very life."
"Monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; that of entirely white actions is entirely white; and that of mixed actions is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned entirely black actions as well as mixed ones, you should apply yourselves only to entirely white actions.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the Suvarṇābhāvadāna, within the collection of twenty-two avadānas.
XXI. The Avadāna of Vapuṣmān.
Then that Lord of Sages, the Lion of the Śākyas, a mine of virtues, having gazed upon the assembly of monks, spoke this avadāna concerning Vapuṣmān. (Dak_21.1)
The monks said:
O Blessed One, All-Knowing Teacher, having heard our auspicious words, you ought to speak further concerning those who have performed merit for the sake of the Buddha. (Dak_21.2)
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, monks! Furthermore, on one occasion, there lived in that great city of Kapilavastu a certain Śākya.
He was wealthy, possessed of great riches and a large retinue; his possessions were vast and extensive, he was as abundant in wealth as Vaiśravaṇa, and he rivaled Vaiśravaṇa himself.
From a family of equal status, he took a wife."
He played, took delight, and amused himself with her.
While he was thus playing, taking delight, and amusing himself, his wife became pregnant and gave birth to a son who was handsome,
beautiful to behold, pleasing, fair-skinned, surpassing human appearance yet not having fully attained divine appearance, and whose body had delicate skin.

He was of great renown and had attained a purified body. When his birth took place, a great celebration for his birth was held, and his name was established; they asked, "What shall be the name of this child?"
The kinsmen said,
"Since his body is divine, let the boy's name be Vapuṣmān."
The handsome boy was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.

He was reared and nourished by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other excellent, refined provisions; he grew rapidly like a lotus in a lake.

He was faithful, noble, of virtuous intent, dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, and a lover of the Dharma; he was honored, revered, and saluted by all the world.
Furthermore, whatever regions Vapuṣmān goes to and traverses, they all become pure for him; such is one who is renowned for his great power of merit.
Then, at another time, he went to the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then he beheld the Blessed Buddha, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
his body resplendent with the eighty secondary characteristics, graced by a fathom-wide halo, possessing a radiance exceeding that of a thousand suns,
like a moving mountain of jewels, auspicious on all sides; and upon seeing him, in the presence of the Blessed One—
With his mind purified and having conceived serene faith, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
The Blessed One, having understood his disposition, underlying tendencies, element, and nature, delivered a discourse on the Dharma that penetrates the Four Noble Truths.
Upon hearing it, Vapuṣmat shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he obtained permission from his parents and went forth in the teaching of the Blessed One.

By applying himself with diligence and exertion, he understood the entire wheel of saṃsāra to be unstable and unsteady; having struck down all conditioned states by realizing their nature as subject to decay, falling, scattering, and destruction, he realized arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions.

He became an Arhat, free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like the palm of a hand or the open sky, indifferent toward the axe or sandalwood, having rent the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, and turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor; he became one worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods, including Indra and Upendra.
Then the monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable Sir, what deeds were performed by Vapuṣmān such that he obtained such a physical form and attained arhatship?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, in former births, Vapuṣmān performed and accumulated actions that had gathered their requisite conditions, whose causes had matured, which stood before him like a surging flood,
and which were inevitable."
"Who else shall experience the actions performed and accumulated by Vapuṣmān?
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element."

Actions performed—whether wholesome or unwholesome—ripen not in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor even in the wind element, but rather in the very aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that have arisen.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one eons ago, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Vipaśyin appeared in the world—
one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
He dwelt in dependence upon the royal capital of Bandhumatī.
Eventually, after the Perfectly Awakened One Vipaśyin had completed all the works of a Buddha, he passed away into the realm of nirvana without remainder, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
Then King Bandhumat, having performed the funeral rites for the body, erected a stūpa made of the four jewels, one yojana in circumference and one krośa in height.
And there, King Bandhumat, together with his circle of sons, surrounded by a host of ministers and attendants, held a festival for the stūpa.
Then, on a certain day, a certain poor man entered the courtyard of the stūpa; there he saw that the flowers had withered and that the color [of the ground] had been defiled by dust.
Thereupon, recollecting the virtues of the Buddha and having conceived a sense of serene faith, he took up a broom.
The stūpa was swept clean and its withered flowers were removed.
Then, seeing the stūpa free from dust and stainless, he was filled with serene faith; prostrating at its feet, he made this aspiration:
"By this wholesome production of the thought of awakening, may I become a possessor of such qualities as these;
may I please a Teacher such as this, and never displease him."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the poor man, he is this Vapuṣmān. Because he swept the stūpa, he has become handsome; because he made a vow, he has realized arhatship in this present life."
"Monks, for actions that are exclusively black, the ripening is exclusively black;
for those that are exclusively white, the ripening is exclusively white; and for those that are mixed, the ripening is mixed.

Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black as well as those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves solely to actions that are exclusively white. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Furthermore, monks, listen again.

And those who, having gathered and purified the floral offerings (nirmālya) from all sides here, take refuge in them and serve them with minds full of devotion to the Perfectly Awakened One; // Dak_21.4 //
"Those who practice for awakening shall be free from afflictions and grief, beautiful to behold, with pure faculties, majestic, and lotus-faced. (Dak_21.5)
Having heard that, all the monks were filled with joy, exclaiming, "It is so, Tathāgata!
and they became even more intensely devoted to the stūpa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the narrative of Vapuṣmat, within the collection of twenty-two avadānas.
XXII. The Avadāna of Sandalwood.
Then, monks, the Blessed One was addressed as follows.
O Blessed One, having heard your excellent speech, I have attained great joy;
how then could another be so devoted to worship and devotion? (Dak_22.1)
Or is there such a person? Speak further to me, O Teacher.
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, monks! At one time, while wandering on a tour through the Magadha country together with a great community of monks, I arrived at the bank of the Ganges.
Now at that time, not far from the bank of the Ganges, the monks saw a ruined stūpa, a shrine worn away by wind and sun; having seen it, they asked the Blessed One:
'Blessed One, whose stūpa is this?'"
The Blessed One said:
There was a Pratyekabuddha named Candana; [the story] is as follows regarding him.
The monks asked:
"Lord, from where did the Pratyekabuddha Candana arise, and how was his name and manifestation brought about?"
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, do you wish to hear how the Pratyekabuddha Candana was born and how his name came to be?"
"So be it, Venerable Sir."
Therefore, monks, listen well and pay close attention; I shall speak.

Long ago, monks, in the past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. His kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. He was a righteous king of dharma who ruled his realm according to the Dharma.
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Rudra, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities.

Specifically, he supplicated the deities of groves, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, the deities who receive offerings, and even those deities who are innate, those who share his religious practice, and those who are constantly attached to him.
Furthermore, there is this worldly proverb: [that one may obtain a son through such prayers].
As for the claim that sons and daughters are born as a result of prayers,
that is not so;
if it were otherwise, each person would have a thousand sons.
It is just as with a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);
nevertheless, sons and daughters are born through the presence of three conditions,
even though he remains intent on such prayers.
In his park there was a great lotus pond,
where a lotus of immense size had grown;
it increased day by day, yet it did not bloom.
Then the park-keeper informed the king,
and the king said, "Let this lotus be protected."
Then, at another time, at sunrise, that lotus blossomed, and upon the pericarp of that lotus sat a boy in the cross-legged posture.

He was handsome, beautiful to behold, gracious, fair-skinned, with a golden complexion, a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, a prominent nose, joined eyebrows, and a high-bridged nose; he was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Adorned with the eighty minor marks, his body was radiant;
from his mouth issued the fragrance of a lotus,
and from his body the scent of sandalwood.
Then the park-keeper informed the king;
having heard this, the king went to that garden accompanied by his ministers and the women of his harem. Upon seeing him, the boy addressed the king.
"Come, father! I am the son for you who have no son."
Then the king, thrilled, satisfied, and overjoyed, said: "It is exactly so, my son, just as you say."
Then the king, having entered the lotus pond, took the boy from the pericarp of a lotus and placed him upon the palm of his hand.
And wherever that boy places his feet, there lotuses appear.
Then, the name Candana was given to him.
When the boy Candana had gradually grown up and reached the prime of youth, the citizens petitioned the king:

"Your Majesty, our city festival is now at hand; it would be fitting for Your Majesty to release Prince Candana so that he may enjoy the festival with us and adorn the entire city with lotuses. The king said:
"So be it."

Then Candana, adorned with all his ornaments and surrounded by the sons of ministers, went out from the royal palace accompanied by various musical instruments being played, in order to enjoy the city festival.
As he walked there, with every step he took, beautiful and delightful lotuses appeared; they emerged from a single ray of light.
As soon as they are touched by those sunbeams, they wither and dry up.
Then, for that being of pure essence and virtuous intention, who had planted roots of merit under previous Buddhas, there arose through that vision a correct mental attention (*yonisomanasikāra*):
"Just as these lotuses, having merely sprung up, are beautiful, yet wither and dry up when scorched by the rays of the sun,
so too is this body."
As he was thus reflecting, weighing, and examining, the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening became manifest before him.
Standing right there in the midst of that very assembly of people, he realized pratyekabodhi.

When the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm offered him saffron robes, he put them on and flew up into the expanse of the sky; he then began to perform various miraculous feats— emitting fire, raining down water, radiating heat, and flashing lightning—
at the sight of which the king, along with his ministers, merchants, and companions, attained great faith.
And various roots of merit were planted.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, this is the arising and the manifestation by name of the Pratyekabuddha Candana.
The monks questioned the Venerable One.
"Venerable sir, what actions were performed by the Pratyekabuddha Candana, such that his body is fragrant and his faculties are sharp?"
The Blessed One said:

Monks, in the past there appeared a perfectly awakened Buddha named Kāśyapa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having completed all the work of a Buddha, that Buddha established himself in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In that regard, in former times, this Candana had a stūpa for hair and nails constructed;
having conceived faith in the Blessed One Kāśyapa, he went forth as a monk.
There, he performed the sprinkling of perfumes upon the stūpa and offered flowers, and he cultivated the path toward *pratyekabodhi*.
Then that Pratyekabuddha, having performed the work of a Buddha, passed into Nirvana because of his pure intention.
Then his disciples had a stūpa built in his very name;
it was thus designated as "the stūpa of him alone."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Teacher;
having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped the Teacher, we shall dwell in dependence upon him.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Blessed One said this; with uplifted minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the Story of Candanā, within the collection of twenty-two avadānas.

It is difficult to find the opportunity to hear the encouragement toward merit, as well as the merit of renunciation; likewise, the bathing of the image, the offering of incense, the parasol, and the dedication of relics. // 1 //
The mandala, food, drink, clothing, and the description of flowers and so forth; prostration, the radiant lamp, the monastery, and the crest-ornament. // 2 //
The discarded flower offerings, the water, and the sandalwood—these twenty-two discourses have been extensively proclaimed in various ways for the further praise of giving. (3)
XXIII. Discourse on Generosity (1). On that occasion, monks, the Blessed One said this to them. Regarding clothing: then, monks, the Blessed One spoke as follows.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear what was done in the past;
O Hero, may all of that be told for the increase of the merit of the worlds. (Dak_23.1)
When this had been said, the Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Compassionate One, spoke:
"O monks, listen to the merit for the increase of the merit of the worlds."
Generosity is indeed a great treasure that follows one and cannot be shared by thieves or others; it is the washing away of the dust of the faults of stinginess and greed from the mind,
and generosity is a comfortable vehicle that removes the exhaustion of the path of saṃsāra.
Generosity is a true friend that provides manifold comforts and is constant until the end.

Whether it be the accumulation of wealth, splendor, the quality of authoritative knowledge, residence in the city of the thirty-three gods, or the excellence of physical beauty—whatever one desires, all that is obtained through giving. Thus having calculated this meaning, who would not give gifts?
Faith is indeed the mother of virtue; therefore, let it be established from the very beginning in the minds of virtuous people.
For one devoid of the mine of faith is indeed not capable of grasping the mass of jewels that are the true Dharma of the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Just as one who has fallen from his supernatural powers reaches a state of lack of sovereignty,
so too one who has fallen from the faculties of faith will not attain the state of awakening.
Therefore, a wise person should constantly direct a serene mind toward the Sugatas and those who act for their benefit;
for there is nothing else that pacifies all faults as faith does, which burns away the entire multitude of defects.
Giving is said to be of four kinds, even for the poor and the young;
yet giving to a worthy recipient and in a fertile field is the most excellent form of giving.
Miserable, poorly clothed, and bewildered, with begging bowls marked upon their hands, they indeed demonstrate to the world such a fruit for one who does not give. (Dak 23.9)
With bodies like scorched pillars, these beggars wander from house to house like hungry ghosts, perpetually tormented by hunger and raising their arms while crying "Give!
Even when they turn back, they are met by packs of dogs that have been driven far away.
Generally, these people have given food to no one at all, whether it be little or even just once.
Thinking thus, O man, you should therefore strive diligently in giving;
for in this abode of existence, there is no other friend superior to that gift. (Dak_23.11)
"Long ago, monks, at one time, I was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great Saṅgha.

When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had offered the Jeta Grove to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and had gradually given one hundred koṭis for the Blessed One’s teaching, the thought occurred to him:"
"What is there to marvel at in this—

that I give gifts or perform meritorious deeds? Rather, for the sake of showing favor to the poor, let me solicit alms from the body of people residing in Śrāvastī so that I may attend upon the Blessed One together with his community of disciples."
"In this way, great benefit will be conferred upon the multitude of people, and much merit will be generated by him."
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada reported this matter to the king.
The king caused a proclamation by bell to be made throughout all of Śrāvastī:

"Listen, venerable citizens residing in Śrāvastī! On the seventh day from today, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, mounted upon the back of an elephant, [will proceed] for the sake of the Tathāgata and his community of disciples."
Desiring to solicit alms for the sake of the horse-keeper, he said:
"Whatever amount each of you is able to relinquish, that should be given."

On the seventh day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, mounted upon the neck of an elephant, began to solicit offerings for the sake of the Tathāgata and his community of disciples. Thereupon, those who possessed whatever measure of wealth they had began to give that much: some gave bracelets, some armlets, some golden necklaces, some finger-rings, and some pearl necklaces.
Some [give] gold, some fine gold, and some even as little as a kārṣāpaṇa;
the householder accepts them for the sake of favoring others.

Now, there was a certain woman who was extremely poor; after three months of great hardship, she had earned a single piece of cloth. Wearing that cloth, she stepped out onto the street and saw Anāthapiṇḍada approaching from afar, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and drums.
She questioned a certain lay follower:
"If this householder is so wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments that he can even see his hidden treasures buried beneath the earth,
why does he wander for alms among other families?"
She was addressed by the lay follower:
"For the sake of benefiting others, she provides assistance for those who are unable to feed the Blessed One together with the community of disciples;
how might many people, having gathered together, be able to provide for the Blessed One?"
Then, a thought occurred to that girl:
"I am one who has not performed meritorious deeds; I do not have the power to provide a meal by myself for the Blessed One together with the community of disciples.
What if I were to give something from here?"
Looking at her own possessions, she saw nothing except a cloth;
she began to reflect:
"If I give this cloth while remaining right here, I shall be naked. What [if...]
"Now, having climbed onto the roof of the shelter, I shall cast down a cloth."
Then, having climbed onto the roof of the shelter, she removed a cloth from her own body and threw it over Anāthapiṇḍada.
Seeing the cloth, the householder perceived her:
"Surely this is all the wealth she possesses, which she has thrown over me while staying in the shelter."
He issued a command to his own men:
"Go, sirs, and investigate by whom this cloth was thrown down."
They looked at her and saw that she was sitting in a crouching posture. Then they questioned her, and she said:
"Whatever wealth I possessed, having heard the praises of the Blessed One's virtues, I gave it to the community of monks headed by the Tathāgata, being terrified by the fear of poverty."
Then they informed Anāthapiṇḍada;
thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, overcome with great wonder, clothed that girl in various garments and ornaments.
Then she, having a short lifespan, passed away and was reborn among the sublime gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
As soon as she was reborn, such garments appeared for her as had never belonged to any other son of the gods or daughter of the gods.
Indeed, it is the natural law that three thoughts arise in a son of the gods or daughter of the gods shortly after they have been reborn.
"From where have they passed away? Where have they been reborn? By what karma?
She saw that they had passed away from among humans and were reborn among the sublime gods of the Trayastriṃśa heaven because of their gift of a cloth to the Blessed One.

Then, a celestial maiden who had offered garments—wearing swaying, stainless earrings, her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, her crest variegated with jewels and gems, and her limbs anointed with saffron, tamāla leaves, spṛkkā, and other perfumes—filled her lap that very night with divine flowers: blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-lotuses, white lotuses, and mandāraka flowers; and having illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with a magnificent radiance, she [approached] the Blessed One.
Having scattered flowers before the Blessed One, they sat down to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the disposition, latent tendencies, elements, and nature of the celestial maiden who had offered the cloth,

delivered a Dharma teaching conducive to the realization of the Four Noble Truths; upon hearing which, the celestial maiden who had offered the cloth shattered with the thunderbolt of knowledge the mountain of the view of a self-identity, which rose up with its twenty peaks, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the truths, she uttered this inspired exclamation three times: "Venerable Sir,

what has been done for us by the Blessed One could not have been done by our mother, nor by our father, nor by the king, nor by the deities, nor by our beloved circle of kinsmen and relatives, nor by our departed ancestors, nor by ascetics and brahmins."

The oceans of blood and tears have been dried up; the mountains of bones have been crossed; the gates to the lower realms have been closed; the gates to heaven and liberation have been opened; and we have been established among gods and humans. And he said:
(Dak: 226) Through your power, the most terrible path to the lower realms, fraught with many defects, has been closed;
the highly meritorious path to heaven has been opened, and the path to Nirvāṇa has been found by me. (Dak_23.12)
Through taking refuge in you, I have today attained the pure and flawless [vision] with the most purified eye;
I have reached the peaceful state beloved by the Noble Ones, and I have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of suffering.
O Lord of Men, honored by humans and gods, free from birth, old age, death, and disease;
O Sage, whose appearance is so difficult to obtain even in a thousand lifetimes, today your sight has become fruitful for me.
Thus [it is said].
Then, bowing down and having saluted his two feet with her long pendants of pearls, she was filled with joy;
and having circumambulated the Conqueror of Enemies from the right, she departed for heaven, facing the world of the gods.

Then the divine maiden who had presented the cloth, like a merchant who has gained profit, like a farmer with a bountiful harvest, like a hero who has won a battle, or like a sick man freed from all disease, returned to her own abode with the very same splendor with which she had come into the presence of the Blessed One.
(Dak: 227) Then, monks, as they dwelt devoted to the practice of vigilance during the first and last watches of the night,
they saw a sublime radiance in the presence of the Blessed One.
Seeing this, they became doubtful and asked the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, did Brahmā Sahāpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four world-protectors approach the Blessed One for a vision of him during this night?"
The Blessed One said, "Monks, it was neither Brahmā Sahāmpati, nor Śakra the lord of gods, nor even the four world-protectors who approached me for the sake of seeing me.

Rather, it was the daughter of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, who, while he was soliciting alms for his son Chandaka, gave him a robe and passed away; she has been reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, who possess all manner of pleasant enjoyments and garments."
"She has attained [the fruit]," he said. "She approached me this very night; I taught her the Dharma, and having seen the Truths, she has since departed for her own abode."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We shall perform services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and not acts of harm. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Having heard that, all the monks were awakened and greatly rejoiced.
(Dak: 228) (2) Śibi:
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and said:
Listen further, Maitreya; I shall speak again of the fruits and benefits of giving.
"Excellent, Blessed One," he said; and the Blessed One spoke this to him.
For human beings, merit is a lamp in the darkness, a protection in times of fear, a kinsman in calamities, the unsurpassed medicine for diseases, and a boat in the great ocean of saṃsāra. (Dak 23.16)
Generosity destroys poverty; ethical discipline wards off miserable rebirths;
wisdom destroys ignorance; and meditative cultivation destroys cyclic existence.
When a person gives their own wealth with a pure mind, at that very moment, that mass of merit is designated as "giving. (Dak 23.18)
Generosity is all-encompassing happiness, the remover of great fear, fortune, and the bestower of great wealth; it is the ground of manifold, vast, and skillful means, adorned with all virtues.
Therefore, generosity is the pacifier of many faults and the dispeller of the terrors of saṃsāra.
Men should diligently perform that which brings about auspiciousness and thoroughly dries up hunger, thirst, and other [afflictions].

When the Tathāgata Maitreya was formerly a bodhisattva, he fulfilled the perfection of generosity by relinquishing his hands, feet, eyes, head, flesh, blood, beloved sons, wife, daughters, kingdom, limbs, pleasures, enjoyments, and even his own body; for the sake of others' welfare, through that very [practice], he attained the state of sovereignty as a Tathāgata.
As it is heard in tradition:
(Dak:

229) Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a king named Śibi reigned over the royal capital of Śibighoṣā. It was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, crowded with many people, and free from strife, quarrels, tumult, and civil unrest.
He rules his kingdom—which is free from thieves and disease, abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo, entirely without thorns, and as dear to him as an only son.

And that King Śibi was faithful, auspicious, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all, and one who gives without attachment, abiding in a great mind of relinquishment.
Rising early in the morning, he enters the sacrificial enclosure and bestows food upon those who seek food,
clothing upon those who seek clothing, and makes gifts of wealth, grain, silver, gold, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and so forth.
And he does not reach satiety through conditioned phenomena consisting of merit.
He provides food and clothing for the people of the inner apartments, for the princes, the ministers, the army officers, and the merchants and country folk.
Then this thought occurred to King Śibi:
"These human beings have been fully satisfied by him;
what remains is the small creatures—by what means are they to be satisfied? Thus he reflected.
Having renounced his entire wealth and possessions, clothed in a single garment, and with nothing remaining but his own body, he fell into reflection.
This thought occurred to him:
"I shall give my own body to the lowly creatures."
Having carved his own body with a weapon, he goes to where the gadflies and mosquitoes are and, having offered his body there, satisfies them with his blood as if they were his only beloved son.
Then, Śakra, the lord of the gods, directed his vision of knowledge downward.
This thought occurred to him:
"Does this King Śibi perform such deeds for the sake of sentient beings out of mere self-interest, or out of compassion? Let me now test him."
Then, having transformed himself into the guise of a vulture with the color of crushed collyrium, he approached King Śibi and began to pluck out his eye with his beak.
Even so, the king did not fall into terror;
rather, looking at the vulture with eyes wide with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he said:
"My child, since you are being dispatched from my own body, let this be done out of affection."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, being thus won over, manifested himself in the guise of a brahmin and, standing before King Śibi, spoke.
"Excellent, O King! Let both these policies be granted to me."
The king said:
"Great Brahmin, take whatever you desire;
let it be taken, for there is no obstacle for me in this matter."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, becoming even more deeply pleased, vanished his brahmin disguise, stood in his own form, and, encouraging the king, said:
"Excellent, excellent, O King! Your intellect is well-determined, your resolve is unshakable, and your great compassion is directed toward sentient beings.
Since you are indeed fearless regarding those things that cause terror, before long you shall, by means of this exertion, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Having spoken thus, Śakra, the lord of the gods, vanished right there.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Śibi, I was he.
Even then, I had no satiety with meritorious formations; how much less so now!
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall give gifts; we shall perform meritorious deeds.'"
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
"By the power of the merit of giving and the strength of generosity performed in previous lives, may I become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha."
(232) (3) Furthermore, the Blessed One, being of beautiful form, addressed the community of monks once more and taught the Dharma, most sweetly, in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
Just as honey from a beehive is free of bees, so too did an assembly of many hundreds hear the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unflinching ears.
Then the monks, overcome by doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how these beings have become vessels for the jewel of the Dharma, thinking that it must be heard with such great reverence."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, listen to how the Dharma was heard and mastered by the Tathāgata with a sense of reverence; listen well and pay close attention, and I shall speak."
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, a king named Surūpa reigned in the city of Vārāṇasī.

He ruled a kingdom that was prosperous, flourishing, well-supplied with food, and teeming with many people; it was free from strife, quarrels, riots, and civil unrest, devoid of thieves and disease, and abundant in rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo—entire, secure, and cherished like an only son.

That king was faithful, noble, and of virtuous intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of the Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of everything, and one who gave without attachment.
And he was established in great generosity.
That king had a queen named Sundarikā, who was beautiful, lovely to behold, gracious, and endowed with all major and minor limbs.
And he had an only son named Sundaraka, who was beloved, handsome, dear, pleasing, and endowed with patience.
Then, at another time, a longing for the Dharma arose in King Surūpa.
He assembled all his ministers and said to them, "O village chiefs, search for the Dharma for me; the Dharma has pleased me."
Then those ministers, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the king:
"O Great King, the Dharma is difficult to encounter. O Great King, it is said that through the arising of a Buddha in the world, the arising of the Dharma occurs."
Then the king, having fastened a golden casket to the top of his banner, had a proclamation made by the sounding of bells throughout the entire realm:
"To whoever shall preach the Dharma to me,
I will give this golden casket and honor him with great ceremony."
Then, after a long time had passed, no teacher of the Dharma was to be found.
Then that king, for the sake of dharma, yearns and trembles with fear.
Then, Śakra, the lord of the gods, directed his vision and knowledge downward;
he saw the king being struck for the sake of the Dharma,
and this thought occurred to him:
"What if I were now to examine King Surūpa? he thought.
Then, having manifested himself in the form of a yakṣa with deformed hands, feet, and eyes, he spoke thus to the king who was seated in the midst of his many assemblies.
"Are you not indeed a seeker of the Dharma? I shall speak the Dharma to you."
Then that king, having experienced joy and gladness from hearing the Dharma, spoke this to Akṣa:
"Speak, O Guhyaka; I shall listen to the teachings."
The Guhyaka said:
"O Great King, indeed, the dharmas long for one who is happy;
I am hungry, so please give me food."
Then, having heard this, the king summoned his men.
"Various kinds of food and delicacies were being brought for him."
The Yakṣa said:
O King, I do not attain satisfaction with human food;
rather, listen to my intention.
"Excessively warm meats and fresh blood—such are the food and drink of the yakṣas, O Padmākṣa of unbroken vows. (Dak_23.20)
"Freshly slaughtered meat and blood is my food; give me this handsome only son."
Upon hearing this, the king fell into profound despair:
"At last, today, I have obtained the sound of the Dharma, yet even that was acquired at an immeasurable price."
Then, having heard that, Prince Sundara fell at his father's feet and made this petition to the king.
"Forgive me, O Lord; let the intention of the Lord be fulfilled. Grant me to this Guhyaka for the purpose of providing his food."
Then the king gave that only son— beloved, charming, dear, pleasing, and patient—
to the yakṣa for the sake of the Dharma.

Then, seeing his own limbs and minor members being repeatedly torn apart one by one and devoured, and his blood being drunk, exactly as it had been shown to the king and his assembly through the empowerment of the yakṣa’s supernatural power,
the king, who longed for the Dharma, did not fall into despair.
That Guhyaka said to the king:
"I am not yet satiated, O King; give me more," he said.
Then the king gave him his beloved wife;
she too was presented by him in that very same manner.
Thereupon, he spoke again to the king.
"O King, even now he has not yet attained satisfaction."
Then the king said to the yakṣa:
"My child, I have given you my only son and my wife; what more do you request?"
The Guhyaka said:
"Give me your own body; by this, I shall attain satisfaction."
The king said:
"If you give me your own body, how shall I hear the Dharma?
First, tell me the Dharma; once I have grasped the Dharma, I shall relinquish my body."
Then the Guhyaka, having established the king in his promise, taught the Dharma before an assembly of many hundreds.
From what is dear arises sorrow; from what is dear arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from what is dear, there is no sorrow—how, then, could there be fear? (Dak 23.21)
Thus.
(Dak: 236) Then, upon hearing this verse, the king’s mind was gladdened; with a sense of joy and mental well-being arising within his faculties, he spoke to the yakṣa:
"O Guhyaka, let this body of mine be done with as you wish."
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, perceiving that the king was as unshakable as Mount Meru regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
caused his yakṣa form to vanish and stood before him in his own form. With eyes blossoming with faith, he took his son with one hand and his wife with the other, and, encouraging the king, spoke:

"Excellent, excellent, O noble being! You are one of firm armor; before long, by means of this resolve, you shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and this shall be your reunion with your beloved ones."
Then the king said this to Śakra, the lord of the gods:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! You have fulfilled our aspiration for the Dharma."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, monks? He who at that time, on that occasion, was the king named Surūpa, was I myself.
The youth Sundara was Ānanda.
And Sundarikā was none other than Yaśodharā."
"Even then, monks, for the sake of the Dharma, I made the sacrifice of beloved kinsmen and the sacrifice of my own life; how much more so now!
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Dharma.'"
"Monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'Having honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped the Dharma, we shall dwell in reliance upon it.'"
Thus ends the story of the discourse on giving from the *Dvāviṃśatyavadāna*.
(Dak: 238) [XXIV.
*Puṇyotsāhāvadānasūtra*:
Then the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Omniscient One, having gazed upon all those people gathered in the assembly, again taught the True Dharma.
"Listen, sons of good family, to this true Dharma which I have proclaimed—the means for accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, the cause of welfare for all beings. (Dak_24.1)
First, for the sake of accomplishing the wisdom of perfect enlightenment, a bodhisattva,
having made the vow for perfect enlightenment, should practice the desired giving.
Then, having diligently desisted from even those ten evils,
one should maintain pure ethical discipline and practice excellent self-restraint.
Then, having completely conquered the afflictions and abiding in the four divine abodes,
one should always maintain the vow of patience and strive for the welfare of the world.
Therefore, maintaining great enthusiasm for the Dharma in order to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings,
one should abandon attachment to evil friends and cultivate that which possesses great virtue.
Therefore, having abandoned cherished desires and being dispassionate toward sensual enjoyments,
one should fix the mind with great steadiness and meditate upon that which is for the welfare of the three worlds.

Therefore, having abandoned attachment to enemies, one who is devoted to perfect enlightenment should strive for the supreme jewel of awakening within the ocean of wisdom for the welfare of the world.
Having fulfilled these six perfections in their proper order and having conquered all the hosts of Māra, he shall attain the wisdom of perfect enlightenment.
Thus, possessing great supernormal knowledge through the excellence of his glory, wealth, heroism, and virtuous qualities,
he shall accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings and attain the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Thus, having fully understood this, if you desire the state of perfect buddhahood,
you should fulfill all the perfections in their proper sequence.
Having maintained the vow for perfect enlightenment, practicing the four divine abodes,
and having rendered service to the Three Jewels, proceed for the welfare of the world.
By the power of this merit, may you all become masters who have conquered the senses;
having attained the state of an Arhat, you shall reach the stage of perfect enlightenment.
Having heard what was thus commanded by the Lord of Sages, all the monks replied, "So be it," and being enlightened, they rejoiced. (Dak_24.13)
The entire assembly, having heard this and being thoroughly pacified,
responded, "So be it," and, being enlightened, offered their joyful approval.
Thus ends the Sūtra on the Discourse of Encouragement toward Merit within the glorious Collection of Twenty-two Avadānas.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. May there be auspiciousness!
